Speed_note: Authentise claims digital design warehousing gives 'reduced lead times and downtime', but no page shows lead times being estimated or valued (Authentise digital design warehousing blog; FlowsAM page).

name: Materialise CO-AM software platform
year: Unknown start year for CO-AM (current in 2026; DigiFabster quoting integration Nov 2023)
developer: Materialise NV (Belgium)
earlier_versions: Materialise Streamics (date not found): Materialise AM production-management system used at Avio Aero; the entry treats it as the predecessor of CO-AM's AM MES, which the sources read do not confirm.
description: Production software stack: Magics build preparation (nesting, metal supports, pre-print checks), AM MES for work orders, capacity and throughput, quality data with NCR/CAPA, and multi-site visibility and secure data delivery. Cost estimation is not described natively.
NRE_note: Magics and the Build Processor automate build preparation (metal supports, nesting, pre-print checks of error-prone areas), but the effort is not costed (Materialise CO-AM page).
Production_note: Quoting is offered only through the DigiFabster portal feeding CO-AM order management, and its pricing inputs are not documented; the CO-AM, MES and planning pages describe no cost calculation (PR Newswire 2023; Materialise MES and CO-AM pages).
QA_Qual_note: Nonconformance and CAPA tracking, traceability and regulatory and ITAR compliance features are offered, but no qualification workflow is described and qualification is not modelled or costed (Materialise CO-AM page).
QA_Insp_note: Quality checklists on manufacturing travelers and sensor and image data for quality assurance are provided, but there is no inspection cost or scope by part class (Materialise MES and CO-AM pages).
Storage_note: The CO-AM, MES and planning pages do not mention parts inventory or digital inventory beyond storing lifecycle data for reorders, and no product documentation was found (Materialise product pages).
Shared_Capital_note: Nesting and lot management to maximise machine use and an ROI analytics view are described, but machine cost or utilisation is not calculated in any source read (Materialise planning and MES pages).
Shared_Capacity_note: Work orders are scheduled by due date on Gantt charts across the production floor and data are viewed across connected facilities, but the pages do not show capacity contention setting lead time or cross-site pooling (Materialise planning and CO-AM pages).
Speed_note: Magics, part of CO-AM, estimates build time per machine with a self-learning method, but lead time or availability is not shown to be computed; lead-time reduction is only claimed (Materialise Magics build-time tutorial; CO-AM page).

name: Oqton MOS (Manufacturing OS) with 3DXpert add-on
year: Start year not confirmed; MOS current in 2026
developer: Oqton (Ghent, Belgium); acquisition by 3D Systems announced Sep 2021 ($180M); on 1 Oct 2025 3D Systems agreed to sell Oqton MOS and 3DXpert to Hubb Global Holdings (closing expected Q4 2025)
description: Cloud manufacturing operating system linking ERP/MES/PLM with AI-automated nesting, print prep, build monitoring, KPI reporting and traceability for regulated production.
NRE_note: Build files are prepared with 3DXpert (orient, nest, support, slice, DfAM, simulation) and MOS claims to free engineers from manual tasks, but engineering or preparation effort is not costed (oqton.com MOS and 3DXpert pages).
Production_note: MOS itself only exchanges quotes, while the 3DXpert add-on's print estimation computes material cost by volume plus machine-time cost (hourly rate x estimated time) per build, with no labour or post-processing terms (3DXpert print-estimation tutorial; oqton.com 3DXpert page).
QA_Qual_note: MOS claims to help 'gain certifications and qualify quicker' and to capture all data needed for certification and traceability, but no qualification effort or cost is modelled (oqton.com MOS pages).
QA_Insp_note: MOS links each production step to quality inspection results and detects issues in real time from machine data, and 3DXpert offers AM inspection reports, but no per-part inspection cost or scope is calculated (oqton.com MOS and 3DXpert pages).
Storage_note: The Digital Warehouse replaces physical inventory with a digital one so parts are produced and paid for only when needed, but holding cost or stock is not modelled (oqton.com/manufacturing-os).
Shared_Capital_note: 3DXpert costs machine time at a flat hourly rate times estimated build time, and MOS claims better machine utilisation through smart job allocation, but no utilisation, volume or per-part allocation of nested builds is documented (3DXpert print-estimation tutorial; oqton.com MOS page).
Shared_Capacity_note: MOS is said to 'balance workloads across sites' and the Digital Warehouse can send files to a qualified facility anywhere, but no capacity or queue model is described (oqton.com MOS pages).
Speed_note: 3DXpert estimates printing time from user-set build rates and recoating time (print time only), and MOS scheduling balances machine availability and delivery deadlines and claims shorter lead times, but lead time is not computed or valued (3DXpert print-estimation tutorial; oqton.com MOS page).

name: Autodesk Fusion with Netfabb
year: Origin year not confirmed; Netfabb 2019 release Nov 2018; sold as Fusion with Netfabb (2025 features page)
developer: Autodesk
earlier_versions: Autodesk Netfabb 2019 (Nov 2018): standalone Netfabb release whose simulation supported parameter (PRM) file development; the product is now sold as Fusion with Netfabb.
description: Build preparation (repair, 2D/3D packing, supports), quoting/manufacturing reports and thermo-mechanical simulation of metal PBF/DED builds to predict distortion. Dedicated cost estimation is not listed on the current features page.
NRE_note: Build preparation, simulation-based PRM file generation and distortion compensation are offered to cut trial builds, but this effort is not costed (Autodesk features page; Netfabb 2024 help, About Netfabb).
Production_note: The report generator outputs part volume, support volume and, for some machine engines, a build-time estimate 'for estimates, quotations', but the documented report fields include no cost or price (Netfabb 2024 help, report generator and report field reference).
QA_Qual_note: The documented editions and capabilities cover build preparation, slicing and thermo-mechanical simulation only, so qualification is outside the documented scope (Netfabb 2024 help, About Netfabb; Autodesk features page).
QA_Insp_note: The documentation names no inspection or testing function; simulation predicts hot spots and lack of fusion before the build but does not set or cost inspection (Netfabb 2024 help, About Netfabb; Autodesk features page).
Storage_note: Netfabb is build-preparation and simulation software, so inventory is outside its documented scope (Netfabb 2024 help, About Netfabb).
Shared_Capital_note: 2D and 3D automatic packing places many parts in one build volume and reports part count, but machine cost and its spread across parts are not calculated (Autodesk features page; Netfabb 2024 report field reference).
Shared_Capacity_note: Netfabb packs and prepares builds for one machine workspace and does not address capacity shared across sites or users (Netfabb 2024 help, About Netfabb).
Speed_note: A build-time estimate (NETFABB_ENGINE_BUILDTIME) is available for selected machine engines, but lead time or availability is not computed (Netfabb 2024 help, report field reference).

name: Etteplan AMOTool
developer: Etteplan (Finland), AMO team; Business Finland support
description: Quick metal AM cost estimator from part height and volume covering material, printing and post-processing; compares with conventional manufacturing, gives ROI, recommends orientation to maximize parts per plate and indicates if redesign would pay off.
NRE_note: Indicates whether redesign would be profitable and how much material must be removed for viability, but does not estimate redesign cost (3Dnatives 2020; Metal AM 2020).
Production_note: Launch coverage says it estimates material, printing and post-processing cost from part height and volume and compares with conventional manufacturing, but the calculation and any other inputs are undocumented and the tool is withdrawn (3Dnatives 2020; Etteplan release).
QA_Qual_note: Four launch articles list only material, printing and post-processing costs and say nothing on qualification, and the tool page is withdrawn, so this cannot be settled.
QA_Insp_note: None of the four launch articles says whether inspection is part of the post-processing cost, and the tool page is withdrawn.
Storage_note: AMOTool estimates single-part cost from part height and volume, a scope that excludes inventory (3Dnatives 2020).
Shared_Capital_note: Recommends the orientation that maximises parts per build plate, but how machine cost is amortised or spread across parts is not described (3Dnatives 2020).
Shared_Capacity_note: AMOTool estimates single-part cost and does not address capacity shared across sites or users (3Dnatives 2020).
Speed_note: None of the four launch articles mentions print time or lead time, and the tool page is withdrawn, so this cannot be settled.

name: ExOne Production Metal Cost Calculator
developer: The ExOne Company (later ownership changes not verified in this session)
description: Online per-part cost estimator for binder-jetted metal parts on ExOne's four Pro-series printers, from material, machine, part dimensions and volume, including capital investment, throughput, material, binder and printhead replacement.
NRE_note: The launch release and the gated calculator page list material, machine, part dimensions, nesting and volume inputs and capital, throughput, material, binder and printhead costs 'and more', but do not say whether setup or engineering effort is included; the calculator itself is behind a form.
Production_note: Computes a per-part binder-jet cost from material, machine, part dimensions and volume, covering capital, throughput, material, binder and printhead replacement (BusinessWire Jan 2021 release; 3DPI).
QA_Qual_note: The documented scope is a per-part printing cost based on buying one Pro-series printer, which plainly excludes part qualification; the page only notes that some materials are still under qualification by ExOne (calculator access page; BusinessWire release).
QA_Insp_note: Neither the launch release nor the calculator access page mentions inspection or post-processing, and the listed cost elements end with 'and more', so inspection could be included.
Storage_note: The calculator gives a per-part binder-jet cost, which excludes inventory (BusinessWire release).
Shared_Capital_note: Initial capital investment and throughput are cost elements spread over the entered production volume, with a nesting input for parts per build (BusinessWire release; calculator access page).
Shared_Capacity_note: The estimate assumes purchase of one ExOne Pro-series printer and does not address capacity shared across sites or users (BusinessWire release).
Speed_note: Throughput speed is a cost factor and machine build rates are quoted, but no source shows whether print time or lead time is output; the calculator is form-gated.

name: DigiFabster (AM quoting and e-commerce)
year: Unknown (active by Nov 2021; integrated with Materialise CO-AM Nov 2023)
developer: DigiFabster (US-based)
description: ML-assisted instant quoting and e-commerce for AM service providers, using one-off per-build costs (e.g., recoat time driven by part height in powder bed) and per-part material and machine time; order data flows into Materialise CO-AM.
NRE_note: Cost-based pricing includes one-off setup and programming costs and time-based pricing includes programming time, but design, digitisation and parameter development are not covered (Instant Quoting page).
Production_note: Quotes are computed from geometry analysis with machine, operator and programming time, or operation, material, setup and programming costs, split into one-off and per-part costs (Instant Quoting page; 3DPI 2021 guest post).
QA_Qual_note: The quoting, features and service-bureau pages and the 2021 guest post do not mention qualification or certification, and no user documentation is public.
QA_Insp_note: Help articles show user-defined post-production options priced per part, per setup or per area, but no source shows inspection set up as one, so it can be neither confirmed nor ruled out (DigiFabster help: post productions).
Storage_note: DigiFabster is a quoting and order-management tool for manufacturers, so inventory holding is outside its documented scope (features list).
Shared_Capital_note: Time-based pricing applies a machine time rate and the 2021 guest post suggests charging model height as a one-off because parts share recoat time, but machine capital and its spread over utilisation are not shown (Instant Quoting page; 3DPI 2021).
Shared_Capacity_note: DigiFabster quotes and manages orders for one shop; capacity shared across sites or users is outside its documented scope (features list; service-bureau page).
Speed_note: The quoting, features and service-bureau pages and the 2021 guest post discuss quote turnaround, not production lead time, and do not say whether lead times or delivery dates are quoted.

name: Rickenbacher integrated SLM cost model
developer: L. Rickenbacher, A. Spierings, K. Wegener (ETH Zurich / inspire AG)
description: Adapts Alexander et al.'s generic cost model to SLM, covering pre- and post-processing steps plus a regression-based build-time estimate for mixed build jobs. It allocates build cost to parts by volume and build height so that parts of different size and complexity sharing one build each get a fair cost. Building parts simultaneously gave a 41% average cost reduction in the case study.
NRE_note: Geometry-data preparation and build-job assembly are costed per job and divided over the parts in it, which is recurring build prep with no redesign, reverse engineering or parameter development (Dogea et al. 2023 description).
Production_note: Per-part cost from preparation, job assembly, set-up, build (machine rate x build time plus material), removal, substrate separation and post-processing (Emerald abstract; Dogea et al. 2023).
QA_Qual_note: Two reviews reproduce the full cost equation as seven process-step terms (geometry-data preparation, job assembly, set-up, build, removal, substrate separation, post-processing), so qualification lies outside the model's documented scope (Costabile et al. 2017; Dogea et al. 2023).
QA_Insp_note: The reproduced equation has no inspection term, but inspection could sit inside the post-processing term and the paywalled paper could not be read to settle it (Costabile et al. 2017; Dogea et al. 2023; Emerald abstract).
Storage_note: Outside the documented scope: the model allocates SLM process-step costs to parts in shared build jobs, which does not involve inventory (Emerald abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: Build cost (machine hourly rate x build time) is allocated among parts from different projects sharing a build job by volume and build height, so filling the build space lowers unit cost (41% average reduction); the machine rate itself is given, not derived from capital (abstract; Costabile et al. 2017; Dogea et al. 2023).
Shared_Capacity_note: Pooling happens only within one machine's build jobs as a cost effect, with no lead-time or multi-site capacity effect (abstract; secondary descriptions).
Speed_note: Build time for a job is estimated by a linear regression on 24 builds (job volume, support area, layer-dependent fraction) and split among parts by an allocation algorithm, but only for cost; lead time is not reported (Costabile et al. 2017; Khanna et al. 2024).

name: Lindemann et al. (2013) DMRC lifecycle-cost model with TD-ABC
developer: C. Lindemann, U. Jahnke, M. Moi, R. Koch (Paderborn University, Direct Manufacturing Research Center)
earlier_versions: Lindemann, Jahnke, Moi, Koch (2012), 'Analyzing Product Lifecycle Costs for a Better Understanding of Cost Drivers in Additive Manufacturing', SFF Symposium 2012: earlier DMRC cost-driver analysis whose results the 2013 lifecycle-cost paper builds on.
description: Lifecycle cost model following the DIN/IEC 60300-3-3 phases: concept, design and development, production, installation, usage/maintenance, and disposal. Production is costed with time-driven activity-based costing across build-job preparation, build, part and support removal, and post-processing. Build rate, machine cost, material cost and utilization come out as the dominant drivers.
NRE_note: The design and development phase costs technical drawings, component design, QM planning, a prototype and test phase and production planning, and build-job preparation is a TD-ABC process (SFF 2013).
Production_note: TD-ABC of build-job preparation, build, part/support removal and post-processing with machine, material, personnel, energy, consumables and complexity factors per build job (SFF 2013).
QA_Qual_note: A prototype and test phase and QM planning are costed as design-and-development lifecycle elements, but material/process qualification or certification is not modelled beyond that lump (SFF 2013).
QA_Insp_note: Quality control is a TD-ABC production cost element bundled with post-processing (support removal, surface treatment), with no NDI/CT or coupon-testing line (SFF 2013; Khanna et al. 2024).
Storage_note: Usage-phase logistics include spare-part storage at about 22% of acquisition value, but AM's effect on stock levels is only discussed, not modelled (SFF 2013).
Shared_Capital_note: TD-ABC allocates machine cost by resource time with an explicit 75% utilisation assumption (about 673 parts/yr per machine), and utilisation is named a dominant cost driver, though it is not varied (SFF 2013).
Shared_Capacity_note: Capacity appears only as an illustrative parts-per-year figure and predicted build rates; no pooling or contention is modelled (SFF 2013).
Speed_note: TD-ABC times each process (including build time from build rate) only as cost drivers; lead time is not modelled, and the EUR 100,000/day aircraft-on-ground cost is cited only as motivation (SFF 2013).

name: Atzeni & Salmi DMLS vs. die-casting break-even model
developer: E. Atzeni, A. Salmi (Politecnico di Torino)
description: Builds cost models for DMLS and high-pressure die casting of the same DfAM-redesigned aerospace part to find the volume at which AM becomes competitive. It concludes AM can compete for small-to-medium batches.
NRE_note: Pre-processing is costed per build as setup time times operator rate, but the DfAM redesign of the part is not shown as a one-time engineering cost (Khanna et al. 2024 review; abstract).
Production_note: Per-part DMLS cost is built up from material (volume x unit price), pre-processing, processing (machine cost over parts per build) and post-processing (operator time, heat treatment), against a die-casting model (abstract; Khanna et al. 2024).
QA_Qual_note: The abstract and two reviews that describe the model (Khanna et al. 2024; Baumers et al. 2017) do not mention qualification or certification, and no open full text was found (IRIS record has no file).
QA_Insp_note: The reviews list material, pre-processing, processing and post-processing (operator, heat treatment) terms without inspection, but absence cannot be confirmed without the full text (Khanna et al. 2024; Baumers et al. 2017).
Storage_note: The documented scope is a per-part production cost comparison by batch size against die casting, which excludes inventory (abstract; Khanna et al. 2024).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine cost (5-year straight-line depreciation, about 90% of AM part cost) is divided by the number of parts in a multi-part build that assumes the build space is used efficiently (Khanna et al. 2024; Baumers et al. 2017, Table 5).
Shared_Capacity_note: The model costs a single part on one DMLS route at different batch sizes, so capacity pooling across sites or users is outside its scope (abstract; reviews).
Speed_note: Neither the abstract nor the two reviews mention lead time or build-time reporting, though a comparison with die casting could treat tooling lead time; the full text could not be reached.

name: Baumers et al. (2017) total-cost and capacity-utilisation model (IJPR)
developer: M. Baumers, P. Dickens, C. Tuck, R. Hague (University of Nottingham), with L. Beltrametti and A. Gasparre on the 2017 paper
earlier_versions: Baumers, Dickens, Tuck, Hague (2016), Technol. Forecast. Soc. Change 102:193-201: production-cost model for EBM and DMLS (about GBP 2.39 vs. 6.18 per cm3 deposited) showing machine productivity drives cost; the 2017 model adds total cost with build-failure risk, filling build volume with other geometries, and the value of design adaptation.
description: Activity-based production cost models that combine direct costs with time-allocated indirect (machine and overhead) costs, voxel-based build-time estimates, and computational packing of the build volume. The 2017 version adds per-layer build-failure risk and the discounted value of design adaptation. It shows single-geometry builds overstate unit cost by 157% on average compared with full mixed builds.
NRE_note: Only per-build machine setup and unloading labour (180 min, about EUR 72 per build) is costed; design, redesign and re-validation costs are explicitly excluded (arXiv full text).
Production_note: Unit cost is built from material, energy, build-time-allocated indirect cost, setup labour and 37 min/part post-processing labour, inflated for build-failure risk; the 17-4PH blower costs about EUR 56-58 per unit in mixed builds (arXiv full text).
QA_Qual_note: Re-validation and qualification costs are explicitly omitted, which the authors say may be significant (arXiv full text).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection is only folded into 37 min/part of manual post-processing labour together with support removal, surface finishing and washing, and the scope statement elsewhere lists inspection as excluded (arXiv full text).
Storage_note: In-process inventory, warehousing and logistics costs are explicitly excluded (arXiv full text).
Shared_Capital_note: Indirect machine cost (about EUR 23/h) is allocated by build time and volume share, and filling unused build volume with other geometries ('fungible' capacity) cuts unit cost, so capital is spread with an explicit utilisation and multi-part-build assumption (arXiv full text).
Shared_Capacity_note: Build-volume utilisation is modelled by packing other parts into the same build, but on one machine with no effect on lead time; scheduling and lead time are left to future work (arXiv full text).
Speed_note: Lead time is explicitly excluded from scope and named as future work (arXiv full text).

name: Laureijs/Fuchs (CMU) process-based cost model: metal AM vs. forging
developer: R. E. Laureijs, J. Bonnín Roca, S. P. Narra, C. Montgomery, J. L. Beuth, E. R. H. Fuchs (Carnegie Mellon University; E. R. H. Fuchs lab, Engineering & Public Policy)
description: Process-based cost model built on data from 14 anonymous firms (AM producers, powder and equipment suppliers, a university lab) and the Forging Industry Association. The AM route is modelled from the build step through stress relief (DMLS only), wire EDM, HIP, shot peening and destructive testing. At 1,000/yr the AM bracket costs about $3,200 vs. about $400 forged. With a 10-year fuel-saving NPV ($1,300 base, up to $3,000 per bracket), AM is competitive at 2,000-12,000/yr. Powder price and batch size (set by build orientation) are the top sensitivities. Cutting destructive testing from 1 part in 8 to 1 in 100 saves about $150/bracket at 10,000/yr, and about $410 when combined with vertical builds. FAA configuration control is modelled as 'one machine, one part' dedication of the AM machines.
NRE_note: Explicitly excluded: the model assumes the design is already optimised and converted to STL and starts at the build step, so redesign enters only as the lighter geometry (ASME full text as read in the earlier pass; the ASME page could not be reopened this session).
Production_note: Per-bracket cost for DMLS, EBM and forging is built up from process-step inputs, reject rates and best/base/worst ranges across 1,000-12,000 brackets/yr (ASME full text, Figs. 4-7; ScienceGate abstract).
QA_Qual_note: FAA configuration control is modelled only as a 'one machine, one part' dedication rule that raises AM machine cost per part at low volume; certification activities themselves are not costed and recertification is discussed only in words (ASME full text).
QA_Insp_note: Destructive testing is modelled as a yield loss (base 1 part in 8, swept to 1 in 100, worth about $150/bracket at 10,000/yr), but testing labour, equipment and AM NDI/CT are not costed (ASME full text, Fig. 8; ScienceGate abstract on reduced testing).
Storage_note: Inventory and spares are not analysed; lead-time reduction appears only in the introduction and a footnote on military field repair (ASME full text).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine cost per part depends on annual volume and batch size per build (set by vertical vs horizontal orientation, Fig. 9), with AM machines dedicated to the bracket while forging equipment is shared (ASME full text).
Shared_Capacity_note: Production is modelled at a single facility with no pooling of capacity across sites or users (ASME full text).
Speed_note: Time value is not modelled; the lifecycle benefit is fuel saving from weight reduction, not availability or lead time (ASME full text; ScienceGate abstract).

name: Bonnín Roca (CMU) process-based cost model + facility-location model for decentralized metal AM
developer: J. Bonnín Roca, P. Vaishnav, R. E. Laureijs, J. Mendonça, E. R. H. Fuchs (Carnegie Mellon University EPP; Universidade de Lisboa / IN+ via CMU Portugal; Bonnín Roca now at TU Eindhoven). M. G. Morgan is not a co-author of this paper; he co-authored the team's regulation papers.
description: A location-dependent process-based cost model (local labour and land costs) feeds an uncapacitated facility-location MILP. The MILP picks the cost-minimising number and location of AM sites, trading production scale economies against transport and inventory costs. The optimal number of sites barely changes across technology-improvement scenarios, and as demand grows the factory moves toward the highest-demand airports. Decentralisation pays only for non-critical parts that can share the same equipment with minimal certification requirements, at combined volumes in the tens of thousands per year. At lower volumes it pays only for parts that need no HIP. Expensive post-processing equipment is what favours centralisation.
NRE_note: The abstract and section snippets do not say whether design, reverse-engineering or build-preparation cost is included; no open full text or dissertation PDF could be reached (the CMU repository PDF is not fetchable), so this stays unconfirmed (ScienceDirect abstract; IN+ seminar abstract).
Production_note: A process-based cost model of AM production, with HIP as a post-processing step that drives the result, feeds the location optimisation (ScienceDirect abstract; IN+ seminar abstract).
QA_Qual_note: Certification works as a scoping condition: decentralisation pays only for non-critical parts on shared equipment 'with minimal certification requirements', and no qualification cost term is visible (ScienceDirect abstract).
QA_Insp_note: The abstract and snippets do not mention inspection or testing, and whether the predecessor Laureijs destructive-testing yield is carried over could not be checked without the full text (ScienceDirect abstract).
Storage_note: Inventory cost is an explicit term traded off against production and transport cost when choosing the number and location of sites (ScienceDirect abstract); the inventory formulation itself is not visible.
Shared_Capital_note: Production scale economies are traded off against the number of sites, and parts that share the same equipment, or skip costly HIP equipment, favour decentralisation (ScienceDirect abstract; IN+ seminar abstract).
Shared_Capacity_note: The optimisation sets the number and location of AM sites serving airports, but the accessed text shows no capacity contention or effect on lead time or service level (ScienceDirect abstract and snippets).
Speed_note: Lead-time reduction appears only as a motivation in the introduction, and whether lead time enters the inventory or transport cost terms cannot be seen in the abstract and snippets, so the earlier Partial rested on inference (ScienceDirect abstract and introduction snippet).

name: Paderborn DMRC Trade-off Methodology (TOM), 2017 version (Kruse, Reiher & Koch)
developer: C. Lindemann, T. Reiher, U. Jahnke, R. Koch; A. Kruse (Paderborn University, DMRC)
earlier_versions: Lindemann, Jahnke, Reiher & Koch (2014), SFF Symposium paper 'Towards a sustainable and economic selection of part candidates for AM': original workshop-based part-selection matrix with an early cost-estimation module. | Lindemann, Reiher, Jahnke & Koch (2015), Rapid Prototyping Journal 21(2):216-227 (doi:10.1108/RPJ-12-2014-0179): journal version reporting 90% overlap with independent expert selections in an ESA project; the 2017 version adds knock-out gates, four value categories, company and product questionnaires, and an Excel implementation.
description: Three-phase workshop (information, assessment, decision) in which non-experts and AM experts score candidate parts in a trade-off matrix. Criteria cover size limits, part class, assembly suppression, post-processing need, material applicability, design rules, property improvement and processing time, then material change, buy-to-fly, lead time and an AM-vs-milling cost ratio. Redesign and economic evaluation follow, and the 2017 revision adds knock-out gates and four value categories.
NRE_note: The decision phase gathers redesign requirements (black-box principle, InformationForms) and compares redesign approaches, but redesign and data-preparation effort are not costed (SFF 2014).
Production_note: An AM-vs-milling cost ratio and an early cost-calculation module give a first production-cost estimate without a documented build-up, and a full cost comparison is only planned in the 2017 version (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).
QA_Qual_note: Material applicability (industry use, public data) and space-specific requirements are scored and printable material is a knock-out gate, with no certification step (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).
QA_Insp_note: Full papers read; post-processing need is scored but quality inspection is not a criterion (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).
Storage_note: Avoiding tooling and tool warehousing is mentioned and the 2017 questionnaire asks about spare-part and tool management strategy, with no inventory criterion or calculation (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).
Shared_Capital_note: Full papers read; machine availability in-house or at providers is only a size-feasibility check and the TOM has no investment criterion (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full papers read; equipment availability is checked only for build-chamber size, and capacity sharing is not addressed (SFF 2014).
Speed_note: Lead, process and post-processing time and time-criticality are scored criteria on a 1-5 scale, not computed outputs (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).

name: VTT/Aalto digital spare parts program (DIVA / DIVALIITO): screening, metal PBF cost tool, qualification workflow
developer: M. Salmi, J. Partanen, J. Tuomi, S. Chekurov, N. Kretzschmar et al. (Aalto University); S. Metsä-Kortelainen, A. Jussila et al. (VTT)
description: Four-phase spare-part classification adapted from Knofius et al.: technical (material, size), photo-based geometry review, ranking, then economic (price, resupply lead time, annual consumption, MOQ). Only ~2% of one firm's items were feasible. It adds an STL-based metal PBF cost tool and illustrative AM vs. conventional business cases that include downtime. Its cost tool was later released as AMDSP 2.0, which is listed separately.
NRE_note: 3D-model availability is a technical screening criterion (though it could not be assessed systematically), and digitisation and redesign are not costed (DIVA report).
Production_note: The STL-based metal PBF cost tool sets orientation and supports automatically and splits cost into machine amortisation (8-yr depreciation), work and material with 74% powder packing, up to 95% recycling and 10% follow-up time; cases include an Inconel 718 pin at about EUR 55 vs EUR 90 (DIVA report).
QA_Qual_note: DIVALIITO sets out a six-step qualification workflow based on DNV GL CG-0197 (MPS and test plan, notified-body review, qualification build with witness specimens, component and powder test lists), but it is not tiered by part class or costed (2020 report; DIVA report).
QA_Insp_note: Hardness, porosity, Charpy, tensile, chemistry and microstructure tests on printed parts and witness specimens are listed, but not costed or set by part class (DIVA report; 2020 report).
Storage_note: The cost tool accepts storage and transport costs, and the enclosure business case quantifies stock reduction from printing on demand: average stock 10 vs 1 pcs, storage cost EUR 100 vs EUR 1, plus logistics-to-stock costs (DIVA report Table 4).
Shared_Capital_note: The PBF cost tool depreciates the printer over 8 years, but no utilisation, operating-hours or parts-per-build input is described (74% is the powder packing ratio), and spreading capital through service providers' wider customer base is mentioned only qualitatively (DIVA report).
Shared_Capacity_note: Five supply-chain models (OEM, maintenance provider, 3D database operator, printing service provider and end-user centric) and platform networks of AM service providers are described qualitatively, with no capacity model (DIVA report; 2020 report).
Speed_note: The enclosure business case quantifies downtime (EUR 1,000/h) and delivery time (20 vs 19 days) to show AM can be cheaper overall, and re-supply lead time is a screening criterion (DIVA report Table 4).

name: Klahn-Leutenecker-Meboldt (ETH Zurich) design-strategy and indicator method
developer: C. Klahn, B. Leutenecker, M. Meboldt (ETH Zurich; inspire AG)
description: Separates a manufacturing-driven strategy (substituting AM for an existing process, possibly later in the lifecycle) from a function-driven strategy (redesign for performance). It proposes indicators for parts that gain most from AM through process advantages vs. design advantages.
NRE_note: The strategy choice sets how much redesign is warranted (function-driven designs need major redesign to return to conventional production), but redesign effort is not quantified (Procedia CIRP full text).
Production_note: Cost is a screening outcome and a reason for the manufacturing-driven strategy, and the cases compare quoted unit costs by lot size (SLS about EUR 6.88 vs EUR 107.83 for prototype moulding at 25 units), but there is no cost model (Procedia CIRP Fig. 4; ICED 2015 Table 1).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification is not part of the strategies or indicators; the CIRP case mentions only customer testing of 50 SLS parts (Procedia CIRP and ICED 2015 full texts).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection is not addressed in either paper (Procedia CIRP and ICED 2015 full texts).
Storage_note: Inventory, spare parts and obsolescence are not among the indicators or strategies; reduced inventory appears only in a background list of general AM benefits citing Wohlers (ICED 2015 full text, Sec. 2, 5.1; Procedia CIRP).
Shared_Capital_note: AM machine investment is not discussed; the papers note only that AM avoids part-specific tooling and CAM investment (Procedia CIRP and ICED 2015 full texts).
Shared_Capacity_note: Capacity is not addressed beyond a remark on growing build rates and service-provider competition (Procedia CIRP and ICED 2015 full texts).
Speed_note: The manufacturing-driven strategy uses AM for time reasons, citing about 3 weeks for prototype moulds and 3 months for series tooling in the case, but time is not computed or valued (Procedia CIRP; ICED 2015).

name: Purdue/Virginia Tech Decision Engine for AM in defense acquisition
developer: W. Tsutsui, Q. Shi, I. Walter, A. Wei, C. Williams, D. DeLaurentis, J. Panchal (Purdue University; Virginia Tech)
description: Expected-utility engine that ranks AM and conventional routes on total cost, total time and part mass, with a bounding-box go/no-go check. Cost comes from a Gibson et al.-style model (prorated machine purchase, operation, material, labour). Hybrid WAAM ranked highest in both scenarios.
NRE_note: Per-batch human time for printer facilitation is costed as labour, but the topology-optimised redesign enters only through lower mass and its design, CAD/CAM or file-preparation effort is not costed (NPS paper SYM-AM-23-069, cost model and Table 3).
Production_note: Cost per alternative is built from prorated machine purchase, machine operation, material (feedstock price times mass) and labour from human time, with build time from scan length and process parameters and a ±10% uncertainty (NPS paper, Table 3).
QA_Qual_note: The full paper models no qualification or certification term; only a note that the hWAAM part needs heat treatment (NPS paper).
QA_Insp_note: The full paper models no inspection or testing term (NPS paper).
Storage_note: Inventory reduction appears only as a general AM benefit in the introduction and the decision engine does not evaluate it (NPS paper).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine purchase is prorated into cost and parts per batch (5-8) are listed, but the proration basis (life, utilisation or parts per machine) is not stated and machine sharing is not modelled (NPS paper, cost model and Table 3).
Shared_Capacity_note: The full paper does not model machine counts, shared machines or pooled capacity; build volume is only a go/no-go check (NPS paper).
Speed_note: Total time for the 100-part lot (machine time from scan length plus human time) is computed and weighted 0.3-0.4 in the utility, but lead time, queueing and availability are not modelled (NPS paper, Table 3).

name: Zaman et al. integrated material & AM process selection (Ashby + AHP)
developer: U. K. uz Zaman, M. Rivette, A. Siadat (Arts et Métiers ENSAM, LCFC Metz); S. M. Mousavi (Shahed University, Tehran)
description: Translates requirements, screens materials and processes with Ashby material indices, then ranks them with AHP (validated with SAW) on function, cost and environment. Criteria include machine cost, labour cost, build speed, accuracy and build volume.
NRE_note: Design or engineering effort is not a criterion or cost term in the method; a longer design cycle is mentioned only in the literature review (ENSAM author copy).
Production_note: Per-part material cost is computed with the Yim and Rosen model (support, recycling, volume, price, density), while machine cost and labour cost enter only as AHP criteria, so no full per-part cost is built up (ENSAM author copy, Eq. 1, Table 11).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification and certification are not addressed anywhere in the method (ENSAM author copy).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection is not in the method; metrology and quality control appear only as challenges in the literature review (ENSAM author copy).
Storage_note: Inventory is not addressed anywhere in the method (ENSAM author copy).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine cost is an AHP ranking criterion (7.9% global priority), but it is not amortised and sharing or utilisation is not modelled (ENSAM author copy, Table 11).
Shared_Capacity_note: Capacity is reflected only as machine build volume; throughput and shared capacity are not modelled (ENSAM author copy).
Speed_note: Build speed (printing speed on a 50x50x20 mm reference part) is the most heavily weighted machine criterion (26.9%) and 'time constraints' are noted as requirements, but no build or lead time is computed (ENSAM author copy, Table 11).

name: Liu-Zhu-Ye design-integrated AM process & machine selection
developer: W. Liu (Aston University), Z. Zhu (University of Sheffield), S. Ye (University of Cambridge)
description: Four-stage method run alongside design: must-have screening (volume, lead time, accuracy, surface, durability), AHP technical ranking, feature-based re-evaluation after detailed design, and per-machine cost estimation. The cost step adapts Fera et al.'s model, adding print success rate, labour, energy and maintenance; an SLM280 was selected at $277/part.
NRE_note: The cost equation includes per-build geometry preparation (Cprep: supports, orientation), build-job assembly and machine set-up, but one-time redesign or design effort is not costed (Aston accepted manuscript, Eq. 1).
Production_note: Per-part cost is estimated for each feasible machine from preparation, set-up, build (incl. material) and post-processing, divided by print success rate and grossed up for labour, energy and maintenance (adapted Fera et al.; SLM280 at $277.33/part) (Aston accepted manuscript, Eq. 1-2).
QA_Qual_note: The full method (screening, AHP ranking, re-evaluation, cost) contains no qualification or certification element (Aston accepted manuscript).
QA_Insp_note: Post-processing (support removal, bead blasting) is costed, but no inspection or quality-check term appears anywhere in the method (Aston accepted manuscript).
Storage_note: Inventory is not addressed anywhere in the full method (Aston accepted manuscript).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine maintenance enters as a fixed rate (e.g. $20k/yr, $3.5/h), but machine purchase, depreciation, utilisation and parts per build are not modelled (packing index left to future work) (Aston accepted manuscript).
Shared_Capacity_note: Capacity sharing is not addressed anywhere in the full method (Aston accepted manuscript).
Speed_note: Required lead time (12 weeks in the case) is a must-have screening threshold against tabulated process lead times (4 weeks AM vs 8-12 weeks conventional), but lead time is not computed (Aston accepted manuscript, Table 2).

name: Fera/Costabile/Lambiase (Salerno) MiProCAMAM mixed-build cost-allocation model
developer: M. Fera, F. Fruggiero, G. Costabile, A. Lambiase, D. T. Pham (University of Salerno and co-authors)
description: Step-wise cost model (data preparation, build-job assembly, setup, building, removal) with skill-specific labour rates and OEE-adjusted times. Mixed-build costs are allocated per geometry with a coating-time algorithm adapted from Rickenbacher. Outputs are cost per part, completion time and capacity-utilisation indicators.
NRE_note: Per-build preparation (orientation, supports) and build-job assembly are costed from operator and workstation rates (Eq. 18-19); redesign is mentioned in the introduction but no one-time redesign, reverse engineering or parameter development is modelled (UNISA preprint).
Production_note: Cost per part for each geometry is the sum of preparation, build job, setup, building (machine, gas, energy, material with powder waste) and removal costs (Eq. 17-23), validated on Baumers' 85-part B01 build (UNISA preprint).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification is not addressed anywhere in the model or case (UNISA preprint, full text).
QA_Insp_note: Quality control is named as a post-processing phase but explicitly neglected in the cost calculation; production rejects enter only as the quality loss in the OEE time adjustment (UNISA preprint, Eq. 7-8).
Storage_note: Inventory is not addressed; the model covers one build job in a job shop (UNISA preprint, full text).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine cost per hour is purchase cost divided by depreciation years and annual uptime hours (Eq. 21), and build costs are allocated across the geometries of a mixed build with capacity-utilisation indicators (Eq. 9-15, 25-26) (UNISA preprint).
Shared_Capacity_note: Build-chamber capacity utilisation and adapted utilisation are computed for the mixed build (Eq. 25-26), but the model covers one machine and one build with no queue, scheduling or cross-site pooling, which the authors leave to future work (UNISA preprint).
Speed_note: Outputs completion time per geometry in days from assembly, setup, build and removal times (Eq. 16), but post-processing, queueing and delivery are excluded and time is not valued (UNISA preprint).

name: Di & Yang DMLS cost model with dynamic process planning
developer: L. Di, Y. Yang (University of Texas at Arlington)
description: Production cost = energy + labour + material + overhead, where overhead covers machine amortisation, maintenance and administration by build time. It is coupled with a layer-wise process-parameter search that cut total cost 12.7%. Mixed-batch cost is allocated by mass × geometric complexity.
NRE_note: Labour cost includes setup and pre-processing hours per build (Eq. 7) and a geometry-based algorithm selects layer-wise parameters, but one-time parameter development or design effort is not costed (MDPI full text).
Production_note: Total cost = energy + labour + material + overhead with unit cost per part; a single Ti part costs USD 119.98, falling to 104.70 with dynamic process planning (MDPI full text, Eq. 1-10).
QA_Qual_note: No qualification cost or time term; the authors list the lack of quality and mechanical-property constraints as a limitation (MDPI full text).
QA_Insp_note: No inspection or testing cost line in the model (MDPI full text).
Storage_note: Inventory and storage do not appear in the model (MDPI full text).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine investment is amortised over a 3-year life by build time (Eq. 10) and mixed-geometry batch cost is allocated to parts by mass and geometric complexity (Eq. 2); utilisation enters only for material (MDPI full text).
Shared_Capacity_note: Single machine build costing; capacity, queues or multiple sites are not modelled (MDPI full text).
Speed_note: The model computes build and scan time (t_build) to drive energy, gas and overhead costs, a print-time-only time model; lead time or availability is not reported or valued (MDPI full text).

name: Barclift et al. powder-reuse depreciation extension to PBF cost model
developer: M. Barclift, S. Joshi, T. Simpson, C. Dickman (Pennsylvania State University)
description: Extends an existing PBF cost model with sum-of-the-years'-digits depreciation of reused powder by build cycle. Fixed-material-cost models can undervalue high-value virgin-powder jobs by ~3-11% or 13-75%, depending on material and the allowed number of reuse cycles.
NRE_note: Per-part geometry preparation, build-tray layout and machine setup are costed (terms inherited from Rickenbacher et al.), but the paper states that re-design and engineering of an existing component are not captured (SFF full text).
Production_note: Total cost per part (Eq. 12) sums preparation, tray assembly, setup, build (machine and gas rates x build time), removal, separation and post-processing, with melted powder priced by reuse cycle (SFF full text).
QA_Qual_note: The paper notes that reused-powder acceptance is agreed between supplier and purchaser but costs no powder, material or part qualification (SFF full text).
QA_Insp_note: CT scanning is mentioned only as a possible extra post-processing step in the limitations; no inspection or testing is costed (SFF full text).
Storage_note: Storage appears only as a labour activity within part removal; there is no inventory or carrying cost (SFF full text).
Shared_Capital_note: Build time at a fixed machine operating rate ($60/h) is split among the parts in a build and setup/removal are divided by part count, but machine capital depreciation and utilisation are not modelled (SFF full text, Table 1, Eqs. 2-5).
Shared_Capacity_note: Sharing across machines, jobs or customers is not modelled; supply-chain modelling is named only as future work (SFF full text).
Speed_note: Build time per part is estimated (Eq. 3) as a cost driver, a print-time-only time model; lead time, queuing and delivery are not modelled (SFF full text).

name: Kamps et al. integrated cost + LCA model for LBM gears
developer: T. Kamps, M. Lutter-Guenther, C. Seidel, T. Gutowski, G. Reinhart (Fraunhofer / TU Munich; MIT)
description: Cradle-to-gate integrated cost and life-cycle-assessment models covering full process sequences. Lightweight design is the most significant lever for both cost and energy.
NRE_note: The abstract names lightweight design (a redesign) as the most significant lever for cost and energy, but whether the one-time design effort is costed is not visible; full text was not reachable (BL catalogue abstract; ScienceDirect, Fraunhofer Publica and CAS catalogue blocked).
Production_note: The paper presents an integrated cost model that estimates gear cost across complete process sequences (machining, hobbing, LBM) for low-volume, high-variant production (BL catalogue abstract).
QA_Qual_note: Only the abstract could be read (full text paywalled; Fraunhofer Publica and other records blocked) and it does not mention qualification.
QA_Insp_note: Only the abstract could be read; it covers complete process sequences but does not say whether gear inspection or testing is costed.
Storage_note: The abstract scopes the models to cradle-to-gate production cost and energy, which plainly excludes inventory (BL catalogue abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: Only the abstract could be read; it does not show how LBM machine cost is allocated or whether builds are shared.
Shared_Capacity_note: The abstract scopes the work to cradle-to-gate cost and energy of gear manufacturing process sequences, which plainly excludes printer capacity pooled across sites or users (BL catalogue abstract).
Speed_note: Only the abstract could be read; lead time is not mentioned, but a low-volume LBM versus hobbing comparison could plausibly include it.

name: Dias et al. (2022) WAAM process-based cost model (Sustainability)
developer: M. Dias, J. P. M. Pragana, B. Ferreira, I. Ribeiro, C. M. A. Silva (Instituto Superior Técnico, University of Lisbon)
earlier_versions: Dias (2021) IST MSc thesis 'Economic and Environmental Potential of Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing' (July 2021): original Excel process-based cost model and cradle-to-gate LCA of a 316L part; the 2022 Sustainability paper publishes this work with co-authors.
description: Excel process-based cost model of setup, deposition and machining. Fixed costs cover equipment annualised and scaled by utilisation, building and overhead; variable costs cover wire, baseplate, gas, labour, energy and a scrap credit. WAAM beats machining from solid at all volumes studied and beats die casting up to ~2,000-2,300 parts, with buy-to-fly as the most sensitive parameter.
NRE_note: Pre-processing (3D modelling, planning) and post-processing are explicitly excluded from the cost model so the routes can be compared fairly, so no design or engineering cost is included (Sustainability full text, sec. 2).
Production_note: Per-part cost vs annual volume is built from wire, baseplate, gas, labour, energy, equipment, tooling, building and overhead for WAAM and the conventional routes (Sustainability full text).
QA_Qual_note: Full text read; qualification or certification is not part of the model (Sustainability full text).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection falls in the post-processing stage that the model explicitly excludes (Sustainability full text).
Storage_note: Full text read; inventory is not addressed (Sustainability full text).
Shared_Capital_note: Machinery is annualised over its life and scaled by a utilisation rate set by cycle time, annual production, rejection rate and uptime for non-dedicated machines (Sustainability full text).
Shared_Capacity_note: The model sizes the number of WAAM-plus-machining sets needed to reach annual production at 240 x 8 h/yr uptime, so capacity is modelled, but at one site and with no effect on lead time (Sustainability full text).
Speed_note: Deposition (from wire feed speed), inter-layer cooling and machining times are computed per part, but only to allocate cost; lead time is not reported (Sustainability full text).

name: Cranfield WAAM early-stage cost estimation models (vs. CNC machining)
developer: Cranfield University: J. Guo (MSc by Research, supervisors J. Mehnen, Y. Xu) and Y. Zhai ('Early cost estimation for additive manufacture', MSc by Research, supervisor H. L. Lockett)
description: Feature-based cost (and GHG) models that let designers estimate WAAM cost from CAD features and compare it with machining. Wire cost and buy-to-fly ratio drive the WAAM advantage; in Zhai's Ti case, WAAM cost £1,800 vs. £2,150 for CNC, with setup 28%, wire 27% and welding labour 25%.
NRE_note: Zhai's model costs WAAM setup (28% of product cost in the Ti case) from a process plan, but the review notes no approach covers AM design activities and neither thesis abstract mentions one-time design or reverse-engineering cost (Busachi et al. 2017 review; thesis abstracts; full theses not online).
Production_note: Per-part WAAM cost is built from process-plan times, wire, welding and setup costs and hourly rates, and compared with CNC (Zhai Ti case GBP 1,800 vs 2,150; Guo's tool reads CAD features) (thesis abstracts; Busachi et al. 2017 review).
QA_Qual_note: Neither thesis abstract nor the review summary mentions qualification, and the full theses have no public files on the Cranfield records, so whether it is costed cannot be established.
QA_Insp_note: The review lists setup, wire and welding as the cost elements and does not mention inspection; the full theses are not online, so whether inspection is costed cannot be established (Busachi et al. 2017; Cranfield records).
Storage_note: Both models are design-stage per-part cost (and carbon) estimators for WAAM vs CNC, a scope that excludes inventory (thesis abstracts).
Shared_Capital_note: Process times are converted to cost with hourly rates for operators, machines and software, but how equipment capital, depreciation or utilisation enter those rates is not shown (Busachi et al. 2017 review of Zhai).
Shared_Capacity_note: Both models are single-part design-stage cost estimators, a scope that excludes pooled print capacity (thesis abstracts).
Speed_note: The model computes deposition and machining times (WAAM 3.7 h deposition plus 0.5 h milling vs CNC 1.3 h) as cost drivers, but no lead time or availability (Busachi et al. 2017 review of Zhai).

name: Wilson et al. DED turbine-blade remanufacturing (repair vs. replace) assessment
developer: J. M. Wilson, C. Piya, Y. C. Shin, F. Zhao, K. Ramani (Purdue University)
description: Reverse-engineers the missing blade volume from a scanned mesh with a prominent-cross-section algorithm, deposits the repair by laser direct deposition, and validates geometry and tensile strength. A cradle-to-gate comparison of energy and CO2 finds repair favourable when less than ~18% of blade volume is missing.
NRE_note: Geometry reconstruction (PCS cross-section algorithm, spline rebuild in CATIA, Boolean repair volume) is central, but the scan was hypothetical and digitising and CAD reconstruction are explicitly excluded from the energy analysis and not costed (author PDF).
Production_note: Compares energy and CO2 only; the paper has no cost or economic analysis (author PDF).
QA_Qual_note: Two tensile specimens show the repaired material is as strong as the original, but qualification is explicitly excluded from the analysis and no certification path is given (author PDF).
QA_Insp_note: A CAD distance analysis of the repair (max deviation 0.145 mm) is reported, but inspection is not costed or prescribed per part (author PDF).
Storage_note: Inventory and spares are not discussed in the full paper (author PDF).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine capital is not discussed in the full paper (author PDF).
Shared_Capacity_note: Capacity and sites are not discussed in the full paper (author PDF).
Speed_note: Deposition time (14 and 18 min) and process cycle times are reported and feed the energy comparison, a print-time-only time model; end-to-end repair lead time is not analysed (author PDF).

name: Wilson-Schmitz hybrid AFSD + scanning + CNC activity-based cost model
developer: N. Wilson, R. Patterson, E. Charles, M. Landis, J. Kincaid, R. Garcia, G. Corson, T. Schmitz (University of Tennessee, Knoxville; Oak Ridge National Laboratory MDF; Northwestern University)
description: Activity-based cost models for each step of a hybrid sequence (AFSD deposition, structured-light scanning, milling, turning), with direct costs and indirect costs (space, depreciation, maintenance). The hybrid route cost ~$1,008 vs. ~$834 for machining only, and labour was 65% of the hybrid cost.
NRE_note: Setup labour for each step (e.g., 18 min AFSD, 30 min milling) is costed, but part-program generation for deposition and machining is explicitly omitted and no redesign is costed (NSF PAR full text).
Production_note: Direct (material, labour, energy, tooling) and indirect (depreciation, maintenance, space) costs are computed per step for the hybrid and machining-only routes (about $1,008 vs $834) (NSF PAR full text).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification is not mentioned in the cost model (NSF PAR full text).
QA_Insp_note: The structured-light scanning step is a costed per-part metrology activity (about $175), but it serves preform alignment and toolpath generation; acceptance inspection of the finished part is mentioned as possible but not costed (NSF PAR full text).
Storage_note: Inventory is not addressed (NSF PAR full text).
Shared_Capital_note: Straight-line depreciation (equipment cost, salvage, life) and maintenance are allocated by process time, with no utilisation, annual-hours or volume input (NSF PAR full text).
Shared_Capacity_note: The model costs one part's process chain and has no shared or pooled capacity (NSF PAR full text).
Speed_note: Lead time is stated to be outside the model; the authors note the large wrought stock was unavailable and the machining-only part could not have been made in the same time frame, a qualitative point (NSF PAR full text).

name: NIST SP 1176 / Thomas & Gilbert AM cost review and taxonomy
developer: D. S. Thomas, S. W. Gilbert (National Institute of Standards and Technology)
decision_levels: Process/machine choice; Adopt or make-vs-buy; Capacity placement/sharing
description: Literature review that sorts AM costs into well-structured costs (material, machine, build-envelope utilisation, build time, energy, labour) and ill-structured costs (build failure, setup, inventory, transport, supply-chain vulnerability). It gives conceptual supply-chain cost equations but no new calibrated model.
NRE_note: The reviewed per-part models carry per-build setup labour (Hopkinson and Dickens setup times of 10-120 min) and preparation at about 3-9% of cost (Lindemann), but design cost is only noted as the exception to cost-free customisation and no one-time engineering is modelled (NIST SP 1176, Secs. 3.3, 3.2, Table 3.1).
Production_note: The report sets out per-part cost models from machine, material, labour, build time and post-processing (Hopkinson and Dickens; Ruffo et al. C = material x mass + indirect rate x build time) and its own total-cost decomposition for AM vs traditional (NIST SP 1176, Secs. 4.1, 4.3).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification and certification are not treated as cost items anywhere in the full report (NIST SP 1176).
QA_Insp_note: Quality assurance is named as a concern needing standard methods to evaluate accuracy, surface finish and feature detail, and build failure is listed as an ill-structured cost, but neither is costed (NIST SP 1176, Secs. 3, 3.3).
Storage_note: Inventory is quantified only at the macro level (holding cost of $52 billion at an assumed 25% of inventory value) and appears as a finished-goods inventory term in the cost decomposition, but AM's effect on stock is not modelled (NIST SP 1176, Secs. 3.1.1, 4.3).
Shared_Capital_note: Utilisation and multi-part amortisation appear only in summaries of other studies (Hopkinson and Dickens; Ruffo); the report's own cost equations have no amortisation or utilisation term, and it says only that filling the build chamber lowers unit cost (NIST SP 1176, Secs. 4 and 6).
Shared_Capacity_note: Centralised vs distributed production is discussed by quoting Khajavi et al.'s F-18 case ($1.0M vs $1.8M per year) and Holmström et al., not computed by the report (NIST SP 1176, Sec. 3.1.2).
Speed_note: Time appears as a conceptual term in the 'total advantage' equations and in narrative on lead time and supply disruption, with no lead-time calculation or value of time (NIST SP 1176, Secs. 3.1.2, 3.1.4, 4.4).

name: Ghadge aircraft spare parts AM system dynamics model
developer: Abhijeet Ghadge, Georgia Karantoni, Atanu Chaudhuri, Aravindan Srinivasan (Heriot-Watt University; Aalborg University)
description: System dynamics simulation comparing CM base-stock inventory across RDCs and service locations with on-demand AM at service locations; AM inventory ~25% of CM and 5-year holding cost ~$1M vs >$4.5M.
NRE_note: Design and digitisation appear only as qualitative benefits in the literature table; the Vensim models have no NRE variable (author version, Appendices 1-2).
Production_note: The paper only expects 'a moderate increase in the unit cost of (new) raw material and 3D production' in words; production cost is not a model input or output (author version).
QA_Qual_note: Quality standards appear only as a qualitative limitation in the literature table; no qualification variable is modelled (author version).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection and testing are absent from the model equations and parameter tables (author version, Appendices 1-2).
Storage_note: Aggregate inventory and accumulated holding cost ($15/unit) are computed for both networks: AM inventory about 25% of CM, 5-year holding cost about $1M vs $4.5M (author version).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine acquisition cost is not a model input; equipment cost is mentioned only in general terms (author version).
Shared_Capacity_note: A single aggregate AM capacity stock (105,000 units) is depleted by production across service locations, but it never binds and has no effect on lead time or service; there is no per-site pooling (author version, Appendix 2).
Speed_note: Stochastic lead times (CM replenishment mean 6, AM production mean 4) drive safety stock and inventory, and backorders are computed only in the CM model, so AM's availability effect is not computed; grounding cost is qualitative (author version).

name: Sgarbossa conventional vs additive spare parts inventory comparison (Poisson demand)
developer: Fabio Sgarbossa, Mirco Peron (NTNU); Francesco Lolli, Elia Balugani (University of Modena and Reggio Emilia)
decision_levels: Part selection; Process/machine choice; Adopt or make-vs-buy
description: Periodic-review Poisson inventory model choosing manufacturing option, review period and order-up-to level, with technology-specific unit costs (from experts) and AM-vs-CM failure-rate ratios from fatigue literature; decision trees show backorder cost (~EUR 3,500/unit split) is the main driver and that AM wins whenever storage is zero.
NRE_note: Different design costs for AM and CM parts and possible redesign of AM parts are explicitly left to future work; there is no NRE term in Ctot = Ch + Cb + Cp (accepted manuscript, Eq. 3, conclusions).
Production_note: Unit production cost per option is entered by technology (SLM, LENS, casting, wrought, forging), part size and post-process (polishing, annealing, HIP), from expert-estimated EUR/cm3 ranges (accepted manuscript, Tables 4-6).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification is not mentioned; reliability enters only through literature-based AM vs CM failure-rate ratios (accepted manuscript, full text).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection and testing are not mentioned; only post-processing (polishing, annealing, HIP) is in the unit cost (accepted manuscript, Table 5).
Storage_note: Holding cost (30% per year of unit cost) is computed on average stock under the optimal order-up-to level, with storage limits Smax = 0 and 1 tested (accepted manuscript, Eq. 3).
Shared_Capital_note: AM machine capital is absent from the full text and limited AM equipment capacity is named as future work; unit cost is a single per-option input (accepted manuscript).
Shared_Capacity_note: Single-item, single-stock-point model; limited AM equipment capacity and multi-item approaches are left to future work (accepted manuscript, conclusions).
Speed_note: Expected backorders over review period plus lead time are computed and costed, with CM lead times of 4-12 weeks and AM lead time equal to total production time (accepted manuscript, Eq. 3, Table 6).

name: Peron failure-rate-uncertainty AM vs CM spare parts model with inspection tools
developer: Mirco Peron, Andrea M. Coruzzolo, Rob Basten, Nils Knofius, Francesco Lolli, Fabio Sgarbossa
description: Periodic-review Poisson inventory model with materials-science-based failure-rate uncertainty showing AM is penalized far more than CM by uncertainty; porosity assessment or in-situ monitoring pays off only if it cuts uncertainty by ~5-6 percentage points.
NRE_note: The 2024 abstract does not mention design or one-time engineering cost, and the same authors' 2022 IFAC precursor (full text) has only holding, backorder and production cost terms; the 2024 open-access PDF on UNIMORE IRIS could not be fetched (URL rejected by the proxy), so whether the extension adds NRE is not shown.
Production_note: The 2024 abstract says the model weighs AM's high production costs against inventory savings, but the full text could not be opened, so whether unit cost is computed or entered is not confirmed; the same authors' 2022 precursor uses per-technology unit costs (abstract; IFAC 2022).
QA_Qual_note: AM failure-rate uncertainty derived from fatigue data, attributed to the newness of the process, acts as a proxy for missing qualification data and its cost penalty is computed, but no qualification activity, test set or cost is modelled (2024 abstract; 2022 IFAC precursor).
QA_Insp_note: Porosity assessment and in-situ monitoring are costed as investments and the model computes the uncertainty reduction that justifies each (about 5 and 6 percentage points) (UNIMORE IRIS abstract).
Storage_note: Holding cost (about 30% per year of unit cost) is computed on expected on-hand stock under the optimal order-up-to level for AM and CM, quantifying AM's inventory reduction (2024 abstract; 2022 IFAC precursor, Eq. 1).
Shared_Capital_note: Neither the 2024 abstract nor the 2022 precursor full text includes AM machine capital (unit production cost is a single input), but the 2024 full text could not be fetched to confirm the extension adds none.
Shared_Capacity_note: A single-item periodic-review inventory model with fixed lead times (0.1 weeks for AM), so capacity shared across sites or users is outside its documented scope (2024 abstract; 2022 IFAC precursor).
Speed_note: The 2024 abstract names AM's short lead time as the source of its inventory savings, but the full text could not be opened, so whether backorders or lead time are computed is not confirmed; the 2022 precursor computes backorder cost (abstract; IFAC 2022).

name: Ahlsell automotive slow-moving spare parts AM supply chain cost model
developer: Levin Ahlsell, Didar Jalal, Patrik Jonsson (Chalmers); Siavash H. Khajavi, Jan Holmstrom (Aalto)
description: Total supply chain cost model (production price, inbound/outbound transport, ABC-based warehousing, and service costs incl. vehicle-off-road downtime, badwill, lost sales) over the part life cycle; 3 of 14 parts show savings; metal AM parts cost ~1,756% more and need 72-99% cost cuts to break even.
NRE_note: The model explicitly leaves out the cost of developing or adjusting 3D drawings and the engineering labour of redesign; production cost is only the supplier purchase price (Chalmers full text, method and Discussion).
Production_note: Part-specific unit prices for each technology are model inputs (AM prices from supplier quotes on 3D drawings, annual quantity and material; TM prices from the OEM database), which meets the per-technology unit-cost input test even though the AM price has no build-up (Chalmers full text).
QA_Qual_note: The model explicitly excludes the cost of quality controls to approve a spare part and has no qualification term (Chalmers full text).
QA_Insp_note: Quality-control cost is explicitly excluded, and quality-check time is also left out of the AM lead-time estimate (Chalmers full text).
Storage_note: ABC-based warehousing cost (capital cost on stock value, goods-in, overhead, building and more) is computed from average inventory, which differs by method: TM one-shot lifetime buy versus AM annual replenishment with a one-piece safety stock (Chalmers full text, Table 4).
Shared_Capital_note: AM production is outsourced and machine capital sits inside the supplier price (with margin), so capital and its sharing are outside the model's scope (Chalmers full text).
Shared_Capacity_note: Only one centralised outsourced AM supplier is modelled and its capacity never constrains lead time; the authors state a dispersed AM supply chain was not investigated (Chalmers full text).
Speed_note: Vehicle-off-road penalty cost, badwill and lost sales are computed from service level, with the AM stockout penalty set by the AM lead-time input and the TM penalty at the maximum fee (Chalmers full text, service cost equations).

name: Strong two-stage p-median model for metal AM post-processing hubs
developer: Danielle Strong, Michael Kay, Brett Conner, Thomas Wakefield, Guha Manogharan (Penn State and collaborators)
description: Two-stage p-median facility location model choosing hub locations and capacities and assigning demand across machine shops and heat-treatment facilities, minimizing fixed, operating and transport costs; 22 hubs grow to 35 as demand rises.
NRE_note: Only the abstract was reachable (Elsevier paywall; no open copy, thesis or repository text found); it lists total cost as fixed, operational and transport costs and does not mention design or engineering cost.
Production_note: Operational costs of hybrid-AM processing at hubs enter the total cost, but at hub level with no part-level build-up (Penn State Pure abstract).
QA_Qual_note: Only the abstract was reachable and it does not mention qualification, so whether it is modelled cannot be established.
QA_Insp_note: Only the abstract was reachable; it covers heat treatment and machining but does not say whether inspection is in the operational costs.
Storage_note: Only the abstract was reachable and it does not mention inventory, so whether it is modelled cannot be established.
Shared_Capital_note: The p-median model trades fixed hub costs against operational and transport costs when choosing hub locations and capacities (22 hubs growing to 35 with demand) (Penn State Pure abstract).
Shared_Capacity_note: Outputs include hub capacity utilisation and demand assignment across machine shops, heat-treatment facilities and hubs, but the abstract shows no effect on lead time or service (Penn State Pure abstract).
Speed_note: Only the abstract was reachable; it reports transport cost but not lead time or delivery time, so whether speed is modelled cannot be established.

name: Barz two-stage capacitated facility location model with AM buy-to-fly ratio
developer: Andreas Barz, Tobias Buer, Hans-Dietrich Haasis
description: Two-stage capacitated facility location problem showing that lower buy-to-fly ratios (AM) cut transport costs and shift production sites closer to customers, with the site count roughly unchanged.
NRE_note: The objective has only first- and second-stage transport costs and site-opening fixed costs, so design or engineering effort is not modelled (open-access full text).
Production_note: Production costs are explicitly excluded: the paper states direct production costs are independent of the site and are not considered in the experiments (open-access full text).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification is not part of the model, whose only AM parameter is the buy-to-fly ratio in the flow-balance constraint (open-access full text).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection is not part of the model, which costs only transport and site opening (open-access full text).
Storage_note: Storage of raw materials or final products at production sites is explicitly forbidden, so inventory is not modelled (open-access full text).
Shared_Capital_note: Fixed costs of opening capacitated production sites are traded against transport cost, but these are generic site costs rather than AM machine capital, and economies of scale are explicitly excluded (open-access full text).
Shared_Capacity_note: Site capacities (100-500 units) constrain single-sourcing assignment of customers to sites, but the model has no lead-time, delivery-time or service-level effect (open-access full text).
Speed_note: Lead time, delivery time and service level are absent; the paper lists slower production time only as future work (open-access full text).

name: Doudnikoff NCSU/USMA military spare parts network model (extends McDermott et al.)
developer: Letai M. Doudnikoff (advisor Brandon M. McConnell), North Carolina State University
earlier_versions: McDermott, Winz, Hodgson, Kay, King & McConnell 2021 (Journal of Defense Analytics and Logistics 5(2):179; from McDermott's 2020 NCSU MS thesis, with the Winz et al. 2020 readiness-vs-cost working paper): the original Monte Carlo + Croston/SBA intermittent-demand + MILP (s,S) model comparing no-AM, centralized and distributed AM. It found centralized AM wins for lumpy demand and distributed for stable demand. Doudnikoff 2021 reuses this model and its 1-1-4 network and modifies it for isolated military sustainment networks, first-machine placement and AM fixed-cost/capacity trade-offs.
description: MILP inventory policy plus Monte Carlo simulation (60 periods) for first-machine placement and isolated-network studies; distributed first machine lowers operating and transport cost, but no-AM is cheapest once AM fixed cost is included; returns to added AM capacity diminish.
NRE_note: The MILP objective covers TM and AM production, transport, carrying and backorder costs only, and part specifications are not modelled, so no design or engineering cost appears (NCSU thesis, ch. 3).
Production_note: AM per-part production cost is a model input but is set equal to TM cost for simplicity (Assumption 4), a lumped unit cost with no build-up from machine time or material (NCSU thesis, ch. 3).
QA_Qual_note: The thesis assumes equal build quality for AM and TM (Assumption 3), which takes qualification out of scope (NCSU thesis, ch. 3).
QA_Insp_note: No inspection or testing term appears in the cost objective, and build quality is assumed equal to TM (NCSU thesis, ch. 3).
Storage_note: The MILP sets order-up-to levels and charges inventory carrying cost at DCs and service locations, with reorder points set from a service-level parameter (NCSU thesis, ch. 3).
Shared_Capital_note: AM fixed cost per machine per day ($121/$241/$512 in Table 3.1, with sensitivity) is charged by the number of machines in the network, and centralized vs distributed placement and added capacity are traded off; variable machine cost is not modelled and the $2,000-5,000 metal figure is only a footnote (NCSU thesis).
Shared_Capacity_note: AM capacity per node and period constrains output (one part type per period), and a centralized AM node at the DC serves several service locations, so capacity contention drives backorders; total capacity is split evenly when distributed (NCSU thesis, ch. 3-4).
Speed_note: Transport lead times (7 periods TM-to-DC, 2 periods DC-to-SL) drive reorder points, and backorders and backorder penalty cost are model outputs (NCSU thesis).

name: Coyle naval aviation AM sustainment screening + DES (NPS)
developer: David M. Coyle (Naval Postgraduate School)
description: Top-down screen of Navy aviation inventory for AM candidates followed by an Innoslate discrete-event simulation (adapted from Jedeck 2015) comparing local stock, OEM order and local AM for one part: AM $3,145 in ~10 days vs OEM $7,005 in 545 days; at quarter print speed AM costs 17% more but stays far faster.
NRE_note: The DES assumes a 3D CAD file, PMI and a complete TDP already exist; reverse-engineering cost and time (SD-22's three to six months is cited) are omitted from the model and flagged as possibly decisive, with PLM/digital thread recommended (full thesis, Sec. V.B.1, VI).
Production_note: Per-part build-up for local AM: setup $100, machine run $550.10 for an 18.6 h build, removal $100, post-processing $1,000 and feedstock at $47.62/lb, as triangular distributions, with half- and quarter-print-speed sensitivity (full thesis, Tables 3-4, Sec. V.B.3).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification of AM and reverse-engineered parts is identified as a gap and future research but is not modelled or costed (full thesis, Sec. VI.A, VI.C).
QA_Insp_note: Final inspection is a per-part activity in the AM branch at $400 and 1 day (full thesis, Table 4).
Storage_note: Holding cost for the local-stock branch is computed as h = i x c (10% of the $7,004.77 unit cost, $700.48 per unit per year) and compared with the order and AM branches (full thesis, Sec. V.B.3.a).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine time is priced as a single run cost ($550.10 for 18.6 h, from Ray 2017 ABC models) with no depreciation, utilisation or multi-part-build input (full thesis, Table 4).
Shared_Capacity_note: One part per print run on one EOS M290 at the FRC, with no queue, capacity contention or multiple sites in the DES (full thesis, Sec. V.B).
Speed_note: The DES outputs time per activity and a Gantt chart for each supply branch (AM about 10 days vs. 545 days for an OEM order, about 30 minutes for a local pull), and long lead time is a candidate selection criterion; readiness is not dollarised (full thesis, Sec. V.C, VI.A).

name: Busachi/Erkoyuncu (Cranfield, Babcock) AM framework and decision support for Royal Navy support services
developer: Alessandro Busachi, John Erkoyuncu, Paul Colegrove (Cranfield University); Richard Drake, Chris Watts, Stephen Wilding (Babcock International)
decision_levels: Part selection; Process/machine choice; Adopt or make-vs-buy; Capacity placement/sharing
description: Soft-systems framework with eight phases (mission, platform, configuration, critical-to-availability parts, AM technology, DfAM, manufacturing configuration, dynamic simulation) and availability equations in which on-platform AM removes administrative and procurement delay; authors state benefits still need quantification.
NRE_note: Design time is an explicit DSS input and output (DesTim, Table 10) that the thesis says may lead to high costs, and the FDM model costs bidding and geometry preparation at a high level; 3D scanning for parts without CAD is a framework step (PhD thesis sec. 7.2; Procedia CIRP 2018; IJSAEM 2018).
Production_note: Per-part WAAM cost is computed from welding, deposited material, substrate, shielding gas, setup and non-productive costs using machine, engineering and machining rates, e.g. GBP 75,732 for case component 1 (PhD thesis ch. 5 Eqs. 4-15, sec. 8.2).
QA_Qual_note: Part qualification is named as the main constraint and is a framework phase, but no qualification cost or time is modelled, and expert reviewers flagged qualification as missing (IJSAEM 2018; PhD thesis secs. 6.2, 8.1).
