QA_Insp_note: QA appears in the process map and a 3D scanner for QA is listed in the FDM cost breakdown, but the thesis has no inspection cost term and says scanner activities still need to be modelled; WAAM NDT methods are only listed (PhD thesis sec. 5.4; Procedia CIRP 2018).
Storage_note: Lower platform inventory and freed space are cited as benefits, but no inventory equation exists (IJSAEM 2018; PhD thesis sec. 8.3).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine rate is investment divided by utilised time times utilisation rate with overheads (Eq. 6), and setup cost is spread over batch size (Eq. 14) (PhD thesis ch. 5; Procedia CIRP 2018 Eq. 1).
Shared_Capacity_note: AM location configurations (in-port, support vessel, forward base, on-platform) are compared and change logistic delay time, but no machine count, capacity limit or queue is modelled, so platforms never contend for a shared facility (IJSAEM 2018; PhD thesis secs. 7.1, 8.1).
Speed_note: The DSS computes travel time, logistic delay time, downtime and operational availability from distance, platform speed and delay inputs, e.g. availability 96.47% to 99.25% when LDT falls from 661 h to 6.7 h; the IJSAEM paper itself gives these equations only conceptually (PhD thesis Eqs. 16-21, Table 18).

name: Strieby USMC expeditionary metal AM cost-effectiveness analysis
developer: LtCol Stephen F. Strieby, USMC (Naval Postgraduate School, Acquisition Research Program)
description: Cost-effectiveness ratio (total system cost / parts produced over a 5-year life, from representative print times) for four metal AM processes with sensitivity on print and sintering times; recommends hybrid wire-arc AM.
NRE_note: The MCO 4700.4 design, test-fit and approval workflow is described and design time per unique part is named as a using-unit cost, but it is not monetised in the CEA (NPS report, ch. V).
Production_note: Cost per part is purchase price divided by lifetime operating hours times a representative production time per process; material, labour and maintenance are excluded and parts are not specific (NPS report, ch. V, Tables 14-15).
QA_Qual_note: The CEA assumes all parts are approved and all printers meet qualification standards, but the report describes the MCO 4700.4 design, test-fit and approval workflow and recommends a standardised test print to verify printers and set an accepted engineering risk; nothing is costed (NPS report, ch. V-VI).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection and NDT are not discussed or costed anywhere in the CEA (NPS report, full text).
Storage_note: Raw-material inventory is excluded and spares inventory is not modelled; only general reductions in 'logistical supply lines' are expected (NPS report, ch. V-VI).
Shared_Capital_note: Each system's purchase price is amortised over 15,600 lifetime operating hours (12 h/day, 5 days/week, 5 years) and the parts produced in that time, a utilisation and volume assumption; maintenance is assumed zero (NPS report, ch. V).
Shared_Capacity_note: Assumes an in-theatre printer can be tasked by any organisation in the task force with a prioritisation process, but no queue or contention is modelled; a queuing study of XFAB numbers for a service level is future work (NPS report, ch. V-VI).
Speed_note: Representative production time per process sets parts produced and is the main sensitivity, but lead time, readiness and availability are explicitly not computed (NPS report, ch. V).

name: NASA-STD-6030 Additive Manufacturing Requirements for Spaceflight Systems (2021)
developer: NASA (Marshall Space Flight Center; NASA Engineering and Safety Center)
earlier_versions: MSFC-STD-3716 (2017): Marshall standard for L-PBF spaceflight hardware; superseded by NASA-STD-6030 in 2021, which extended it to other AM processes. | MSFC-SPEC-3717 (2017): Marshall specification for control and qualification of L-PBF metallurgical processes; superseded in 2021 by NASA-STD-6030 and companion NASA-SPEC-6033.
description: Classifies each AM part by consequence of failure (Class A/B/C, plus Exempt), then structural demand and a points-based AM risk score (inspectability, removable as-built surfaces, supports, wall thickness) into subclasses A1–A4/B1–B4, and tailors the QA requirements (QMP, material property suite, witness testing, NDE, preproduction articles, part process qualification) to each class.
NRE_note: Requires a registered Qualified Metallurgical Process (QMP, per machine), a Part Production Plan and a Qualified Part Process frozen after the AM Readiness Review, so parameter development and build preparation are mandatory deliverables, but none is costed (NASA-STD-6030 Sec. 4-5, AMR-47/48).
Production_note: No per-part production cost content; the standard is a requirements document (NASA-STD-6030 text).
QA_Qual_note: Prescribes qualification by class in countable form: QMP-A/B/C scaled to part class, a lot-mature material property suite needing at least 5 feedstock lots and 10 build/heat-treat lots for A/B (removed for C), six tensile coupons to qualify Class C, and a preproduction article evaluation for every Class A/B part (AMR-31); no costs are given (NASA-STD-6030 Sec. 4-5).
QA_Insp_note: Sets per-build witness testing by class (independent builds: 6 tensile for A1-B4, 2 for C, plus microstructure, HCF and chemistry by subclass; continuous builds: 4 tensile for A1-B4) and full surface and volumetric NDE for Class A and B (AMR-17, AMR-19), removed for Class C (NASA-STD-6030 Tables 5 and 7).
Storage_note: Inventory reduction is not addressed; serialisation is mentioned only for managing part and inventory risk (NASA-STD-6030 text).
Shared_Capital_note: Spreads one-time qualification across parts without numbers: a QMP registered to a machine can produce parts of equal or lower class, sub-QMPs inherit a parent QMP on equivalent machines, and lot-mature design values apply to parts of all classes built under an equivalently controlled QMP (NASA-STD-6030 Sec. 5, AMR-47/48).
Shared_Capacity_note: Capacity shared across sites or users is not addressed (NASA-STD-6030 text).
Speed_note: Part lead time or availability is not addressed; schedule appears only as programmatic risk when witness results lag production (NASA-STD-6030 text).

name: USAF Structures Bulletin EZ-SB-19-01: Durability and Damage Tolerance Certification for AM Aircraft Structural Metallic Parts
developer: U.S. Air Force, AFLCMC/EZ (Engineering Directorate)
description: Sets durability and damage-tolerance certification requirements for metal AM structural parts by ASIP category (Fracture Critical Traceable/Non-Traceable, Durability Critical, Normal Controls), using equivalent initial damage size at category-specific exceedance probabilities and validated NDI capability. It recommends gaining experience in order of escalating criticality (NC, then DC, then FC).
NRE_note: Requires demonstrated process control (machine qualification, software version control, periodic requalification, strictly controlled parameters), which presumes parameter development, but none of it is costed (EZ-SB-19-01, secs. 2, 3.2).
Production_note: Full bulletin read; cost appears only as stability and supportability criteria ('predictable costs', 'cost-effective' inspection), and part cost is not addressed (EZ-SB-19-01).
QA_Qual_note: Sets class-specific analysis criteria (EIDS exceedance 1e-1 for NC, 1e-3 for DC/FC, 1e-7 for FC damage tolerance), but test frequencies, EIDS test counts and dissection plans are 'as approved by the procuring agency', so the campaign cannot be costed by class (EZ-SB-19-01, secs. 2.2, 3.3, 4).
QA_Insp_note: Requires NDI capability with POD at 95% confidence, coupons from production parts, dissection or validated in-process monitoring, and dimensional verification for all parts, with frequencies left to the procuring agency and no split by category (EZ-SB-19-01, secs. 3.3-3.5).
Storage_note: Full bulletin read; inventory and spares are not addressed (EZ-SB-19-01).
Shared_Capital_note: Recommends gaining experience on NC, then DC, then FC parts, with DC parts pursued once EIDS data mature, so qualification data is built up and reused across parts without costs (EZ-SB-19-01, secs. 2.2, 4).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full bulletin read; machines appear only for traceability and EIDS variation across machines, not capacity sharing (EZ-SB-19-01, secs. 3.7, 4.1).
Speed_note: Full bulletin read; it says only that cost-effective inspection and repair methods should be available or developed 'in a timely manner', and part lead time is not addressed (EZ-SB-19-01).

name: USAF Flight Systems Bulletin EN-FSB-25-01 (Preliminary Qualification Data Requirements for Metallic AM) and Part Family Qualification approach
year: Unknown (bulletin number suggests 2025; the public abstract gives no date)
developer: U.S. Air Force (approach presented by M. Benedict at TMS 2026; issuing office not stated in the public abstract)
description: Separates material qualification from part certification and defines a standard minimum data set for screening new AM processes, materials and vendors on stability, producibility and predictability. It replaces 'point qualification' of each part with 'Part Family Qualification'.
NRE_note: The bulletin explicitly separates material qualification from part certification and covers preliminary data to screen new processes, materials and vendors, so one-time part engineering is outside its documented scope (TMS 2026 abstract).
Production_note: Per-part production cost is outside the documented scope of a qualification-data bulletin (TMS 2026 abstract).
QA_Qual_note: Defines a standard minimum data set to judge material stability, producibility and predictability and whether further qualification investment is worthwhile, and calls point qualification 'slow and expensive', but no costs or test counts are public (TMS 2026 abstract; the bulletin itself is not posted).
QA_Insp_note: Only a conference abstract describes the bulletin and it does not list the data set's contents; an Army RFI cites EN-FSB-25-01 only by number and a USAF vendor-qualification article does not mention it, so whether NDI or CT is required is not established (TMS 2026 abstract; Govly RFI 2026; Military & Aerospace Electronics).
Storage_note: Spare-part shortages are named only as motivation; inventory is outside the documented scope of a qualification-data bulletin (TMS 2026 abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: Moves from requalifying each part after any machine or process change to Part Family Qualification, which spreads qualification across a family of parts; qualitative only (TMS 2026 abstract).
Shared_Capacity_note: Print capacity is outside the documented scope of a qualification-data bulletin (TMS 2026 abstract).
Speed_note: The abstract says AM can overcome lead times of up to years and that Part Family Qualification aims to cut the time of full material qualification, a time-saving claim with no lead time computed (TMS 2026 abstract).

name: NAVSEA AM qualification framework: Guidance letter Ser 05T/2018-024 severity levels, T9074-AX-GIB-010/100 material selection requirements, and PBF/DED Technical Publications
year: 2018 (guidance letter); 2020 (PBF Tech Pub); 2021 (DED Tech Pub, anticipated)
developer: Naval Sea Systems Command (NAVSEA 05T, AM Technical Warrant Holder); DED tech pub developed with NSWC Carderock and EWI
description: Part failure-consequence severity (NAVSEA 5100.12-M Levels 1–7/N/A) determines whether material selection requirements and process/material qualification apply, whether a Technical Data Package is needed, and who approves. The process Tech Pubs then prescribe procedure qualification, part verification builds and a production conformance test plan.
NRE_note: Prescribes one-time engineering deliverables by part class (a NAVSEA-approved TDP for severity Levels 1-6, and an approved DED Procedure before procedure qualification) but puts no cost or effort on them, so it is a requirement rather than a cost term (guidance letter; DED tech pub).
Production_note: The letter says only that AM enables 'cost-effective, on-demand manufacturing of critical parts'; per-part costing is outside the framework, and NAVSUP's separate cost/part tool is being integrated into TDP development (Ser 05T/2018-024; Rettaliata 2020).
QA_Qual_note: Severity level sets the required qualification: Levels 1-5 invoke T9074-AX-GIB-010/100 and process/material qualification, Levels 1-6 a risk assessment that sets the approval authority, and the Tech Pub prescribes countable steps (procedure qualification build, PQTR, sacrificial part verification build with witness coupons, test reports); no costs (Ser 05T/2018-024; Hovanec 2021).
QA_Insp_note: Conformance testing per build is required, NDE test types are set by material group with MIL-STD-2035 Class 1 acceptance, but production NDE and destructive-test schedules are set part by part in each Production Conformance Evaluation Plan rather than by severity class, with no counts or costs (Ser 05T/2018-024; Hovanec 2021).
Storage_note: The guidance letter's documented scope (severity, qualification, approval) does not address inventory (Ser 05T/2018-024).
Shared_Capital_note: Procedure qualification is done once per process/material combination and then applies irrespective of part geometry while essential elements are kept, so qualification is reused across parts, but this is not costed (Hovanec 2021).
Shared_Capacity_note: Neither the guidance letter nor the Tech Pub briefing addresses capacity shared across ships, depots or users (Ser 05T/2018-024; Hovanec 2021).
Speed_note: The letter claims only that AM 'can shorten the design-to-production cycle', with no lead-time or readiness calculation (Ser 05T/2018-024).

name: DNV-ST-B203 Additive manufacturing (Edition 2025-11)
year: 2017 (DNVGL-CG-0197); first ST-B203 edition reported as 2019 (not confirmed); editions Dec 2022 and 2025-11
developer: DNV (formerly DNV GL)
earlier_versions: DNVGL-CG-0197 (2017): class guideline on AM qualification and certification; testing extent set by criticality, no per-category counts; read in full. | DNVGL-ST-B203 Additive manufacturing of metallic parts, first edition (year Unknown): covered two metal AM technologies. | DNV-ST-B203 edition of Dec 2022: added DED-arc, PBF-EB and binder jetting, combined manufacturing, NDT acceptance criteria, and guidance on part families and AMC selection; the 2025-11 edition adds polymers, a CO2 footprint method and grouped part approvals.
description: Assigns parts to AM categories AMC 1–3 by criticality (an informative appendix guides AMC selection). The category sets the qualification route: AMC 1 needs a facility audit and a build process qualification, and AMC 2/3 add part family qualification. Appendices give inspection/test plans and NDT guidance.
NRE_note: The standard has an informative appendix on design of AM parts and build process qualification fixes the build process, but neither is costed (DNV ST-B203 pages).
Production_note: The documented scope (procurement, qualification, quality management, production testing and inspection, plus design and carbon-footprint appendices) contains no cost estimation (DNV ST-B203 pages).
QA_Qual_note: The AM category sets countable qualification steps (AMC 1: facility audit plus at least one BPQ per material; AMC 2/3: plus part family qualification) per DNV certification-services slides, and CG-0197 calls part-by-part certification 'costly, time consuming'; exact AMC criteria and test counts were not seen because the standard is paywalled.
QA_Insp_note: The standard defines inspection and test plans for PBF and DED and NDT acceptance criteria, with quality approaches scaled to part criticality (DNV pages; 2022 release); the class-by-class production testing (C1 visual only; C2/C3 add per-build tensile, impact, surface and volumetric NDT and dimensional checks) rests on Peron, Cantini & Coruzzolo (IFAC 2023), which is closed access and could not be re-opened in this pass.
Storage_note: The standard's documented scope has no inventory element; DNV's release mentions digital spare parts only as a general AM benefit (DNV pages).
Shared_Capital_note: Manufacturers prequalify per facility, per-material BPQ and per part family, and the part-family guidance 'may extend the validity of qualifications' across parts; no numbers (DNV slides; DNV 2022 release).
Shared_Capacity_note: The documented scope does not address capacity shared across sites or users (DNV ST-B203 pages).
Speed_note: The standard has no time or lead-time element; DNV's release mentions AM's lead-time benefit only in general terms (DNV pages).

name: API Standard 20S Additively Manufactured Metallic Components (AM Specification Levels AMSL 1/2/3)
developer: American Petroleum Institute
description: Specifies process qualification and production control for AM metallic components at three AM Specification Levels. Each higher level raises technical, quality and qualification requirements, and the level is assigned by the product specification, purchaser or manufacturer according to consequence of failure, service severity and inspectability.
NRE_note: Summaries say the manufacturer must establish and qualify the machine, parameters, feedstock and post-processing (essential AM variables, aligned with ASME IX QW-600 in the 2nd edition) before production, a prescribed parameter-development activity with no cost (Inspenet summary; World Oil 2025).
Production_note: The documented scope is process qualification, production control, marking and documentation requirements, which plainly excludes per-part cost estimation (Normservis and Techstreet scope listings).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification requirements rise with AMSL, assigned by consequence of failure, service severity and inspectability, and require representative coupons, mechanical testing and metallography, but per-level test counts could not be verified because the full text is paid; the standard may meet the Yes bar (Inspenet summary; scope listings).
QA_Insp_note: NDE methods (RT, UT, PT, MT, CT, dimensional) are named and the 2nd edition adds an NDT annex on how AMSLs apply with example acceptance criteria, but class-specific inspection scope was not verified (Inspenet summary; World Oil 2025).
Storage_note: The scope (process qualification, production, marking, documentation) excludes inventory; spares appear only as candidate applications (scope listings; Inspenet).
Shared_Capital_note: No summary, scope listing or announcement says whether one process qualification can cover several parts or part families, and the full text was not accessible.
Shared_Capacity_note: The scope (process qualification, production control, marking, documentation) excludes capacity shared across sites or users (scope listings).
Speed_note: The requirements scope excludes lead time; shorter supply times near the asset are cited only as motivation in summaries and announcements (Inspenet; World Oil 2025).

name: FAA AM Roadmap and risk-based certification framework (Gorelik briefings)
developer: Federal Aviation Administration (AM National Team; M. Gorelik, Chief Scientist for Fatigue and Damage Tolerance)
description: Ties regulatory scrutiny to part criticality and maps the qualification path to criticality and volume: point-design certification for low-criticality, high-margin parts; part-family qualification as volume grows; model-enabled qualification later. It gives indicative figures for the barrier to entry and qualification timelines.
NRE_note: Process development is lumped into an indicative barrier-to-entry figure (about $1M for equipment alone vs '$10's of M' realistic, also covering qualification, process controls, characterisation, design data and QA/NDI), with no separate NRE term (Gorelik 2016 National Academies deck).
Production_note: Production cost appears only as background (about 50% of operating cost is labour and 20% depreciation, with powder expected to become the largest item), quoted rather than computed by the framework (Gorelik 2016 National Academies deck).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification paths (point design, part family, model-enabled) are mapped to criticality and volume only qualitatively, but the briefing gives building-block specimen counts, cost and time by test level (e.g. 5,000-100,000 coupons, $8-15M, 2 yrs) and alloy-introduction timelines of 10-15 years, not set by part class (Gorelik 2016 deck; FAA REDAC 2017 roadmap).
QA_Insp_note: NDI capability is a top-5 challenge, probabilistic fracture mechanics with inspection POD and zone-based evaluation are proposed, and a research task will develop POD for CT and laser ultrasonics, but no inspection cost or part-class scope is set (Gorelik 2016 deck; FAA REDAC 2017 roadmap).
Storage_note: The briefings are a certification and research framework whose scope excludes parts inventory, and neither deck mentions it (FAA REDAC 2017 roadmap; Gorelik 2016 deck).
Shared_Capital_note: Part-family qualification is proposed as volumes grow, which implies spreading qualification across parts, but no numbers are given (FAA REDAC 2017 roadmap).
Shared_Capacity_note: The framework's certification scope excludes print capacity and neither deck mentions it (FAA REDAC 2017 roadmap; Gorelik 2016 deck).
Speed_note: The only times given are qualification and alloy-introduction timelines; part lead time or availability is outside the framework's scope (Gorelik 2016 deck; FAA REDAC 2017 roadmap).

name: CMU adaptive regulatory framework for metal AM in aviation (Bonnín Roca et al. 2017)
developer: Carnegie Mellon University, Engineering and Public Policy (with Universidade de Lisboa / CMU Portugal)
earlier_versions: Bonnín Roca, Fuchs, Morgan & Vaishnav 2016, 'Policy needed for additive manufacturing' (Nature Materials commentary): earlier call for process science, standards and adaptive regulation that the 2017 paper develops into a framework.
description: Uses metal AM in aviation as a case study to propose adaptive regulation: standards revised periodically, and firms regulated differently according to their technological capabilities. It gives a general framework in which the right regulatory design depends on industry structure, safety requirements and sources of technological uncertainty.
NRE_note: The framework concerns how regulators revise standards and treat firms of differing technological capability; one-time part engineering cost is outside its documented scope (Research Policy 2017 abstract via TU/e and IDEAS records).
Production_note: Per-part production cost is outside the documented scope of a regulatory-design framework (Research Policy 2017 abstract).
QA_Qual_note: Proposes adaptive certification regulation with periodically revised standards and requirements that differ by firm capability, a qualitative framework with no costs or test counts in the abstract (Research Policy 2017 abstract).
QA_Insp_note: Only abstracts could be read (the full paper and the author's 2017 CMU dissertation PDF were not reachable); the work addresses certification standards, so whether it treats inspection or NDE requirements is not established.
Storage_note: Inventory is outside the documented scope of a regulatory-design framework (Research Policy 2017 abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: Only abstracts could be read (full paper and dissertation PDF unreachable); regulating firms by capability could let qualification carry across parts or users, but no source read shows the paper treating this.
Shared_Capacity_note: Print capacity pooling is outside the documented scope of a regulatory-design framework (Research Policy 2017 abstract).
Speed_note: Part lead time or availability is outside the documented scope of a framework for setting certification regulation (Research Policy 2017 abstract).

name: Rapid qualification framework for powder-bed laser AM parts (Honeywell-led DARPA Open Manufacturing work; Peralta et al.)
developer: Honeywell Aerospace-led team (Peralta, Enright, Megahed, Gong, Roybal, Craig) under DARPA Open Manufacturing
description: A probabilistic, risk-based qualification framework that runs ICME models (melt pool CFD, residual stress/distortion FE, microstructure/strength) with Bayesian calibration in a digital loop, adding physical tests only when the digital results do not show acceptable risk. In-situ monitoring and NDE feed the risk calculation.
NRE_note: ICME process models are used to identify the optimum process window and predict residual stress and deformation, narrowing parameter development, but engineering effort is not costed and no effort figures are given (IMMI 2016 full text).
Production_note: Production cost is not addressed anywhere in the paper (IMMI 2016 full text).
QA_Qual_note: A probabilistic risk framework decides when physical tests are needed; the 40% qualification-time, 20% cost and 40% testing reductions and certification-by-analysis rising from 10% to 20% are programme goals, not computed by a cost model, and no dollar figures are given (IMMI 2016 full text).
QA_Insp_note: Pyrometer quality metrics against a 95% limit flag off-nominal layers and X-ray CT/acoustic microscopy outcomes feed the risk calculation, but no inspection cost, scope or sampling plan is set and in-process data alone cannot accept a part (IMMI 2016 full text).
Storage_note: Inventory is not addressed (IMMI 2016 full text).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine capital and its sharing are not addressed; the remark that the framework allows interchangeability of components and AM processes does not describe sharing capital or qualification across parts (IMMI 2016 full text).
Shared_Capacity_note: Capacity is not addressed (IMMI 2016 full text).
Speed_note: The paper claims rapid qualification enables 'faster response to the market demands' and 'rapid procurement of qualified hardware' (40% qualification-time goal), but part lead time is not computed or valued (IMMI 2016 full text).

name: NIST qualification pathways for AM materials, processes and parts (statistical, equivalence-based, model-based, 'qualify-as-you-go')
year: 2014-2025 (project page created March 2014; project completed; page last updated March 2025)
developer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
description: Frames three qualification routes with different testing burdens and develops measurement science (round-robin protocols, a public materials database, validated process models, in-process measurement) to make equivalence and model-based qualification viable and to spread the cost of statistical testing.
NRE_note: The project's documented scope is measurement science for qualification; part design files and run-parameter development are outside it (NIST project page).
Production_note: Production cost is outside the documented qualification scope and is not mentioned (NIST project page).
QA_Qual_note: Compares the testing burden of statistical, equivalence-based and model-based routes in words and cites full empirical qualification as 'many thousands of individual tests, costing millions of dollars and 5 to 15 years', with no model (NIST project page).
QA_Insp_note: 'Qualify as you go' uses pre-, in- and post-process measurements (including dimensional metrology of critical geometries) to show each part meets spec, as a concept with no scope or cost (NIST project page).
Storage_note: Inventory is outside the documented qualification scope and is not mentioned (NIST project page).
Shared_Capital_note: Aims to 'distribute the burden of testing' through round-robin protocols and a public materials database many contributors can add to, a qualitative sharing of qualification cost (NIST project page).
Shared_Capacity_note: Machine capacity is outside the documented qualification scope and is not mentioned (NIST project page).
Speed_note: Part lead time is outside the documented scope; the only time figure is the 5-15 years of empirical qualification (NIST project page).

name: Seifi et al. qualification and certification pathway review (JOM, 2017)
developer: Seifi, Salem, Beuth, Harrysson, Lewandowski (2016); Seifi, Gorelik, Waller, Hrabe, Shamsaei, Daniewicz, Lewandowski (2017)
earlier_versions: Seifi et al. 2016, Overview of Materials Qualification Needs for Metal Additive Manufacturing (JOM 68, doi:10.1007/s11837-015-1810-0): companion review; source of the AMS4999A test counts and the 'millions of dollars, up to 15 years' figure.
description: Compares statistically based qualification (e.g., AMS4999A), model-based qualification and ICME 'qualify-as-you-go' schemes for metal AM. The 2017 paper maps the standards landscape needed for a Q&C pathway and cites NASA's AM risk criteria (inspectability, surface removal, wall thickness).
NRE_note: Full texts read; design or engineering effort is not addressed (JOM 2016; NIST copy of JOM 2017).
Production_note: Full texts read; lowering production costs is named only as a general challenge, and part cost is not addressed (JOM 2016; NIST copy of JOM 2017).
QA_Qual_note: Gives costable counts for one route (AMS4999A: >50 tensile results per principal build direction for source qualification, >12 per direction on production parts) and says legacy qualification may cost millions and take up to 15 years, with any non-minor deviation triggering requalification; it is a review, not a model (JOM 2016).
QA_Insp_note: Discusses micro-CT and X-ray CT as leading NDT options, the lack of AM NDT consensus standards and NASA's inspectability risk criterion, with no costs or class-specific scope (JOM 2016; NIST copy of JOM 2017).
Storage_note: Full texts read; spares appear only as items needing defined NDT, and inventory is not addressed (NIST copy of JOM 2017).
Shared_Capital_note: The 2016 review names the lack of shared knowledge and materials test results across the AM community, and proprietary machine controls, as barriers to qualification, but pooling of qualification data is not costed (JOM 2016).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full texts read; capacity is not addressed (JOM 2016; NIST copy of JOM 2017).
Speed_note: The 2017 review claims AM could make essential parts on demand in days rather than months, as motivation only, with no time model (NIST copy of JOM 2017, p. 2).

name: Cost model for the economic evaluation of in-situ monitoring tools in metal AM (Colosimo, Cavalli, Grasso)
developer: Politecnico di Milano
description: A per-part cost model comparing as-is production, in-situ monitoring, and monitoring with diagnosis. It uses scrap fraction, false-alarm and missed-detection rates, inspection time and monitoring equipment cost to find the scrap rates at which monitoring pays off, including a make-or-buy variant.
NRE_note: Build preparation (operator plus workstation/software rate times build-prep time, divided by parts per build) and machine setup are costed per build, but CAD development cost is explicitly excluded and there is no parameter-development term (Polimi author manuscript, Eqs. 9-10).
Production_note: Computes per-part cost from material, pre-process, LPBF process and post-process terms (e.g., 212.74 vs 192.99 EUR/part as-is vs monitoring), validated within about 10% of a service-bureau benchmark (Polimi author manuscript).
QA_Qual_note: The full paper has no qualification or certification cost term; certified medical materials are mentioned only as background (Polimi author manuscript).
QA_Insp_note: Per-part post-process inspection (operator plus metrology rate times inspection time, visual or CMM) is a cost term, combined with scrap fraction, Type I/II monitoring errors and 50k/150k EUR monitoring hardware to find break-even scrap fractions of about 0.02-0.2; CT is named as an optional extra and not included (Polimi author manuscript).
Storage_note: The full paper has no inventory, storage or holding-cost terms (Polimi author manuscript).
Shared_Capital_note: The L-PBF system is charged at an hourly rate from straight-line depreciation plus maintenance and space (EUR 600k over 5 years at a 55% load factor) and build cost is divided by parts per build, so machine capital is amortised into per-part cost (Polimi author manuscript).
Shared_Capacity_note: Capacity shared across sites or customers is not modelled; the make-or-buy variant only blends in-house and service-bureau cost by the fraction outsourced, with no capacity or lead-time effect (Polimi author manuscript, Eq. 19).
Speed_note: The model computes average production time per part (pre-process, process and post-process, including scrapped builds) and annual throughput (about 4,585 vs 4,821 parts/year in the dental case), but has no lead time, delivery or value of availability (Polimi author manuscript, Eqs. 16-17).

name: Process-based cost estimation model for metal AM spare parts with explicit qualification-test line items (Sheikh et al.)
developer: Hamad Bin Khalifa University (Sheikh, Hadid, Padmanabhan, Elomri, Kerbache, Alabtah, Khraisheh)
description: Total part cost is the sum of design, material, manufacturing (print, debind, sinter), post-processing and 'part qualification' cost. The qualification term sums per-part tests for dimensions, corrosion, strength, hardness and density.
NRE_note: Design cost is an explicit term: 3D-scanner use (initial cost over annual usage hours times scan time), software licence spread over parts produced, and designer time times rate, $80-220 per part in the cases (IEOM full text, Eqs. 2-3, Table 3).
Production_note: Per-part cost is built from material (metal and ceramic rod weight times price), printing (setup labour, depreciation, maintenance and energy times print time), debinding, sintering and post-processing (heat treatment, machining, finishing) (IEOM full text, Eqs. 4-19).
QA_Qual_note: The 'part qualification' term is a flat per-part lump of test fees (dimensional $30, corrosion $50, strength $40, hardness $25, density $20); there is no material or process qualification campaign or approval (IEOM full text, Eq. 20, Table 3).
QA_Insp_note: Per-part test costs are explicit line items totalling $120-165 per part, about 11-20% of part cost; how the unit fees were derived is not explained (IEOM full text, Table 3).
Storage_note: Inventory or stock is not mentioned anywhere in the full paper (IEOM full text).
Shared_Capital_note: Printer and furnace capital enter as flat depreciation per hour times processing time with no utilisation, batch or volume input; only the 3D scanner is spread over annual usage hours (IEOM full text, Eqs. 3, 7-12).
Shared_Capacity_note: Capacity, batching and distributed production are not modelled; the conclusion notes economies of scale are not accounted for (IEOM full text).
Speed_note: Lead time is not modelled; downtime and lead-time reduction appear only in the introduction and literature review (IEOM full text).

name: ASTM E3166-20e1 Standard Guide for Nondestructive Examination of Metal Additively Manufactured Aerospace Parts After Build
developer: ASTM Committee E07
earlier_versions: ASTM E3166-20 (2020): original edition, now listed as historical; reissued as E3166-20e1 with an editorial change that the ASTM page does not describe.
description: Surveys established and emerging NDT methods (CT, eddy current, optical metrology, penetrant, process-compensated resonance testing, radiography, thermography, ultrasonics) against AM flaw types, with a method-versus-flaw table and factors for selecting methods.
NRE_note: The scope (Sec. 1) covers post-build NDT methods only; design files and process parameters are outside it, with process control assigned to ASTM F42 (Sec. 1.12) (ASTM scope page).
Production_note: The scope covers selection and application of NDT methods, not production cost (ASTM scope page).
QA_Qual_note: Excludes control of input materials, equipment and processes (Sec. 1.12), fracture-critical part inspection requirements (1.13) and accept/reject criteria (1.14) (ASTM scope page).
QA_Insp_note: Surveys CT, ET, PT, PCRT, RT, IRT, UT and optical metrology against AM flaw types to support method selection, but recommends no course of action (Sec. 1.11), sets no scope by part class (parts classed only by processing state, 1.6) and gives no costs (ASTM scope page).
Storage_note: Inventory is outside the documented NDT-method scope (ASTM scope page).
Shared_Capital_note: Equipment cost and sharing are outside the documented NDT-method scope (ASTM scope page).
Shared_Capacity_note: Production capacity is outside the documented NDT-method scope (ASTM scope page).
Speed_note: Lead time and availability are outside the documented NDT-method scope (ASTM scope page).

name: In-situ NDE (INDE) with probability-of-detection framework for L-PBF (ORNL; Snow et al.)
developer: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (Snow, Scime, Ziabari, Fisher, Paquit)
description: Detects 200–1000 µm subsurface flaws from fused process-monitoring data using machine learning, with XCT as ground truth, and generates POD/PFA curves and an a90/95 metric following NDE practice, so in-situ monitoring can be assessed as an inspection method.
NRE_note: The documented scope is in-situ flaw detection from fused process-monitoring data validated against XCT, which plainly excludes design-file or parameter-development cost (ORNL abstract).
Production_note: The documented scope is flaw detection and POD/PFA assessment, which plainly excludes per-part production costing (ORNL abstract).
QA_Qual_note: The abstract frames the method against the current qualification paradigm for critical L-PBF parts, which relies on expensive NDI and limits use cases, and the ORNL release quotes Snow that lacking a POD number makes parts hard to qualify and certify; no qualification cost or effort is modelled (ORNL abstract; EurekAlert release).
QA_Insp_note: Detection capability is quantified (POD/PFA curves, a90/95, flaws ~200-1000 um) but inspection cost is only claimed qualitatively as a 'less expensive alternative' to ex-situ XCT, with no cost or time figures (ORNL abstract; EurekAlert release).
Storage_note: The documented scope is an in-process flaw-detection method, which plainly excludes inventory (ORNL abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: The documented scope is flaw detection, which plainly excludes machine capital or its sharing (ORNL abstract).
Shared_Capacity_note: The documented scope is flaw detection on single builds, which plainly excludes pooled print capacity (ORNL abstract).
Speed_note: The documented scope is flaw detection; the release only says conventional evaluation demands more time and labour, and no lead time or availability is computed (ORNL abstract; EurekAlert release).

name: VEXTEC VPS-MICRO model-assisted AM certification (AFWERX SBIR; AFRL QUASAR)
developer: VEXTEC Corporation
description: Probabilistic microstructure- and defect-based fatigue software. It aims to predict EIDS distributions and part performance from specimen-level data so that part-level testing can be limited to validation ('risk-based certification').
NRE_note: VEXTEC lists 'AM Process Development' as a use, runs virtual sensitivity studies of build parameters on microstructure and claims 'significant cost/time savings', but engineering effort is not costed (vextec.com AM page; America Makes TRX webinar 2021).
Production_note: The AM page says VPS-MICRO can optimise post-build selective machining, which it says can be up to 20% of part cost, but the tool predicts fatigue risk and computes no part cost (vextec.com AM page and AM news feed).
QA_Qual_note: Model-assisted certification combines limited physical testing with fatigue simulation so parts are tested only when confidence is high, and a Phase III effort demonstrated reduced testing to qualify an LPBF component, but no test, cost or time reduction is quantified (vextec.com AM page; TRX webinar 2021).
QA_Insp_note: The SBIR framework links in-process monitoring and non-destructive part evaluation data to fatigue prediction, and the deck names NDE and post-process inspection as a cost driver, but no inspection cost or scope is set (TRX webinar 2021; vextec.com AM page).
Storage_note: VPS-MICRO is fatigue-performance prediction software; inventory is outside its documented scope (vextec.com software and AM pages).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine capital and its sharing are outside the documented scope of a fatigue-prediction tool; the deck names machine-specific allowables databases only as a burden of current practice (vextec.com software page; TRX webinar 2021).
Shared_Capacity_note: Print capacity is outside the documented scope of a fatigue-prediction tool (vextec.com software and AM pages).
Speed_note: VEXTEC says the testing burden 'has direct impacts on both the schedule and cost of AM part availability' and that its approach cuts long lead times and gives early confidence, but no lead time is computed (vextec.com AM news feed; TRX webinar 2021).

name: NASA-CMU Additive Manufacturing Ecosystem for qualification of AM processes and materials in aviation
developer: NASA Ames Research Center (K. Datta) and Carnegie Mellon University (A. Rollett)
description: A six-project research ecosystem for qualifying AM machines, which then supports certification of part production. It names qualification difficulty and cost as the main barriers.
NRE_note: The 'AM Flaw Management' and 'Qualification Aware Process Maps' projects develop processing windows with multiple qualified parameter points, a parameter-development activity, but no cost is given (TechPort data sheet).
Production_note: Names technology cost as a main barrier, notes post-processing can cost as much as fabrication, and targets lower manufacturing cost for short runs and replacement parts, with no cost model (TechPort data sheet).
QA_Qual_note: Builds a qualification ecosystem (porosity-limited processing windows, fatigue data, a data-driven qualification model, supplier training tiers) that links machine and process qualification to part certification, without costs (TechPort data sheet).
QA_Insp_note: The data sheet sets porosity limits and measures porosity effects on fatigue for qualification data but does not say whether per-part inspection is addressed, and no project outputs were found (TechPort data sheet).
Storage_note: None of the six listed projects (flaw management, process maps, post-processing, database analytics, training, scaling to production) addresses inventory (TechPort data sheet).
Shared_Capital_note: That machine qualification spreads across many certified parts and small suppliers is implied but not stated, and no machine cost or sharing is given (TechPort data sheet).
Shared_Capacity_note: The 'Scaling to Production' project configures production cells for hundreds to thousands of parts per year, but capacity shared across sites or users is not among the listed projects (TechPort data sheet).
Speed_note: Anticipates shorter time-to-production as a benefit, with no lead-time figures or model (TechPort data sheet).

name: 3DXpert (build preparation with print time and cost estimation)
year: Estimation feature documented 2019; 'Cost estimation and reports' still listed Feb 2026
developer: Developed by 3D Systems (TCT ties it to the 2015 Cimatron acquisition). On 1 Oct 2025, 3D Systems agreed to sell 3DXpert and Oqton MOS to Hubb Global Holdings, with closing expected Q4 2025. 3D Systems' FY2025 10-K says it 'divested of the 3DXpert business in 2025'. Feb 2026 product material is issued by Oqton Inc.
description: Metal AM build-prep software (part positioning, supports, lattices, print strategies). Its Estimation Parameters dialog computes print time from published build rates (part/support/lattice rates, recoat time). It then costs material per cm3 and machine time at an hourly rate, reporting volume, time and cost for parts, supports and lattices plus total powder required.
NRE_note: The software performs build preparation (positioning, supports, print strategies, 'Automation, Quotation & Setup'), but no preparation, setup or engineering cost field exists in the estimation dialog (2019 estimation guide; oqton.com/3dxpert).
Production_note: Build cost is computed from material cost per cm3 for parts, supports and lattices plus machine time cost (hourly rate x total time from published build rates and recoat time); labour, setup and post-processing are not included and cost is totalled by category rather than allocated per part (2019 estimation guide).
QA_Qual_note: The AM Inspection feature is listed as 'Inspect, Adjust, Certify for future comparisons, generate reports', a build-certification step without any qualification costing (oqton.com/3dxpert).
QA_Insp_note: Build Inspection is listed to 'inspect and correct anomalies and defects' in running builds, but inspection is not costed in the estimation dialog (oqton.com/3dxpert; 2019 estimation guide).
Storage_note: 3DXpert is build-preparation software and the product page places inventory functions in the separate Manufacturing OS, so inventory is outside its documented scope (oqton.com/3dxpert).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine cost enters only as an hourly rate x total build time, with no amortisation, utilisation or per-part allocation of multi-part builds (2019 estimation guide).
Shared_Capacity_note: Documented scope is preparing individual builds; the product page describes no fleet, scheduling or multi-site capacity functions (oqton.com/3dxpert).
Speed_note: Print time is estimated from part, support and lattice build rates plus between-layer recoat time, a print-time-only model; lead time or availability is not computed (2019 estimation guide).

name: Ansys Additive Prep (Cost Estimator)
developer: Ansys, now part of Synopsys (ansys.com product pages redirect to ansys.synopsys.com); Additive Prep runs inside Ansys SpaceClaim
description: Build-preparation tool whose Cost Estimator prices the whole build job. Machine cost comes from build time (laser path and jump times plus recoater time per layer). Material is powder volume over the baseplate area times part height, times density, plus a material-loss %. A profit margin is added. Output is an 'Estimated Total Price' exportable to CSV.
NRE_note: Orientation, supports and scan-pattern build files are generated in the tool, but the preparation effort is not costed (Ansys help 2024 R2).
Production_note: The Cost Estimator prices a build job from scan-path build time times machine cost, powder volume times density plus a loss %, and profit, giving an Estimated Total Price; no labour, post-processing or per-part split is documented (Ansys help 2024 R2).
QA_Qual_note: The cost-estimator help lists only machine, material and profit terms, and the documented five-step build-preparation scope does not include qualification (Ansys help 2024 R2).
QA_Insp_note: The cost-estimator help lists only machine, material and profit terms, with no inspection step (Ansys help 2024 R2).
Storage_note: Additive Prep prepares and prices single build jobs, so inventory is outside its documented scope (Ansys help 2024 R2).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine cost (the largest contributor) is charged per build hour from the SLM machine profile and covers all parts added to the build volume, but no amortisation, utilisation or per-part allocation inputs are documented (Ansys help 2024 R2).
Shared_Capacity_note: Additive Prep prices one build job on one machine and does not address capacity shared across sites or users (Ansys help 2024 R2).
Speed_note: Build time is computed from laser path, jump and recoater times, but only to price machine time and rank orientations; no lead time or value of earlier delivery is output (Ansys help 2024 R2).

name: Ansys Granta Selector (Additive Manufacturing data)
year: Senvol integration announced May 2016; AM Edition in CES Selector 2019; AM data still listed in 2026 R1 help
developer: Granta Design (now Ansys Granta Selector; ansys.com redirects to ansys.synopsys.com); AM machine/material data from Senvol LLC
earlier_versions: CES Selector with Senvol data (May 2016): Granta Design first integrated Senvol machine and material data (550+ machines, 700+ materials) into CES Selector and GRANTA MI. | CES Selector 2019 Additive Manufacturing Edition (2019): Granta Design release covering >950 AM machines, >1,700 materials and >190 conventional equivalents from the updated Senvol Database; now sold as Ansys Granta Selector.
description: Materials/process selection software. The AM Edition embeds Senvol machine and material data. Users can filter machines by process, manufacturer, required part size, cost and compatible materials, and chart AM properties against conventional equivalents to judge whether AM is viable. A generic Part Cost Estimator gives relative costs (+/-20%) across processes, but AM coverage is not documented.
NRE_note: The help documents a materials and process selection database with Senvol AM machine/material data and test data; redesign, digitisation and parameter-development effort are outside that documented scope (2026 R1 help).
Production_note: The Part Cost Estimator gives relative part cost (+/-20%) from material, mass, batch size and ProcessUniverse process records, but neither its help page nor the ProcessUniverse or AM data pages say AM processes are covered, and the worked exercise uses only moulding, rolling and pressing (2026 R1 help).
QA_Qual_note: The AM data provide machine/material records and tensile, creep, fatigue and fracture test data for Ni and Ti AM alloys, but the tool does not gate, plan or cost qualification, which is outside its documented selection scope (2026 R1 help; 3DPI 2016).
QA_Insp_note: The documented selection, data and cost-estimator functions do not address per-part inspection or NDT (2026 R1 help).
Storage_note: The help index and pages show no inventory or stock feature; materials and process selection excludes inventory (2026 R1 help).
Shared_Capital_note: AM machines can be filtered by cost (purchase price) as a selection criterion; the Part Cost Estimator takes load factor and capital write-off time, but its coverage of AM processes is not documented (3DPI 2016; 2026 R1 help).
Shared_Capacity_note: No capacity, site or network feature appears in the help; production capacity is outside the selection scope (2026 R1 help).
Speed_note: The help index shows no lead-time feature and the AM data page mentions no lead time or build rate; lead time is outside the selection scope (2026 R1 help).

name: Ansys Granta MI:Additive Manufacturing
developer: Granta Design (acquired by Ansys; ansys.com product pages now redirect to ansys.synopsys.com)
description: Enterprise database package for AM data. It stores process parameters and logged build data, links supplier information to material batches, and exports properties to simulation. Since 2016 it also exposes the Senvol machine/material database next to a company's own AM data for search and comparison.
NRE_note: The 2017 update offers graphical tools that plot properties against process parameters to 'modify process parameters for optimal results', supporting parameter development, but no engineering effort or cost is tracked or estimated (TenLinks Feb 2017 release).
Production_note: The 2015 and 2017 releases and the 2016 Senvol integration release describe data capture and machine/material selection with no per-part cost estimate, and no product documentation was found to show whether part cost is held or computed.
QA_Qual_note: Captures process parameters, build logs, batch traceability and test data to 'support the qualification and certification' of AM parts and can generate automated qualification reports, but qualification effort or cost is not modelled (CIMdata 2015; TenLinks 2017).
QA_Insp_note: Captures testing and inspection results with build data, and the Sandia AM schema on Granta MI holds visual, NDT and CT inspection and mechanical test records, but inspection cost or class-specific scope is not computed (CIMdata 2015; Sandia SAND2016-8961PE slides).
Storage_note: A materials and process data management system, so spare-part inventory is outside its documented scope (CIMdata 2015; TenLinks 2017).
Shared_Capital_note: Senvol machine data lets users compare AM machines by process, part size and cost as a selection criterion, with no amortisation, utilisation or sharing calculation (3DPI May 2016).
Shared_Capacity_note: As a materials data management and selection system it does not address production capacity shared across sites or users (CIMdata 2015; 3DPI 2016).
Speed_note: As a data management system it does not estimate part lead time or the value of availability; the only time claim is faster time-to-market for AM development (3dprint.com 2015).

name: Altair Inspire Print3D
developer: Altair Engineering (solidThinking unit at launch); altair.com product pages now redirect to siemens.com (ownership change not separately verified here)
description: SLM design and process-simulation tool. It generates and edits supports with the part, picks orientations that minimize supports, runs a thermo-mechanical solver (build, cooling, cutting, springback), flags deformation, overheating and delamination, and exports a print-ready file. No cost-estimation function was found in fetched sources.
NRE_note: The SLM workflow offers build-preparation and parameter work (orientation, supports, a calibration coupon per material and parameter set, distortion-compensated STL export), but none of this effort is costed (Inspire 2022.2 help, SLM, Orientation, Calibration topics).
Production_note: The Inspire 2022.2 help for all nine SLM tools (Print Part, Printer, Orientation, Support, Slice, Export, Calibration, Analyze, Compensation) describes no cost estimate, and the Printer tool takes no cost rate (Inspire 2022.2 help).
QA_Qual_note: The SLM help describes thermo-mechanical simulation and simulation calibration only and does not address material, process or part qualification (Inspire 2022.2 help, SLM, Calibration, Analyze topics).
QA_Insp_note: The SLM help covers no inspection or testing of printed parts; the only measurement is of a calibration coupon used to tune the simulation (Inspire 2022.2 help, Calibration topic).
Storage_note: Inspire Print3D is a design and print-simulation tool for single SLM builds, so inventory is outside its documented scope (Inspire 2022.2 help, SLM topic).
Shared_Capital_note: The Printer tool sets bed size and laser and recoating parameters only, with no machine cost, rate or utilisation, and no cost function exists in the module (Inspire 2022.2 help, Printer topic).
Shared_Capacity_note: As a single-build design and simulation tool it does not address capacity shared across sites or users (Inspire 2022.2 help, SLM topic).
Speed_note: Orientation optimisation estimates and minimises print time (a Time heatmap, with recoating time as a printer input), but lead time or availability is not computed (Inspire 2022.2 help, Orientation and Printer topics).

name: Hexagon Simufact Additive (print cost estimation; part of HxGN Additive Manufacturing Suite)
year: Cost estimation added in Simufact Additive 2020 (announced Nov 2019); bundled in HxGN AM Suite Feb 2024
developer: Simufact Engineering / Hexagon Manufacturing Intelligence
description: Metal AM process simulation. It predicts and compensates distortion, residual stress and temperature. Its PBF Process and Defect Analysis module anticipates warping, porosity and incomplete fusion. It also estimates print-job costs for single components or assemblies, extending to downstream cutting, machining, drilling and grinding, to pick the best build variant.
NRE_note: Distortion compensation, 'right first-time' printing and the PDA module that 'significantly reduce[s] trial-and-error' in parameter tuning support parameter development, but this effort is not costed (Nexus product page).
Production_note: Print-job cost is estimated for single components or assemblies, including subsequent cutting, machining, drilling and grinding, and used to pick the best build variant, but the cost inputs (machine rate, material, labour) are not publicly documented, so the per-part build-up cannot be confirmed (Hexagon 2019 release; MSC 2020 release note).
QA_Qual_note: The Nexus page and 2019/2020 releases describe defect prediction (porosity, incomplete fusion) but never mention qualification or certification, and no product documentation was publicly reachable.
QA_Insp_note: The Nexus page and releases do not mention inspection, and no product documentation was publicly reachable.
Storage_note: Simufact Additive is process-simulation software with build-job costing, so inventory is outside its documented scope (Nexus product page).
Shared_Capital_note: The releases say print-job costs are estimated and compared across build variants, but whether a machine rate, utilisation or parts-per-plate allocation is used is not public.
Shared_Capacity_note: As build-process simulation software its documented scope does not include capacity shared across sites or users (Nexus product page).
Speed_note: The Nexus page speaks only generally of 'saving time', and the releases do not say whether build time or lead time is output.

name: Fieldmade Digital Inventory software with NOMAD deployable micro-factories
year: 2016-present; Equinor digital-inventory project 2019-2020; Nomad LW UK distribution Jan 2023; 1000 Kelvin AMAIZE bundle Jan 2024
developer: Fieldmade AS (Norway; founded 2016 as a spin-off of the Norwegian Defence Research Establishment, FFI)
description: Deployable container micro-factories (NOMAD 01/02/03; Nomad LW) paired with Digital Inventory software. The software gives access to aggregated print-ready files with metadata so parts can be printed at the point of need. Fieldmade also offers 3D scanning/reverse engineering and lists 'qualification assessment and control' as an expertise. The 1000 Kelvin AMAIZE AI print-recipe software is bundled with NOMAD.
NRE_note: Fieldmade offers part design and digitisation (reverse engineering) as a service and bundles 1000 Kelvin AMAIZE to auto-correct print recipes, but no NRE is costed (company site; 3DPrint.com 2024).
Production_note: The digital-inventory platform (spun out as Fieldnode in 2020) lets users 'obtain quotes, lead times, and offers' from different vendors, but no cost-estimation method or inputs are documented (Fieldnode site; company site).
QA_Qual_note: Under 'QA of all parts' the digital-inventory platform 'enables OEMs to pre-select quality standards for parts', a listed requirement with no qualification steps or cost; NOMAD's 2025 testing integration makes no qualification claim (Fieldnode site; 3DPrint.com 2025).
QA_Insp_note: Since 2025 NOMAD integrates Plastometrex PLX-Benchtop indentation testing to check mechanical properties of printed metal parts on site, but inspection is not costed (3DPrint.com 2025).
Storage_note: A parts repository of print-ready designs is meant to replace stocked spares and reduce inventory build-up, and Equinor expects savings 'through reducing inventory', but no stock or holding cost is computed (Fieldnode site; Techstars 2020; Equinor article).
Shared_Capital_note: No source read (company site, Fieldnode site, press) says whether machine investment or utilisation is modelled.
Shared_Capacity_note: Deployable micro-factories put capacity forward, and the digital inventory connects end-users, IP holders and manufacturers ('improved global reach through manufacturing networks') so a file can be printed at different sites, but no capacity or lead-time model is described (Fieldnode site; Techstars 2020; Equinor article).
Speed_note: Vendor lead times are collected with quotes on the platform, and press claims print, test and install 'in just hours' and 'drastically' shorter lead times for Equinor, but no lead time is computed (Fieldnode site; 3DPrint.com 2025; Equinor article).

name: SPEE3D TwinSPEE3D (cold spray toolpath and printability software)
year: Toolpath algorithm upgrade 2020; TwinSPEE3D listed on DirectIndustry (undated); XSPEE3D fall 2022; Expeditionary Manufacturing Unit May 2024
developer: SPEE3D (Australia)
description: Proprietary software for SPEE3D cold spray printers. It automatically generates print or coating toolpaths, identifies unfeasible part features and suggests design modifications, and simulates the full print before production. No part-screening service, parts catalogue, or cost/lead-time estimator was found for SPEE3D.
NRE_note: Automatic toolpath generation for printing or coating, flags for unfeasible features with suggested design changes, and a full print simulation cut build-preparation effort, but none of it is costed (DirectIndustry TwinSPEE3D listing; IMCRC 2020).
Production_note: The vendor listing and IMCRC article mention no cost, material-usage or price output, and no SPEE3D product documentation or catalogue could be opened, so a cost function cannot be confirmed or ruled out (DirectIndustry listing; IMCRC 2020).
QA_Qual_note: The vendor listing does not mention qualification, and no product documentation could be read (DirectIndustry listing).
QA_Insp_note: The listing describes print simulation to catch anomalies before production but not inspection or testing, and no documentation could be read (DirectIndustry listing).
Storage_note: TwinSPEE3D is toolpath and print-simulation software, so inventory is outside its documented scope (DirectIndustry listing).
Shared_Capital_note: The listing and IMCRC article do not say whether machine cost or utilisation is considered, and no documentation could be read (DirectIndustry listing; IMCRC 2020).
Shared_Capacity_note: As toolpath software for a single printer it does not address capacity shared across sites or users (DirectIndustry listing).
Speed_note: The listing describes a full print simulation and IMCRC quotes unquantified user time savings in toolpath generation, but neither says whether print time or lead time is estimated (DirectIndustry listing; IMCRC 2020).

name: Markforged Digital Forge (Eiger / Eiger Fleet with Digital Part Inventory; Digital Source)
year: Eiger Fleet Sep 2021; Digital Source Sep 2023; 'Digital Part Inventory' listed on Eiger page 2026
developer: Markforged (Waltham, MA); acquired by Nano Dimension (closed 25 Apr 2025)
description: Cloud print-prep and fleet platform. Eiger Fleet gives centralized control of distributed printers, users and a digital parts inventory (RBAC, SSO, API) and tracks KPIs for time and cost savings. Digital Source lets OEMs upload designs with locked process settings and encrypted build instructions, licensed to customers or approved print-service providers for on-demand 'manufacturer-certified' parts.
NRE_note: One-click automated print prep, and under Digital Source the OEM rather than the user prepares and locks process settings; NRE is not costed (Eiger page; Digital Source release 2023).
Production_note: Eiger computes a per-part cost when a part is sliced, but it is material cost only (labour and energy are planned), and the ROI dashboard sets the alternative cost at a flat 10x the Markforged cost (Markforged ROI tools blog).
QA_Qual_note: Digital Source lets vendors lock printing process requirements so users receive 'manufacturer-certified parts on demand', but no qualification cost or effort is modelled (Digital Source release 2023).
QA_Insp_note: The Eiger page lists 'quality control via automated part scanning plus intuitive measurement and reporting', but inspection is not costed (Eiger page).
Storage_note: Eiger has a digital part inventory and Digital Source claims 'reduced inventory costs', but stock effects are not computed (Eiger page; Digital Source release 2023).
Shared_Capital_note: The ROI dashboard tracks savings across the cloud-connected printer fleet and a separate Utilization Dashboard tracks printer utilisation, but printer capital never enters the cost, which is material only (Markforged ROI tools blog).
Shared_Capacity_note: Eiger Fleet manages distributed printers and a Utilization Dashboard reports printer utilisation and print time, and Digital Source licenses printing at approved service providers, but there is no queue or lead-time effect (Markforged ROI tools blog; Eiger page; Digital Source release 2023).
Speed_note: Digital Source claims on-site printing 'brings down the time it takes to receive the part', but the ROI tools compute cost savings only, not lead time or downtime (Digital Source release 2023; Markforged ROI tools blog).

name: AMPOWER Additive Manufacturing Cost Calculator
developer: AMPOWER (AM consultancy, ampower.eu)
description: Total-cost-of-ownership calculator. Inputs are part material, dimensions, volume, complexity, quantity and build utilization; outputs are cost per part broken down by process-chain step. Covers technician labor (machine prep, unpacking, support removal, optional data prep), heat treatment and consumables, all overridable. Also gives lead time per part, cost vs 1-10,000 parts/yr, service-bureau market price ranges, and side-by-side comparison of technologies.
NRE_note: Optional digital data-preparation time and cost is included as labour, but there is no reverse engineering, redesign or parameter development (AMPOWER product page).
Production_note: Per-part cost is broken down along the process chain (EUR/ccm or EUR/kg) from material, complexity, labour, heat treatment, consumables and pre/post steps (AMPOWER product page).
QA_Qual_note: The shop page lists the process-chain steps (material, data preparation, machine setup, printing, curing, unpacking, sintering, heat treatment) without qualification, but the Excel tool is user-customisable and its documentation is not public (AMPOWER shop and tools pages).
QA_Insp_note: The listed process-chain steps include no inspection step, but the tools page says the calculator is fully customisable with own processes, so whether inspection can be costed is not established (AMPOWER shop and tools pages).
Storage_note: The calculator's documented scope is per-part cost, production time and throughput by technology and annual quantity, which excludes inventory holding (AMPOWER product page).
Shared_Capital_note: Per-part cost depends on how well the build volume is utilised and on annual quantity (1-10,000/yr), with machine investment named as a main cost driver (AMPOWER product page).
Shared_Capacity_note: Annual throughput is output for production planning, so machine capacity is modelled, but there is no pooling across sites or users and no effect on lead time (AMPOWER product page).
Speed_note: The calculator outputs production time per part broken down along its process chain (data preparation to heat treatment), a partial time model that excludes queueing, inspection and delivery (AMPOWER product and shop pages).

name: Ulu-Huang-Kara-Whitefoot (CMU) concurrent structure + process-parameter optimization for minimum-cost metal AM
developer: E. Ulu, R. Huang, L. B. Kara, K. S. Whitefoot (Carnegie Mellon University, Mechanical Engineering)
description: Couples a process-based cost model (material with 1% scrap, machine investment and maintenance amortised over 7 yr at 7,000 h/yr, energy, labour, 3.5% reject factor) with SIMP topology optimisation. Beam power is chosen per element, so structure and process parameters are optimised together for minimum cost under compliance constraints. Concurrent optimisation cuts cost by up to ~15% and build time by ~21% vs. structure-only optimisation.
NRE_note: Setup time is a constant part of the costed build time (machine and labour per hour), but design effort, build preparation and parameter development are not costed; costs not affected by design or process variables are ignored (author PDF).
Production_note: Per-part cost from build time (scan passes, power, velocity), material with 1% scrap, energy and labour at $26/h, e.g. bracket $675 to $575; post-processing is excluded (author PDF, Table 2-3).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification is not addressed (author PDF).
QA_Insp_note: A single 3.5% reject-rate factor is defined as covering parts rejected in quality control and destructive testing; there are no separate inspection or test line items (author PDF, Table 2).
Storage_note: Inventory is not addressed (author PDF).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine investment ($1.1M) and maintenance are amortised over 7 years at a fixed 7,000 h/yr per hour of production time, while packing, batch size and production volume are explicitly excluded (author PDF, Table 2).
Shared_Capacity_note: Capacity, queues or multiple sites are not addressed (author PDF).
Speed_note: Build time (setup, sintering, powder delivery, cooling) is computed and reported, e.g. 21% faster builds with concurrent optimisation, but this is print time only and is not linked to lead time or availability (author PDF).

name: Nie-Jung-Kara-Whitefoot (CMU) part-consolidation optimization for minimum production cost/time with metal AM
developer: Z. Nie, S. Jung, L. B. Kara, K. S. Whitefoot (Carnegie Mellon University)
description: Generates consolidation candidates from an interface connectivity matrix and removes structurally redundant ones with a 'closed-loop filter'. It then optimises build orientation for minimum support, places parts with a 2-D bottom-left layout, and estimates cost or time; a genetic algorithm searches large assemblies. Consolidating 17 components into 4 parts minimises cost (~20% lower unit cost); merging into 2 parts minimises time (~25%). Full consolidation is rarely optimal because support material and removal costs rise.
NRE_note: Build-job setup (labour and machine time per batch, set by the plate layout) is costed, but redesign of consolidated parts is excluded ('do not consider the topological redesign of parts after consolidation') and no engineering cost appears (CMU PDF).
Production_note: Unit cost from part and support material, machine and maintenance, scrap, energy, setup and support removal, plus assembly (machining, riveting) for unconsolidated interfaces (CMU PDF).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification is absent from the full paper's cost terms (CMU PDF).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection and testing are absent from the full paper's cost terms (CMU PDF).
Storage_note: The paper states its cost estimates exclude inventory; fewer part numbers could cut spares stock, but this is not modelled (CMU PDF).
Shared_Capital_note: The machine rate amortises investment (e.g., $1.1M for EBM) over a 7-year life and 7,000 operating hours per year plus maintenance, and parts are nested into batches by a 2-D layout, so capital is spread by a utilisation and multi-part-build assumption (CMU PDF, cost model and parameter table).
Shared_Capacity_note: The model prices one assembly's production and has no shared capacity, queueing or multi-site element (CMU PDF).
Speed_note: Unit production time (build, batch setup, support removal and assembly) is computed and is an alternative objective, but lead time, delivery and the value of availability are not addressed (CMU PDF).

name: Piili et al. (LUT/Aalto) laser PBF stainless-steel cost estimation by build scenario
developer: H. Piili, A. Happonen, T. Väistö, V. Venkataramanan, J. Partanen, A. Salminen (affiliations not shown on the accessed record; record held by Aalto University)
description: Estimates part cost from build time, machine, material and energy across build scenarios with optimised machine utilisation. Machine investment dominates while energy and material are minor, so time per part is the main lever. A secondary review reports that building as many parts as possible per build cut cost 81-92% vs. building singly.
NRE_note: Only the abstract and a review summary could be read (full text not reachable via Aaltodoc, UTU portal or core.ac.uk), and neither says whether design or build-preparation effort is costed.
Production_note: Part cost is estimated from calculated build times and machine, material and energy costs for each build scenario (Aaltodoc abstract).
QA_Qual_note: Only the abstract and a review summary could be read, and neither mentions qualification; the full paper was not reachable.
QA_Insp_note: Only the abstract and a review summary could be read, and neither mentions inspection or post-processing; the full paper was not reachable.
Storage_note: The documented scope is per-part cost by build scenario on one machine, which plainly excludes inventory (Aaltodoc abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine investment dominates cost and is spread over multi-part builds under optimised machine utilisation; the MDPI review reports full builds cut cost 81-92% vs single parts and 40 concurrent items cut the machine-cost share by 6% (Aaltodoc abstract; MDPI 2024 review).
Shared_Capacity_note: The documented scope is build scenarios on one research machine, which plainly excludes capacity shared across sites or users (Aaltodoc abstract).
Speed_note: Build time per scenario is calculated and drives cost, a print-time-only time model; lead time or availability is not valued (Aaltodoc abstract).

name: Barclift et al. (Penn State) CAD-integrated cost estimation and build-orientation optimization for metal PBF
developer: M. Barclift, A. Armstrong, T. W. Simpson, S. B. Joshi (Pennsylvania State University)
description: Pulls part volume and surfaces through the SolidWorks API and generates internal and external supports as solid bodies, then varies build orientation. This lets designers estimate build time and feedstock (including depreciation of reused powder) while designing. An imprecise support angle underestimates support volume by 34% and build time by 20%. Poor orientation and packing can push powder-depreciation cost to nearly twice the material cost.
NRE_note: The 2017 abstract automates support generation and orientation but does not say whether preparation or redesign labour is costed; the 2016 base model it builds on costs per-build geometry preparation and says redesign is not captured, but the 2017 full text (ASME, paywalled) could not be reached to confirm what it keeps (sciencegate abstract; Barclift et al. SFF 2016 full text).
Production_note: Estimates metal AM build cost per part from CAD geometry: build time, feedstock including generated supports, and reused-powder depreciation (sciencegate abstract; MDPI 2024 review).
QA_Qual_note: The abstract scopes the estimator to build time and feedstock cost inside CAD, which plainly excludes qualification, and the 2016 base model leaves powder acceptability to supplier-purchaser agreement (sciencegate abstract; SFF 2016).
QA_Insp_note: The abstract scopes the estimator to build time and feedstock, and the 2016 base model it extends does not cost inspection (sciencegate abstract; SFF 2016 Sec. 5.4).
Storage_note: A design-stage build-cost estimator inside CAD; inventory is outside its documented scope (sciencegate abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: Packing parts within the build volume is shown to change per-part powder-depreciation cost (computed), but machine capital is not amortised with a utilisation assumption; the 2016 base model uses a flat machine operating rate of $60/h and no machine depreciation (sciencegate abstract; SFF 2016 Table 1).
Shared_Capacity_note: A single-build, design-stage cost estimate; capacity shared across sites or users is outside its documented scope (sciencegate abstract).
Speed_note: Computes build time (an imprecise support angle underestimates it by 20%), a print-time-only time model; lead time and the value of availability are not computed (sciencegate abstract).

name: Budinoff & Shafae geometry-to-cost process-based model for metal L-PBF design alternatives
developer: H. D. Budinoff, M. Shafae (affiliation not shown on accessed page)
description: Process-based cost model of the L-PBF build and post-processing, applied to design alternatives. Costs differ by up to 14% between alternatives, with part mass and build time the strongest predictors. Higher complexity was linked to lower cost but not strongly to reject rates. Scrap and reject rates vary with geometry in conflicting directions.
NRE_note: Only the abstract was readable (the accepted manuscript in the Arizona repository could not be downloaded); it does not say whether design or build-preparation cost is in the model (Springer abstract).
Production_note: Process-based per-part cost of the L-PBF build and post-processing for each design alternative, differing by up to 14% (Springer abstract).
QA_Qual_note: Only the abstract was read; qualification is not mentioned, so whether it is costed cannot be established (Springer abstract).
QA_Insp_note: The abstract shows geometry-dependent scrap and reject rates in the model but does not say whether inspection or testing is costed (Springer abstract).
Storage_note: The documented scope is build and post-processing cost of design alternatives, which excludes inventory (Springer abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not show how machine cost is amortised or whether parts share a build (Springer abstract).
Shared_Capacity_note: The documented scope is per-part cost of design alternatives on one process, which excludes capacity pooling across sites or users (Springer abstract).
Speed_note: The model estimates build time for each design (with mass, the most influential cost factor, and found non-linear in complexity), a print-time-only partial time model, but lead time is not reported (Springer abstract; Brennan & Hanft, SFF 2024).

name: Sartini et al. (UNIVPM) analytic cost model for bound metal deposition
developer: M. Sartini, I. Bianchi, A. Vita, M. Germani, M. Mandolini (Università Politecnica delle Marche)
description: Analytic per-part cost over pre-processing, printing, debinding and sintering. Each phase sums material, machine, labour, energy and consumables, driven by part and support geometry, material, batch quantity and accuracy. Sintering machine and energy dominate the validation case (EUR 565 estimated vs. EUR 576 actual).
NRE_note: Pre-processing labour for set-up and nesting (orientation, supports, slicing, file loading; nesting counted only for the first job) is costed, but CAD design and parameter development are not (Cambridge PDF).
Production_note: Per-part cost sums material, machine, labour, energy and consumables over printing, debinding and sintering from part and support geometry, accuracy setting and batch size, validated within 2% (EUR 565 vs 576) (Cambridge PDF).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification is not modelled; 'quality' is only an accuracy input that sets layer thickness and nozzle diameter (Cambridge PDF).
QA_Insp_note: No inspection or testing cost term appears in any phase (Cambridge PDF).
Storage_note: Inventory is not addressed in the full paper (Cambridge PDF).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine hourly rates cover depreciation, overhead and maintenance at a 57% load factor (4,993 h/yr), and set-up, debind and sinter costs are divided across parts in the batch, with mixed jobs allocated by volume (Cambridge PDF).
Shared_Capacity_note: The model prices one batch on one printer, debinder and furnace and has no shared or pooled capacity (Cambridge PDF).
Speed_note: Build time is computed from extruder path length and print speed, and debind/sinter times are fixed inputs, but these only drive cost; no lead time is aggregated or valued (Cambridge PDF).

name: DeBoer-Diba-Hosseini AM cost calculator (FFF and metal bound powder extrusion)
developer: B. DeBoer, F. Diba, A. Hosseini (Ontario Tech University; Fleming College CAMIIT)
description: Cost calculator covering machine (equipment cost over a payback period and operating hours, power, changeover and setup labour), material (adjusted for shrinkage), post-processing (wash, sinter, argon, debind fluid, loading labour), overhead and profit. In the H-yoke case about 85% of part cost was Metal X capital, so BPE was judged uneconomic unless weight is critical.
