name: RAND 3D printing supply-chain impact matrix and fab-lab concept (PE-229)
developer: RAND Corporation (Simon Véronneau, Geoffrey Torrington, Jakub P. Hlavka)
description: A two-by-two matrix in which the impact of 3D printing grows with site isolation and with ad hoc (unpredictable) demand. The paper proposes a four-machine fab-lab and a process flow: incoming inspection, CT, 3D rendering, AM or CNC, post-production, outgoing inspection, tracking and serialization, then return to service. It calls for a total supply-chain cost comparison but gives no cost model and does not rank parts.
NRE_note: CT metrology can 'generate a 3D printable design' from existing parts and characterising a part without a 3D diagram 'would take about one hour', a quoted estimate that is not costed (RAND PE-229 full text).
Production_note: Says a fab-lab vs centralized comparison 'must involve a total supply chain cost approach' and calls for a 'comprehensive cost-effectiveness evaluation', but gives no per-part cost (RAND PE-229 full text).
QA_Qual_note: Recommends 'rationalizing the certification and testing approach' for AM components, without steps or costs (RAND PE-229 full text).
QA_Insp_note: Incoming and outgoing inspection and CT defect scanning are steps in the fab-lab process flow, and CT is called 'relatively underappreciated', but inspection is not costed (RAND PE-229 full text).
Storage_note: Inventory and holding cost are not discussed, but the impact matrix uses demand variability (ad hoc vs steady) and obsolescence as criteria for where printing pays, a screening use (RAND PE-229 full text).
Shared_Capital_note: The proposed fab-lab is not costed and sharing its equipment is not discussed; pay-per-use appears only as background on civilian hobbyist fab-labs (RAND PE-229 full text).
Shared_Capacity_note: The matrix argues for forward fab-labs at isolated sites with ad hoc demand rather than central production and notes sizing needs a throughput estimate, without a capacity model (RAND PE-229 full text).
Speed_note: Quotes times only: a noncritical part 'in as little as 45 minutes' and readiness gains where items 'cannot otherwise be procured'; nothing is computed or valued (RAND PE-229 full text).

name: RAND Europe AM and obsolescence management in defence (PE-171), with Cranfield obsolescence-resolution cost metrics
developer: RAND Europe (eds. Jon Freeman, Giacomo Persi Paoli). Contributors from armasuisse S+T, US Army ARDEC (G. Di Benedetto) and Cranfield University (J. Erkoyuncu, R. Roy, S. Williams, P. Colegrove, F. Martina, A. Busachi). Funded by armasuisse S+T.
description: A collection of expert perspectives, not a model. The nearest decision elements are a 'window of opportunity' test for obsolescence, a list of resolution options (same component, form-fit-function replacement, emulation, redesign), and Cranfield cost metrics (Table 2) for choosing 'the most cost effective solution'. The cost metrics are not AM-specific.
NRE_note: Cranfield Table 2 gives non-recurring obsolescence-resolution costs by integration level (emulation GBP 52,100 to 2.69m, minor redesign GBP 50,100 to 549,000), but these are generic survey figures, not an AM-specific NRE estimate; the US Navy RESTORE 'SCAN to CAD to FAB' workflow is described without costs (RAND PE-171, pp. 8, 13-14).
Production_note: AM costs are described in words as 'largely predictable' and needing to be competitive, and whether small batches can be made at constant cost is posed as a question; no unit figures (RAND PE-171, pp. 5, 13-14).
QA_Qual_note: Requalification of air/safety-critical components is one of the cost parameters folded into the generic Table 2 non-recurring costs per resolution approach, and ARDEC DMLS 4340 tensile data are reported, but there is no AM-specific qualification costing (RAND PE-171, pp. 10-14).
QA_Insp_note: Per-part inspection is not addressed; the only testing reported is ARDEC tensile testing for process qualification (RAND PE-171, full text).
Storage_note: Proposes digital storage of designs for on-demand remanufacture and notes stock ties up money; Table 2 prices 'existing stock' only as a GBP 300 resolution option, not as an AM inventory model (RAND PE-171, pp. 5, 8, 14).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine investment or its sharing is not discussed; investment appears only as R&D funding for the industrial base (RAND PE-171, p. 9).
Shared_Capacity_note: Raises a national 'strategic reserve of additive manufacturing capabilities' and mobile AM facilities for sustainment contracts, described qualitatively with no capacity or lead-time model (RAND PE-171, pp. 5, 15).
Speed_note: Cites FRCE repairs made with AM 'over a few days' instead of three or more weeks, and frames obsolescence as replacement time exceeding a window of opportunity, but time is not computed or valued (RAND PE-171, pp. 10, 12).

name: Braunberger AFIT MODA and metal L-PBF cost model for AM vs DLA procurement (C-130 parts)
developer: 1st Lt Trever J. Braunberger, USAF, Air Force Institute of Technology (committee: Maj John Situ, Maj Ryan Kemnitz, Alfred E. Thal Jr.)
description: A nine-criterion multi-objective decision analysis. Weights: quality 21.0%, lead time 20.1%, readiness 18.3%, price 14.6%, airworthiness 7.3%, expected life 6.3%, strength 6.2%, weight 4.8%, quantity 1.5%. Score bands: 86–100% is an 'extremely good candidate'; below 60%, use traditional methods. It is paired with an Atzeni & Salmi-based cost model and a guide to AM lab set-up costs ($1.94M for one metal lab). Single-part AM builds averaged $3,174.96 against $2,486.83 DLA prices, 27.6% more. Table 4.3 shows two of six parts cheaper with AM, while the text says three. AM lead times were 9–16 days against 71 to 120+ days.
NRE_note: Pre-processing cost CPRE = (ET x EC) + (TS x CO) has an engineering-time term and the thesis defines NRE as reengineering incl. creating 3D data and programming, but ET/EC values are not given and the implied engineering cost is only ~$25-106 per part per build (Table 4.3, rising per part in multi-part builds, Table 4.4), while one-time reverse engineering (50-150 h, ~$10k), redesign (up to $1M) and parameter development ($150k+, 6+ months) are quoted from SMEs outside the cost model (DTIC full thesis, ch. 3-4).
Production_note: Per-part material, pre-processing, processing (build-time formula, depreciation, energy, maintenance) and post-processing (labour $21.9/h, heat treatment $85/part, test, machining) costs are computed for six parts and for batch builds (DTIC full thesis, Eq. 3-5, Tables 4.3-4.4).
QA_Qual_note: Airworthiness is a MODA criterion (7.3% weight) and parts need a strength test and Chief Engineer approval, but airworthiness approval cost or effort is not quantified and all six parts were chosen as non-flight-safety-critical (DTIC full thesis, ch. 2-4).
QA_Insp_note: Post-processing cost CPOS = (TPOS x CO) + CTEST + CHT + CMACH carries a per-build test-cost line item for the tensile test run after each build ($1,061 grips, test-sample volume in material), though CTEST is not reported separately and volumetric/NDI inspection is explicitly excluded (DTIC full thesis, Eq. 5 and assumptions).
Storage_note: The thesis notes that 'space does cost money' and that storage and transport savings differ by part and location, but calls them difficult to quantify and leaves them out of the equations (DTIC full thesis, ch. 2-3).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine depreciation (8-year amortisation, ~$1.105M M290 package) is charged per build hour and multi-part builds are costed explicitly, cutting per-part cost 33% (2 parachute racks) and 35% (3 bracket mounts); annual machine hours/utilisation are not stated and sharing across sites or users is not modelled (DTIC full thesis, Eq. 4, Tables 4.1 and 4.4).
Shared_Capacity_note: SME interviews call for an integrated network of printing sites for faster turn-around and note distributed production 'may be cost effective' with more automation, but no capacity pooling is modelled (DTIC full thesis, ch. 2 and 4).
Speed_note: AM lead time (9-16 days) is estimated per part against DLA lead times (71 to 120+ days) and scored in the MODA alongside a separate readiness criterion; time is quantified, not dollarised (DTIC full thesis, Fig. 4.2 and MODA).

name: Crean AFIT metal AM per-part cost model and AM capability fielding costs
developer: Capt Ryan C. Crean, USAF, Air Force Institute of Technology (advisor Alan W. Johnson)
description: An Atzeni & Salmi-based cost model (material, pre-processing, processing, post-processing) with a layer-based build-time formula. It matched UDRI builds within 0–5.3%. Single builds averaged $3,144.74 per part and maximum batches $2,615.95. Before NRE, only 1 of 7 parts was cheaper with AM in single builds, and 3 with batching. Fielding one metal capability costs about $1.52–1.66M per alloy family.
NRE_note: Build setup is costed ($90 per build: 2 h at $45/h) and an engineering-hours term sits in the pre-processing equation, but one-time NRE is excluded from per-part cost and only cited outside the model (AFLCMC's ~$1,000,000 and Tinker's ~40 h per reverse-engineered part) (full thesis, ch. III-VI).
Production_note: Per-part cost is built up from material (with waste factor), pre-processing, build time x machine depreciation per machine-hour, energy (3.2 kW), maintenance ($18k/yr), labour ($45/h), heat treatment ($100) and machining (full thesis, Eq. 1).
QA_Qual_note: Missing AM process specifications are discussed as a barrier and flight-critical parts are screened out, but qualification is not costed (full thesis).
QA_Insp_note: A per-build test cost is a line item in the post-processing term: one ASTM E8 tensile coupon per build at $300 ($200 machining, $100 test); volumetric NDI is excluded and the CMM appears only as fielding equipment (full thesis).
Storage_note: Holding-cost and inventory savings are said to vary by part and location and are deliberately left out of the model (full thesis).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine depreciation (EOS M290, ~$1.1M) is charged per machine-hour and spread across multi-part builds (up to 16 parts per build), cutting average cost from $3,144.74 single-build to $2,615.95 max-batch; sharing across users or sites is not modelled (full thesis).
Shared_Capacity_note: The conclusions recommend an enterprise-wide network of metal machines placed by demand, skills and proximity to other bases, but capacity and pooling are not modelled (full thesis, ch. VI).
Speed_note: AM build and post-processing hours are computed (e.g. 46.17 h for one part, 216.48 h for a 16-part build) and current PLT+ALT is reported, but AM lead time is not totalled or valued; NMC-S cost is suggested as future work (full thesis).

name: AMPAT (Additive Manufacturing Process and Analysis Tool), NPS Navy Expeditionary AM capstone
developer: Leslie J. Amodeo, Brian B. Dick, Charles P. Flynn, Rebecca A. Nagurney and Meagan B. Parker (NPS Systems Engineering capstone). Sponsor: Navy Expeditionary Combat Command (NECC).
description: The user filters a database of AM systems on attributes such as build size, material, process, footprint, print speed, cooling, print quality, post-processing, failure rate, operational availability and environment, then assigns weights. The tool outputs a normalized weighted ranking and plots, for example overall score against initial cost. It covers equipment only, not part selection.
NRE_note: The tool has no NRE attribute, but the report mentions an X-FAB 3D scanner for generating models from existing parts and recommends adding a library of parts and part specifications (DTIC AD1150790).
Production_note: Material cost per pound, consumable cost per 100 operating hours and component cost are weighted system attributes in the ranking, but per-part cost is not computed (DTIC AD1150790, Table 2).
QA_Qual_note: The tool has no qualification attribute; the report cites the DON objective to rapidly qualify and certify AM components and recommends AMPAT to help qualified SMEs judge AM technologies for DoD use (DTIC AD1150790).
QA_Insp_note: Print quality is a database attribute and the report says sailor-printed parts need a validation process, but inspection is neither scoped nor costed (DTIC AD1150790).
Storage_note: The report argues on-demand printing eases spare-part stocking; the tool's 'initial spares and inventory cost' attribute refers to the AM system's own spares, and part inventory is not quantified (DTIC AD1150790).
Shared_Capital_note: System initial cost (with maintenance and consumable costs) is entered per AM system and plotted against overall score, but machine cost is not spread over parts or users (DTIC AD1150790, Table 2, Fig. 38).
Shared_Capacity_note: The tool is meant to inform dispersion and prepositioning of AM systems across the fleet, but the team could not build a dispersion plan and capacity is not modelled (DTIC AD1150790).
Speed_note: Print speed, maintenance times and operational availability of each AM system are weighted ranking attributes and part lead-time cuts are argued qualitatively, but no part lead time or readiness is computed (DTIC AD1150790).

name: Sasson & Johnson 3D printing supercenters concept
developer: Amir Sasson, John Chandler Johnson (BI Norwegian Business School)
description: An invited conceptual paper. Firms use direct digital manufacturing (DDM) to separate out low-volume, disruptive parts even at a higher unit cost, then grow into regional multi-product 'supercenters'. These move spares inventory from finished goods at company plants to raw material at shared DDM facilities. There is no quantitative model; the authors call for cost comparisons and simulation studies.
NRE_note: Digital design (creation, modification, copying or scanning) is named as a phase of 3D printing and firms are urged to digitise and publish printable component files to control quality, but the effort is not costed (BI open author version).
Production_note: Higher DDM unit cost (energy and raw material) is accepted for low-volume parts because it stabilises plant operations, argued only in words with illustrative figures (BI open author version).
QA_Qual_note: A lack of safety and quality standards is cited as a constraint on adoption, and part quality is said to depend on the CAD model, but qualification is not otherwise treated (BI open author version).
QA_Insp_note: The full paper does not discuss inspection or testing of printed parts (BI open author version).
Storage_note: Spares inventory is argued to shift from finished goods at company plants to raw material at shared DDM supercenters, with no quantification (BI open author version).
Shared_Capital_note: Supercenters raise utilisation of printing capacity by serving other firms' demand and gain economies of scope in learning and raw-material purchasing, without numbers (BI open author version).
Shared_Capacity_note: Orders are 'redirected to center B' when center A is full, routed only when extra distribution cost is below customer queuing cost, but this pooling is described without a model (BI open author version).
Speed_note: Expedited low-volume orders are moved to DDM to avoid disrupting scheduled production, and local printing is claimed to cut lead time and delivery distance, without quantification (BI open author version).

name: Strong et al. hybrid-AM hub facility-location model (uncapacitated and p-median, 2018)
developer: Danielle Strong, Michael Kay, Brett Conner, Thomas Wakefield, Guha Manogharan (Penn State)
description: An uncapacitated facility-location model places hubs by geography, demand and hybrid-AM processing cost. Hubs land at demand centroids, and location depends only on AM utilization rate. A constrained p-median model grows from 22 to 44 hubs as demand rises. Outputs are candidate US counties, fixed, operating and transport costs, and hub utilization. Transport cost was not a significant factor.
NRE_note: Only the abstract (via the record) and a trade summary were available; the full paper could not be reached (Penn State Pure blocked, Scribd copy empty), and neither mentions design or engineering effort.
Production_note: Hybrid-AM processing and operating cost enter the hub-location model at hub level rather than as a per-part build-up (abstract as summarised in the record).
QA_Qual_note: The abstract mentions meeting GD&T and property requirements but not qualification, and the full paper could not be reached.
QA_Insp_note: The abstract names post-processing steps but not inspection, and the full paper could not be reached.
Storage_note: Neither the abstract nor the trade summary mentions inventory, and the full paper could not be reached.
Shared_Capital_note: Fixed hub cost is traded against hub count (22 to 44 hubs as demand rises) with location driven by AM utilisation rate, and spare traditional-shop capacity is pooled into hubs (abstract as summarised in the record).
Shared_Capacity_note: Hub capacity utilisation is an output and the trade summary recommends expanding existing hub capacity, but no effect on lead time is reported (abstract; Assembly Magazine summary).
Speed_note: Neither the abstract nor the trade summary mentions lead or delivery time, and the full paper could not be reached.

name: ISO/ASTM TS 52930:2021 Qualification principles: installation, operation and performance (IQ/OQ/PQ) of PBF-LB equipment
developer: ISO/TC 261 and ASTM F42 (joint), adopted by CEN as CEN ISO/ASTM/TS 52930
description: Recommended practices for IQ, OQ and PQ of PBF-LB/M machines and connected equipment. Feedstock qualification and post-processing beyond powder removal are excluded. The public scope gives no test list, sample sizes or tiering by part criticality.
NRE_note: The scope is machine IQ/OQ/PQ; process mapping, risk assessment and validation planning are stated to be prerequisites outside it, so one-time part engineering is excluded (ISO scope).
Production_note: Cost is outside the stated scope of machine qualification practices (ISO scope; TOC preview).
QA_Qual_note: Defines IQ, OQ and PQ of PBF-LB machines plus revalidation and a normative process-capability (SPC) annex, but no test counts or part-class tiering are visible (ISO scope; ANSI/iTeh TOC preview).
QA_Insp_note: Only scope and TOC were seen; post-processing beyond powder removal is excluded, but the PQ section and normative Annex A on process capability (SPC) may set ongoing part or specimen checks, so per-part inspection is not established (ISO scope; TOC preview).
Storage_note: Inventory is outside the stated scope of machine qualification (ISO scope).
Shared_Capital_note: Only scope and TOC were seen (including a revalidation section), so whether a qualified machine's IQ/OQ/PQ carries across parts or users is not established.
Shared_Capacity_note: Capacity shared across sites or users is outside the stated scope of machine qualification (ISO scope).
Speed_note: Lead time is outside the stated scope of machine qualification (ISO scope).

name: EASA CM-S-008 Additive Manufacturing, Issue 04 (3 Sept 2025)
developer: European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA); revision discussed at FAA-EASA AM Workshop WG1
earlier_versions: CM-S-008 Issue 01 (4 Apr 2017): first issue. | CM-S-008 Issue 02 (3 Nov 2020): added supporting text for the basic CS materials requirements, guidance on AM in non-critical parts, and emphasis on knowledge transfer and training; issued for public consultation (3-24 Nov 2020). | CM-S-008 Issue 03 (30 Apr 2021): incorporated the comments from the Issue 02 consultation.
description: Adopts the ASTM F3572-22 Class A-D scheme. Section 3 policy covers only new parts or repair-by-replacement of no/low criticality (Class C and D); higher classes are said to be hard to certify near-term. All AM parts need early authority engagement, a threat and design safety assessment, M&P specifications and process control documents, KPPs, statistically covered design values (A/B/C/D/S-basis per MMPDS/CMH-17), and machine OQ plus process PQ over multiple builds. Class C/D may use S-basis data, a minimal representative coupon set and simplified means of compliance; Class D may qualify for minor change approval. POA must treat a new AM process as a significant change.
NRE_note: Calls for identification of key variables and key process parameters and for M&P specifications supported by process control documents, a prescribed parameter-development activity with no effort or cost and no redesign or reverse-engineering content (CM text, Sec. 3.1.1-3.1.2).
Production_note: Per-part production cost is not addressed; the CM is certification guidance (CM text, full read).
QA_Qual_note: Tiered by class (Class C/D may use S-basis data, a minimal representative coupon set and simplified means of compliance; machine OQ and process PQ need statistical relevance over multiple builds), but no build or coupon counts are given and A/B are left case by case (CM text, Sec. 1.3.2, 3.1).
QA_Insp_note: No NDI, first-article, witness-coupon or production acceptance requirement is given for any class; NDT appears only in definitions and the POA section requires only conformity to design data (CM text, Sec. 1.3, 3.5).
Storage_note: Spares and inventory are not mentioned (CM text, full read).
Shared_Capital_note: Part families and machine equivalency are not covered; reuse is allowed only where a part falls within previous regulatory agreement (CM text, Sec. 1.3.2, 3.1.2).
Shared_Capacity_note: Production capacity is not mentioned; only organisational AM capability is required (CM text, Sec. 3.1.2).
Speed_note: Lead time and availability are not mentioned (CM text, full read).

name: FAA Advisory Circular AC 33.15-3 Powder Bed Fusion AM Process for Aircraft Engine Parts (with FAA 2020 AM Report to Congress)
developer: Federal Aviation Administration (Aircraft Certification Service)
description: Design values should be statistically based (MMPDS-level rigor) from a frozen process and stable feedstock. Specimens should span builds, build locations, orientations, thicknesses and powder lots, with debits for features and thermal exposure. Key process variables are frozen within validated windows; changes need requalification; each machine is validated separately. Powder reuse limits are required, ISO/IEC 17025 labs are expected, and periodic destructive sampling is based on SPC. No sample sizes are given. There are no criticality tiers beyond noting that life-limited parts need more (33.14/33.70). The 2020 report says acceptable risk is set by part criticality but defines no formal tiers.
NRE_note: Requires identifying key process variables, running parametric studies to set their tolerances and freezing the process (one-time engineering), with no effort or cost given (AC 33.15-3 secs. 8.1, 8.1.3).
Production_note: The AC's scope is material and process compliance under 14 CFR 33.15, which plainly excludes production cost; the 2020 report does not cost parts either (AC 33.15-3; FAA 2020 report).
QA_Qual_note: Prescribes qualification elements (MMPDS-rigour design values from specimens spanning builds, locations, orientations and powder lots; per-machine validation; requalification on process change) but gives no specimen counts and no part-class tiers (AC 33.15-3 secs. 6.1-6.4, 11.5-11.6).
QA_Insp_note: NDI (including CT) is one option alongside process monitoring, proof testing and periodic destructive sampling set by SPC, with no quantities or class-specific scope (AC 33.15-3 secs. 10.3-10.9, 11.4.2).
Storage_note: Inventory is outside the AC's materials-compliance scope; the 2020 report mentions spare parts only as case-by-case applications (AC 33.15-3; FAA 2020 report sec. 4.2).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine investment is outside scope, and each machine needs its own process validation, so qualification is not shared across machines (AC 33.15-3 sec. 11.5).
Shared_Capacity_note: Production capacity is outside the AC's scope and is not discussed in the 2020 report (AC 33.15-3; FAA 2020 report).
Speed_note: Lead time is outside the AC's scope; the 2020 report notes schedule savings only as background on why industry uses AM, not as part of the approach (AC 33.15-3; FAA 2020 report secs. 4.2, 5).

name: MMPDS Volume II guidelines for AM allowables (2026 handbook edition)
year: 2021-2026 (AM data guidelines presented 2021-2023; Volume II first released 1 July 2024; 2026 edition 1 July 2026; no AM allowables published yet)
developer: Battelle (MMPDS Secretariat) with the MMPDS General Coordinating Committee (FAA, DoD, industry)
earlier_versions: Draft AM allowables guidelines presented by Battelle (Hall, 2021 and 2023): C-, D- and S-basis data minima on which the survey ratings rest. | MMPDS-2024 Volume II (released 1 July 2024): first edition; data-generation and analysis framework only, no material allowables yet (Battelle press release, Aug 2024). | MMPDS 2025 Volume II: annual edition listed on SAE Mobilus; changes not checked.
description: Volume II adds C-basis (lower of spec minimum or T99), D-basis (T90) and S-basis allowables for AM metals, each requiring 'further showing'. Mandatory S-basis minimums: 30 samples per strength property from 3 heats, 3 manufacturing lots, 3 machines and 3 build cycles (fewer for modulus and density). Recommended D-basis: 100 samples, 10 heats, 10 lots, 5 machines, 10 builds. C-basis: 100 samples, 10 heats, 20 lots, 5 machines, 20 builds. If no parametric fit is possible, 299 samples are needed. C-basis needs 20 builds or lots, against 10 lots for conventional A-basis. Lot-release values are being derived for several AMS AM specs.
NRE_note: Part design, reverse engineering and parameter development are outside the scope of a handbook framework for generating and analysing material allowables data (SAE Mobilus Volume II page; Hall slides 2021/2023).
Production_note: Per-part production cost is outside the scope of a material-allowables handbook (SAE Mobilus Volume II page; Hall slides 2021/2023).
QA_Qual_note: The Volume II draft sets costable data minima per allowable basis (S-basis 30 samples, 3 heats, 3 lots, 3 machines, 3 builds; D-basis 100/10/10/5/10; C-basis 100/10/20/5/20, or 299 samples without a parametric fit), but basis is not tied to part class: S-basis for low-criticality parts was still under FAA-EASA discussion (Hall, AMSC 2021 and NRC 2023).
QA_Insp_note: Battelle is deriving lot-release values for AMS AM specs (7024, 7030, 7036, 7038, 7039), which must carry lot acceptance criteria for composition and mechanical properties; per-part inspection or NDI is not addressed (Hall, NRC 2023).
Storage_note: Inventory is outside the scope of a material-allowables handbook (SAE Mobilus Volume II page; Hall slides).
Shared_Capital_note: A published handbook allowable built from data across several machines, heats and builds is one dataset reused by all users of the spec, and AMS 7032 machine-qualification data feed MMPDS, but the sharing benefit is not quantified (Hall, AMSC 2021 and NRC 2023).
Shared_Capacity_note: Print capacity is outside the scope of a material-allowables handbook (Hall slides 2021/2023).
Speed_note: Part lead time or availability is outside the scope of a material-allowables handbook; the slides mention only that two to five alloys are added per year (Hall, NRC 2023).

name: JMADD: Joint Metal Additive Database Definition (America Makes project 5511.001), public B/A-basis allowables framework for L-PBF Ti-6Al-4V
developer: Wichita State University NIAR (presenter; fabrication and testing) with Battelle, Auburn University, Beehive Industries, EOS, Boeing and Penn State CIMP-3D; America Makes project funded by OSD ManTech (AFRL agreement FA8650-20-2-5700)
description: Budget: $4.24M ($1.8M government + $2.44M cost share) over Oct 2020 to Oct 2024. Inputs: three fabricators, three powder suppliers, 19 feedstock lots in Qual 1 and 10+ heats. About 1,733 specimens were defined for Qual 1, covering tension, shear, compression, bearing and fracture toughness, with a CT subset of 216. Qual 2 uses 60 builds. The overall program was described as about 3,600 specimens. Planned follow-ons are machine equivalency (GE M2 vs EOS M290, 18-24 months) and fatigue curves (360 specimens, 8 builds, 24 months).
NRE_note: JMADD's documented scope is a public material and process specification with statistically based allowables for L-PBF Ti-6Al-4V, so part design files and part-specific build preparation are outside it (NIAR briefing AFRL-2024-1140 as read earlier; FAA REDAC 2022 slides).
Production_note: JMADD is an allowables database and specification effort, so per-part production cost is outside its documented scope (FAA REDAC 2022 slides; NIAR briefing).
QA_Qual_note: Gives a lump cost ($4.24M) and a costable test matrix for material allowables only (about 1,733 Qual-1 specimens across tension, shear, compression, bearing and fracture toughness, 60 Qual-2 builds), with no part-class qualification counts or cost model (NIAR briefing; FAA REDAC 2022 slides).
QA_Insp_note: Specifies lot-release tensile testing per build and CT of a 216-specimen subset, which is lot-level acceptance rather than per-part production inspection cost (NIAR briefing).
Storage_note: JMADD is an allowables database and specification effort, so parts inventory is outside its documented scope (FAA REDAC 2022 slides; NIAR briefing).
Shared_Capital_note: Its purpose is publicly available allowables so each user need not regenerate them, with a planned machine-equivalency follow-on, but the saving from this reuse is not quantified (FAA REDAC 2022 slides; NIAR briefing).
Shared_Capacity_note: JMADD does not address print capacity; its scope is material data and specifications (FAA REDAC 2022 slides; NIAR briefing).
Speed_note: JMADD does not address part lead time or availability; its scope is material data and specifications (FAA REDAC 2022 slides; NIAR briefing).

name: MASAAG Paper 124 Issue 2 (2022): qualification and certification of AM parts for military aviation
developer: Military Aircraft Structures Airworthiness Advisory Group (MASAAG), UK Ministry of Defence
earlier_versions: MASAAG Paper 124 Issue 1 (17 Oct 2018): first issue covering structures, propulsion and metals; Issue 2 added Systems and Polymers chapters, a graphical abstract and updated recommendations.
description: Grade A structural parts and Critical engine parts get the full recommendations: the MCRI (Military Certification Review Item) process, a PCD supplied with airworthiness documentation, B-basis allowables per failure mode with minimum coupon and batch counts, and a test pyramid up to component tests. Grade B is at the designer's discretion. Non-critical parts need a consequence-based subset agreed with the TAA. Statistical guidance: about 100 measurements for direct A/B values, 30 as an interim B-value. NDI detectable crack size is linked to inspection intervals for inspection-based fatigue substantiation.
NRE_note: NRE-type activities are recommended without counts or cost: a Process Control Document for critical parts, recorded build parameters and qualified build files, calibration builds on any machine new to the part or after an alloy change, and possible redesign for AM residual stress (MASAAG 124, Exec. Summary, 6.2-6.4, REC6.5, REC6.8).
Production_note: The guidance does not address production cost; cost appears only as the aim of powder reuse to keep material cost down (MASAAG 124, 6.4.1.3; full text read apart from part of the polymer chapter).
QA_Qual_note: Grade A structures get countable requirements (B-basis per failure mode, minimum coupon and batch counts in Table 3-3, a 15-coupon mean fallback, 100 or interim 30 measurements, MCRI, PCD, test pyramid), while Grade B and non-critical parts get TAA-agreed subsets, so counts exist for the top class only (MASAAG 124, 3.1.6, 3.6.1, REC3.3, Exec. Summary).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection scope is set by part class and per build: each Grade A (and Class 1/Group 1 engine) AM part gets inspection of 100% of its surface with part-specific POD, and every powder-bed build carries a witness set of a density cube, powder capsule and tensile coupons (MASAAG 124, REC3.7, REC4.8, REC4.10, REC5.6, REC6.43).
Storage_note: Parts inventory and spares are not addressed; storage appears only for feedstock degradation (MASAAG 124, REC6.2; full text read).
Shared_Capital_note: Reuse is described without numbers: process qualification may later cover several parts 'at least within the same part family', parameters may be fixed for a part or part family, machines other than the qualified ones need pre-qualification builds, and parts are placed to maximise parts per build (MASAAG 124, 4.7.2.2, 6.3.3.3, REC6.8, REC7.18).
Shared_Capacity_note: The guidance does not address print capacity across sites or users; moving parts between machines is treated only as a pre-qualification requirement (MASAAG 124, REC6.8; full text read).
Speed_note: Lead time and availability are not addressed in the guidance (MASAAG 124; full text read).

name: Lloyd's Register LR-GN-046 guidance notes for AM metallic parts (June 2024)
developer: Lloyd's Register (with TWI for the 2016/2017 editions)
earlier_versions: LR/TWI Guidance Notes for Additive Manufacturing (March 2017 edition, read in full; an earlier 2016 edition is reported but not confirmed): joint LR-TWI goal-based guidance for LMD, L-PBF and WAAM parts; LR-GN-046 (2024) refocused it on marine and offshore use.
description: The 2017 edition is goal-based with no fixed part categories. Testing depends on design code, criticality and a functional study. Five certifiable stages (design, materials, manufacturing, post-processing, inspection/testing) can be certified separately by different organisations. Minimum per part: 100% visual and 100% dimensional examination. NDE methods are set by quality level, complexity and criticality. For PBF, good practice is a density block, retained-powder capsule and one tensile set per build. Build parameters are machine-specific. The 2024 edition adds facility approval but its categories were not seen.
NRE_note: Requires a manufacturing plan for each AM part design and machine-specific build-parameter qualification, and lists reverse engineering as a suitability criterion, none costed (2017 edition text secs. 3, 7.1.1, 10; the 2024 text sits behind Regs4ships sign-up and was not read).
Production_note: Material cost, production size and shipping time and cost are listed among the criteria for deciding whether AM is suitable, with no cost calculation (2017 edition text sec. 3).
QA_Qual_note: Five separately certifiable stages and machine-specific parameter qualification, but testing is set by design code, risk matrix and a functional study agreed case by case, with no class-specific counts (2017 edition text secs. 4, 5, 9.3; 2024 page lists facility approval and qualification only by name).
QA_Insp_note: Sets costable minimums for every part and build (100% visual and 100% dimensional examination, a mandatory powder capsule per build, density block and tensile set as good practice) but leaves NDE extent to complexity, criticality and agreement (2017 edition text secs. 7.2.2, 9.1).
Storage_note: The 2017 text does not mention inventory or spares, and the 2024 edition's scope (manufacture, testing and certification) plainly excludes it (2017 edition text; LR guidance notes page).
Shared_Capital_note: Says stage certification reduces effort on later contracts and that using pre-certified organisations cuts part certification cost, a qualitative reuse of qualification (2017 edition text sec. 4).
Shared_Capacity_note: Production capacity and pooling are not addressed in the 2017 text and fall outside the documented certification scope (2017 edition text; LR guidance notes page).
Speed_note: Lead time and shipping time are suitability criteria, and pre-certified organisations are said to shorten certification lead times, not quantified (2017 edition text secs. 3, 4).

name: ABS Requirements for Additive Manufacturing
year: 2018 (Guidance Notes, Sept 2018); 2021 (Guide, April 2021); Requirements edition date Unknown (a linked PDF file name suggests July 2022)
developer: American Bureau of Shipping (ABS)
earlier_versions: ABS Guidance Notes on Additive Manufacturing (Sept 2018): four-stage maturity approval (feasibility, verification, pre-production validation, production); specimen counts agreed case by case; read in full. | ABS Guide for Additive Manufacturing (April 2021): first ABS Guide, covering facility and part approval for PBF and DED; later reissued as the Requirements, which also cover material extrusion (2025 trade coverage); not read.
description: The 2018 Guidance Notes define four maturity stages: feasibility, verification of a cradle-to-grave file, pre-production validation builds witnessed at hold points, and production with monitoring. Qualification depth scales with the part's ABS Tier of Approval; specimen counts are agreed case by case. A critical process-parameter change triggers requalification. A 2023 ABS briefing describes AM Test Levels 1-3 set by risk (likelihood x consequence, consequence mapped to ISO 5817 classes). It lists standard approval tests and rapid-qualification options: in-situ monitoring replacing NDT, reduced scope using existing data, and part- or feature-family qualification. It states only that approval cost is high.
NRE_note: The feasibility and verification stages require design review and checks of converted build files (units, origin, pre-distorted vs resulting geometry) before any build, but this effort is not costed (ABS Guidance Notes 2018 full text; current Requirements portal blocked).
Production_note: Per-part production cost is outside the scope of classification requirements for AM facility and part approval (ABS Guidance Notes 2018 full text).
QA_Qual_note: Staged qualification with ABS-witnessed hold points, depth correlated with the part's Tier of Approval and 2023 Test Levels set by risk, but 'the amount and type of testing varies on a case-by-case basis' with no class-specific specimen counts (ABS Guidance Notes 2018; Qiao ABS slides 2023).
QA_Insp_note: Production NDE must address defect types, locations and probability of detection, a test artifact in each build is recommended and in-situ monitoring may partly replace NDT, but inspection frequency is agreed case by case by criticality with no class-specific scope (ABS Guidance Notes 2018; Qiao ABS slides 2023).
Storage_note: Inventory is not addressed in the guidance text; the 2023 slides mention spare and obsolete parts only as cases where standard qualification is ill-suited (ABS Guidance Notes 2018 full text; Qiao ABS slides 2023).
Shared_Capital_note: ABS proposes qualification by part family, design-feature family or material group and reduced scope using recognised data, though qualified processes 'may be specific to the serial number of a particular AM machine'; no numbers (Qiao ABS slides 2023; ABS Guidance Notes 2018).
Shared_Capacity_note: The guidance notes that a single AM service provider can serve multiple clients and part types, acting as several qualified factories 'under one roof', but capacity or lead time is not modelled (ABS Guidance Notes 2018 full text).
Speed_note: The guidance states AM's value lies in producing 'a low number of complex parts faster than traditional manufacturing methods' and that early detection of failed builds may cut production time, but no lead time is set or valued (ABS Guidance Notes 2018 full text).

name: Indian Register of Shipping Classification Notes: Additively Manufactured Metallic Parts for Marine and Offshore Applications
developer: Indian Register of Shipping (IRClass)
description: Parts are 'class items' (must meet IRS Rules; IRS approves feedstock and manufacturer) or 'certified items' (meet industry/OEM standards; manufacturer qualifies feedstock and design). Criticality is set separately: critical = primary/secondary essential services, non-critical = habitability. Qualification specimen counts are tabulated per category. PBF: tensile 5 (class) vs 3 (certified critical), impact 3 sets vs 1, hardness 6 vs 3, microstructure 4 vs 2, density 3 vs 3. DED tensile: 6 vs 3. Coupons and components get visual and surface NDT; components also get embedded-flaw NDT. Production sampling frequency is set in an agreed inspection and test plan.
NRE_note: Requires CAD model or drawing review and approval for class items, an engineering-analysis report for topology-optimised redesigns and AMPS qualification over a parameter range, without costable effort by class (IRClass CN, secs. 1.6.2, 3.2.3, 5.1.2).
Production_note: Full classification notes read; production cost is outside the scope of a class approval document (IRClass CN, July 2025).
QA_Qual_note: Tables 19-21 prescribe qualification specimen counts per test for certified-critical vs class items and per process (e.g. PBF tensile 3 vs 5, hardness 3 vs 6), which are directly costable (IRClass CN, July 2025).
QA_Insp_note: Requires 100% visual examination and NDT of every delivered part with component-level embedded-flaw inspection, but NDT extent and production test frequency follow an agreed NDT plan or ITP and do not differ by category (IRClass CN, sec. 7.3, Tables 19-20).
Storage_note: Full classification notes read; inventory is not addressed (IRClass CN, July 2025).
Shared_Capital_note: Certified-critical items may be approved as a part family with a risk analysis, and a serial-number change within the same machine model is not a change of machine, so qualification is reused across parts and machines without numbers (IRClass CN, secs. 6.4, range of approval).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full classification notes read; capacity sharing is not addressed (IRClass CN, July 2025).
Speed_note: Full classification notes read; lead time is not addressed (IRClass CN, July 2025).

name: AIA Recommended Guidance for Certification of AM Components, Rev. A (Oct 2025)
developer: Aerospace Industries Association (AIA) Additive Manufacturing Working Group, with FAA participation
earlier_versions: AIA Recommended Guidance for Certification of AM Components, initial report (2020): first AIA AM Working Group guidance; Rev. A (2025) restructured it, added guidance for higher-criticality parts (damage-tolerance, crack-growth and fracture-toughness data, expanded NDI, witness coupons) and aligned with ASTM F3572-22.
description: Criticality is set by FMECA rather than ASTM F3572 classes, and requirements scale with consequence of failure. Higher criticality brings fatigue and damage-tolerance allowables, tighter KPV control, more frequent machine maintenance and stricter requalification. Inspection development needs limits of detection and POD. Performance qualification ends in first-article inspection, and witness coupons are built into production for high-criticality parts. Every machine serial number is qualified independently, though PCDs can be reused. Equivalency is shown statistically. Requalification triggers include software, firmware, component or relocation changes. A section on part-family allowables exists but was not read.
NRE_note: Requires process development (DOE varying up to 8-10 parameters), a parameter set per material and machine model, and fixed PCDs, without costing them (AIA 2025, secs. 6.3, 6.4, 7.2).
Production_note: Notes only that maximising parts per platform generally lowers cost per part (AIA 2025, sec. 6.9.3).
QA_Qual_note: Requirements scale with FMECA criticality (KPV control, maintenance frequency, part-family scrutiny, PQ per machine serial number), but no class-specific test counts are set (AIA 2025, secs. 3, 6-8).
QA_Insp_note: Every part from every machine gets 100% dimensional verification and critical parts keep 100% sampling of select witness coupons until the process is stable, but NDI extent and acceptance criteria are left to criticality with no fixed scope (AIA 2025, secs. 6.5, 13, 14).
Storage_note: Full guidance read; inventory is not addressed (AIA 2025).
Shared_Capital_note: PCDs can be reused across machines and test data pooled across a part family once similarity is shown, but every machine still needs full PQ and no costs are given (AIA 2025, secs. 7.3, 8.2.2).
Shared_Capacity_note: Machine equivalency is treated as a qualification requirement, not capacity pooling; shared capacity is not addressed (AIA 2025, sec. 7.3.2).
Speed_note: Full guidance read; lead time and schedule are not addressed (AIA 2025).

name: Peron/Cantini qualification-cost model for AM vs conventional spare parts (Cantini et al. 2025)
developer: Peron (NTNU), Cantini (Politecnico di Milano / Univ. Firenze), Coruzzolo and Lolli (Univ. Modena e Reggio Emilia), De Carlo (Univ. Firenze)
earlier_versions: Peron, Cantini & Coruzzolo 2023, IFAC-PapersOnLine 56(2):6537-6542 (doi:10.1016/j.ifacol.2023.10.303, open access): base model pricing DNV-ST-B203 class-dependent qualification and production tests; AM break-even falls from 42 parts to 8 (C2) and 6 (C3).
description: Adds three qualification cost blocks to a production-cost comparison. Build process qualification is one-time for all classes (12 tensile, 3 impact, plus hardness, microstructure, porosity, chemistry and visual). Part qualification is one-time and C3 only, covering the full test set including surface and volumetric NDT and dimensional checks. Production testing is per build job: full set for C3, reduced for C2, negligible for C1. A CM batch shares one production test, while each AM build job needs its own. Test prices run from $10 (visual) to $150 (hardness or volumetric NDT), plus $20 per part for transport. Reported break-even quantity below which AM wins: 42 parts without qualification, 42 for C1, 8 for C2, 6 for C3. Sharing a build job among 4 parts raises the C3 break-even to 9. The 2025 extension embeds qualification costs in a spare-parts inventory cost model with holding and backorder costs (abstract only).
NRE_note: The 2023 full paper costs no AM design-file or parameter preparation and lists 'different design routines and related costs' as future work; its only one-time production cost is the CM fixed cost ($22,366), and the 2025 abstract adds no design cost (IFAC 2023 full text; PPC 2025 abstract).
Production_note: Explicit per-part unit costs by technology are model inputs (AM $560.55/part; CM $22.68/part plus $22,366 fixed), taken from Atzeni & Salmi 2012 rather than computed from geometry (IFAC 2023 full text).
QA_Qual_note: One-time build-process qualification (all classes) and part qualification (C3 only) test sets are priced per test by DNV criticality class (IFAC 2023 full text, Eqs. 2-3, Table 4).
QA_Insp_note: Per-build-job production testing is priced by class (full set C3, reduced set C2, visual only C1), with a batch-sharing rule for CM and per-test-job transport cost (IFAC 2023 full text, Eqs. 4-6).
Storage_note: The 2023 paper has no inventory terms; the 2025 paper is titled for spare-parts inventories and its abstract says prior models compare production, holding and backorder costs, but the full text (no file on IRIS UNIMORE or Polimi; DOI blocked) was not read, so whether it computes holding cost is not established.
Shared_Capital_note: One-time qualification cost is amortised over part quantity (break-even N) and tests are shared across parts in a build job (4 parts per job raises the C3 break-even from 6 to 9), but machine capital is not modelled (IFAC 2023 full text).
Shared_Capacity_note: Machine capacity is not discussed in the 2023 full paper, and the 2025 abstract does not mention capacity (IFAC 2023 full text; PPC 2025 abstract).
Speed_note: The 2023 paper uses AM's shorter lead time only as motivation; the 2025 abstract names backorder costs in prior models, but its full text was not reachable, so whether the extension computes backorders or lead time is not established.

name: Verna et al. quality-inspection cost model for low-volume and AM production (2022)
developer: Politecnico di Torino (Verna, Genta, Galetto, Franceschini)
earlier_versions: Verna et al. 2020, Planning offline inspection strategies in low-volume manufacturing processes (Quality Engineering, doi:10.1080/08982112.2020.1739309): earlier inspection-planning model trading inspection cost against alpha/beta errors; the 2022 model adds per-part production cost and a return on inspection investment.
description: A probabilistic model per output characteristic covering defect probability p, false-alarm α, missed-defect β, inspection cost, necessary and unnecessary repair cost, and external failure cost. It yields D_tot (expected undetected defects) and C_tot (quality cost) to compare inspection strategies (2020). The 2022 paper adds quality costs to a per-part production cost model, with a return-on-inspection metric (ROII). In the L-PBF case, production cost was 18.56 €/part and quality-related costs were 14.40-31.69 €/part across three alternatives. In 2020, the most effective strategy cost about 4x the cheapest (€168.81 vs €42.36) with fewer undetected defects. CT was mentioned but not modeled.
NRE_note: Per-job AM system setup (2.5 h) and software job preparation (1.5 h) are costed (2.97 EUR/part pre-process cost), but no one-time design or parameter development is included (2022 manuscript).
Production_note: The 2022 model computes per-part material and manufacturing cost from powder, machine, operator, and pre- and post-process times (18.56 EUR/part in the L-PBF case) (2022 manuscript).
QA_Qual_note: Full manuscript read; qualification is not modelled, and only inspector skill affecting error rates is discussed (2022 manuscript).
QA_Insp_note: Per-part inspection cost (operator plus equipment rate x inspection time, e.g. 3.38-12.50 EUR/part) is traded against detection errors and repair and escape costs across inspection strategies (2022 manuscript).
Storage_note: Full manuscript read; inventory is not addressed (2022 manuscript).
Shared_Capital_note: The L-PBF system is charged at about 38 EUR/h from a 700 kEUR price depreciated over five years at 50% utilisation (plus maintenance, rent, overheads), and job cost is divided over 60 parts per job (2022 manuscript).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full manuscript read; shared capacity is not addressed (2022 manuscript).
Speed_note: Build time (18 h/job) and handling times are fixed inputs used only for cost, and lead time or throughput is not modelled (2022 manuscript).

name: CT vs electromechanical-impedance per-specimen verification cost estimate for metal AM (Strutner et al.)
year: Unknown (SAMPE conference paper; neither the NSF PAR record nor the PDF gives a date; latest reference is 2018)
developer: Virginia Tech (Strutner, Tenney, Tarazaga, Williams) with Northrop Grumman (Kwas); NSF award 1635356
description: Builds a simple per-specimen CT cost estimate. In-house 220 kV CT: $600k capital over 5 years x 2,000 h, i.e. $60/h, scaled to $240/h at a 25% duty cycle. A 2-hour scan therefore costs $480 machine time, plus about $1,000 analysis labour (about 8 h), for about $1,480 per specimen. A service bureau costs about $2,300 ($450/h + $1,000 labour + $400 shipping). Larger parts may cost 5-10x more to analyse. The EMI alternative is estimated at about $324 per specimen (about 90 min).
NRE_note: No design, parameter-development or other one-time engineering cost appears in the full paper (NSF PAR full text).
Production_note: Section 3.4.1 builds each EBM specimen's cost from powder ($160), machine time ($188, from a $1.5M Arcam A2X depreciated over 5 years of 4,000 h and a quarter share of a 10 h build) and de-caking labour ($600), giving at least $947 each (NSF PAR full text, sec. 3.4.1).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification or certification cost is not discussed; EMI is presented only as post-production screening (NSF PAR full text).
QA_Insp_note: Explicit per-specimen inspection cost build-up: in-house CT $1,480 (capital at 25% duty cycle, 2 h scan, $1,000 analysis labour), service bureau $2,300, EMI $324 now and $103 with a clamp-on system (NSF PAR full text, Table 3).
Storage_note: Inventory is not discussed in the full paper (NSF PAR full text).
Shared_Capital_note: Equipment capital is amortised with explicit utilisation assumptions: the $600k CT at a 25% duty cycle ($240/h) and the AM machine over 4,000 h/yr with a quarter-build share per specimen (NSF PAR full text, sec. 3.4).
Shared_Capacity_note: No capacity contention is modelled; the paper only notes that one CT specimen is scanned per day and that external vendors may be used without enough volume (NSF PAR full text).
Speed_note: Scan (2 h) and analysis (about 8 h) times feed the inspection cost only; part lead time, turnaround or availability is not computed (NSF PAR full text).

name: Multivariate equivalency testing framework for AM requalification (Lynch et al., UTEP) with R package MultivariateEquivalency
developer: University of Texas at El Paso W.M. Keck Center and collaborators (Lynch, Villalobos, Valadez Mesta, Gomez Guillen, Mireles, Wicker)
description: Feature-wise equivalence tests on percentile bins of the reference process, with family-wise error control across measured attributes. Simulations map trade-offs among power, detectable effect size, feature count and fabrication/measurement cost. Validation used 40 observations per process and three geometric features. The authors position it as a requalification screen, not a replacement for formal qualification.
NRE_note: Full text read; the framework screens equivalence after a machine, parameter or measurement change and does not cost design or parameter development (JMMP full text).
Production_note: Full text read; per-part production cost is not modelled, and an illustrative artifact cost ($4,165) enters only as a requalification input (JMMP full text, sec. 6).
QA_Qual_note: The framework minimises a composite cost of artifact fabrication and measurement over sample size and feature count for the requalification screen, so qualification test effort is an explicit cost output; the $424,500-$1,269,255 figures in the paper are the cost of a conventional tensile-test procedure it compares against (full text).
QA_Insp_note: Full text read; measurement cost applies to requalification samples, and per-part production inspection is not addressed (JMMP full text).
Storage_note: Full text read; inventory is not addressed (JMMP full text).
Shared_Capital_note: The framework is meant to show that a candidate machine, facility or workflow stays equivalent to a qualified reference, so a qualified baseline can be extended to new machines, but that reuse is not costed (JMMP full text).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full text read; capacity is not addressed (JMMP full text).
Speed_note: Full text read; sequential stopping cuts requalification sample sizes by up to 67.5%, but part lead time or availability is not addressed (JMMP full text).

name: NAVAIR Additive Manufacturing Capability initiative: licensed Material Process Combination (MPC) qualification data packages (Colibrium Additive contract) and FRCE depot certification
year: 2026 (FRCE first certified metal AM parts reported April 2026; Colibrium MPC award reported May 2026)
developer: Naval Air Systems Command (NAVAIR AM Team) with Colibrium Additive (GE Aerospace); Fleet Readiness Center East (FRCE) depot
description: NAVAIR licenses six alloy Material Process Combinations. Each includes characterization data and curves, optimized parameters, consolidated material and process specifications, and design allowables for the tested properties, plus thin-wall fatigue characterization and workforce training. FRCE, working with the NAVAIR AM Team and Fleet Support Teams, qualified, produced and certified its first metal AM parts in under six months, which it called the fastest such effort in NAVAIR. The parts were an AH-1Z pylon fitting, a V-22 landing-gear door stop fitting and a C-130 blanking plate, in aluminum, described as non-flight-critical. No contract value, cost or tiered criteria are public.
NRE_note: The Colibrium package supplies optimized process parameters, manufacturing process instructions and consolidated specifications, removing part of the parameter-development NRE, but this work is not costed separately within the contract (GE Aerospace release Apr 2026; TCT).
Production_note: The GE release, trade coverage and Navy story give a contract value but nothing on per-part production cost, so whether production cost is treated is not established.
QA_Qual_note: NAVAIR's $31M Colibrium contract buys six alloy MPC packages (property data, parameters, specifications, design allowables, thin-wall fatigue data) plus four printers and training as one lump, and FRCE certified its first parts in under six months; there is no tiered or per-part qualification costing (GE Aerospace release; TCT; Navy.mil).
QA_Insp_note: The sources say only that parts meet the same quality requirements as conventional parts and that training covers quality teams, so per-part inspection is not described (Navy.mil; GE release).
Storage_note: The Navy story describes in-house, on-demand production of parts hard to get through traditional supply chains but says nothing about inventory (Navy.mil).
Shared_Capital_note: The releases say the licensed data, four printers and training build in-house capability to produce NAVAIR components at scale, but reuse of an MPC package across parts or sites and machine sharing are not stated (GE release; TCT).
Shared_Capacity_note: The Navy story names FRCE, Lakehurst, NAVAIR HQ and Fleet Support Teams as collaborators but describes no sharing of machines or capacity (Navy.mil).
Speed_note: Releases claim shorter lead times for critical components and less aircraft downtime, and FRCE's certification took under six months, but no part lead time is computed or valued (GE release; Navy.mil).

name: ROK procedure for applying 3D-printed repair parts in operational units (DMSMS / FMECA / localisation screening with DT&E-OT&E qualification)
developer: S. Yoo (ROK Ministry of National Defense), J. Hur (ROK Naval Academy), H. Lee (ROK Navy Force Support System Project Group)
description: Qualitative screening built on existing parts-localisation procedures. Candidates come from three pools: DMSMS-tracked obsolete parts, FMECA risk level 2-3 parts with poor MTBF/MKBF/MRBF, and foreign-sourced parts with high import-substitution value. Each passes DT&E, an installation test, OT&E and a military-suitability determination before being catalogued in a parts database. The programme (since 2017) was extended by a 2025 industry-defence ministry agreement.
NRE_note: The paper describes 3D scanning, reverse modelling and CAD design changes in the printing workflow and has approved parts catalogued with their design data for future production, but this effort is not costed or used in screening (full paper, Korean).
Production_note: Ease of manufacture and cost prioritise the localisation pool and an F-15K HPT cover plate is cited at 90% lower purchase cost, but there is no cost model (full paper, Korean).
QA_Qual_note: Specifies a feasibility review, DT&E, installation test, OT&E (if needed) and a military-suitability determination before cataloguing, but with no class-specific test counts or burden figures (full paper, Korean).
QA_Insp_note: Refers to KCL national quality guidelines that assess printouts for dimensions, mechanical and chemical properties and reliability, with no per-part inspection cost or class-specific scope (full paper, Korean).
Storage_note: The full paper gives no inventory or stock analysis or claim; it argues only that localised production speeds logistics for obsolete parts (full paper, Korean).
Shared_Capital_note: The full paper proposes a Defense Center for 3D printing and service-level training but does not address sharing machine investment across units (full paper, Korean).
Shared_Capacity_note: The full paper gives no printer counts or capacity and no sharing of printing capacity between units or services (full paper, Korean).
Speed_note: FMECA risk 2-3 and MTBF/MKBF/MRBF screening targets parts whose failures cut mission capability, and an F-15K case cut procurement by more than 30 days, but lead time or availability is not computed (full paper, Korean).

name: Satair/Airbus AM spare-part pre-assessment and RapidSpares recertification route
year: 2015-2020 (AM team since c. 2015; first certified metal flying spare 2020)
developer: Satair (Airbus aftermarket subsidiary) AM team with Airbus RapidSpares design offices; production at Airbus Filton Reference Manufacturing shop
description: When a part becomes non-procurable or an AOG order arrives, Satair's AM team runs a short pre-assessment and hands candidates to Airbus RapidSpares design offices for redesign and recertification. In the A320ceo wingtip fence case, AM beat both re-tooling the casting and redesigning for machining. Satair reports more than 300 AM-certified part numbers.
NRE_note: The pre-assessment compared non-recurring cost of AM against re-tooling the casting and redesigning for machining, with AM NRC 45% lower in the wingtip-fence case, a case outcome with no published method (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020).
Production_note: Printing the four-part shipset in one 26-hour build is said to reduce cost per piece, but no per-part cost or cost model is given (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020).
QA_Qual_note: RapidSpares re-certified the former cast part within five weeks via a new certification process and the parts ship with EASA Form 1 from a shop process-qualified in 2019, a case outcome rather than a modelled qualification burden (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020).
QA_Insp_note: The press releases say post-processing steps make the part airworthy but say nothing about inspection or testing, and no fuller description of the route is public (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020; TCT 2020).
Storage_note: The route is triggered when a part is no longer procurable (here, out of production with supplier mould losses), so obsolescence works as a screening trigger, but stock levels or holding cost are not discussed (Satair press release 2020; TCT 2020).
Shared_Capital_note: Four parts are printed together 'to reduce the cost per piece and the printing time per part' in a process-qualified shop with more than 300 AM-certified part numbers, but machine cost or utilisation is not quantified (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020).
Shared_Capacity_note: The press names the Filton Reference Manufacturing shop and notes four more customers requested the same part, but says nothing about how print capacity is shared or allocated (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020).
Speed_note: The route is AOG-triggered and machining redesign was rejected because its 'cost and lead-time implications were not competitive'; total lead time was shorter but no figure is given or computed (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020).

name: ST Engineering AM parts screening, business case and certification workflow (with EOS Additive Minds)
developer: ST Engineering Aerospace (Advanced Manufacturing Design Centre, Singapore), with an EOS Additive Minds capability transfer
description: A late-2018 capability-transfer programme gave ST Engineering a process for parts screening and selection, DfAM, business case analysis and critical-to-quality requirements. ST then built its own workflow covering DfAM, powder management, printing, inspection and post-processing. Parts are printed on demand from certified files under EASA/FAA/CAAS approvals, and more than 120 part numbers are in a production digital catalogue.
NRE_note: DfAM training and assembly consolidation are part of the method, but not costed (EOS/AM Chronicle case study).
Production_note: Business case analysis is a named method step and the brochure quotes '>20% weight and cost savings' on a qualified IN625 part, but no cost model or inputs are published (EOS/AM Chronicle case study; AMDC brochure 2025).
QA_Qual_note: A qualification campaign reached B-basis design values, full proof-load tests were run and EASA granted STC, DOA and POA, but qualification effort is not modelled in part selection (EOS/AM Chronicle case study).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection is a step in the printing process-control workflow that runs through post-processing, with no scope or cost given (EOS/AM Chronicle case study; AMDC page).
Storage_note: Builds a virtual inventory and says printing on demand reduces non-moving inventory; not quantified (EOS/AM Chronicle case study).
Shared_Capital_note: Only a vendor case study, a brochure and the AMDC page describe the method; the business-case step's contents, including machine investment, are not public.
Shared_Capacity_note: Certified print files let parts be produced close to aircraft sites, and the brochure lists 5 qualified machines; no capacity model (EOS/AM Chronicle case study; AMDC brochure 2025).
Speed_note: Claims shorter lead time from on-demand printing of certified files and quotes case results (duct lead time down 90%, a part installed within 7 days of enquiry), not computed by the method (EOS/AM Chronicle case study; AMDC brochure 2025).

name: Leonardo Aircraft Division AM spare-part candidate criteria (safety, feasibility, lead time >180 days, unscheduled removal rate band)
developer: Leonardo S.p.A. Aircraft Division Customer Support (Caselle, Turin) with Politecnico di Torino (A. Pochettino MSc thesis; builds at IAM@PoliTo)
description: Four screening criteria: non-safety-critical (binary); feasibility (geometry, material, volume, cost); procurement lead time over 180 days; and unscheduled removal rate of 0.050-0.500 per 1,000 flight hours. They yielded three use cases: a C-27J main landing gear bracket, an M-346 clevis and an M-345 connector. Leonardo reports more than 100 metal AM parts qualified and flying. This is separate from the earlier pass's Viano business-model entry for the same division.
NRE_note: The bracket CAD was rebuilt in SolidWorks from the drawing and Al 2024 was substituted by AlSi10Mg; the effort is described but not costed (full thesis, ch. 1-2).
Production_note: The feasibility criterion requires AM to be more cost-effective than conventional manufacturing at small to medium volumes, a filter; per-part costs (EUR 69-105 from AMOtool, whose calculation is not shown) are estimated only after selection (full thesis, Table 1.1 and ch. 3).
QA_Qual_note: Safety-critical parts are excluded by a binary gate, and the work relies on Leonardo's existing certification path (AlSi10Mg already certified); qualification is not costed (full thesis, ch. 1).
QA_Insp_note: Each order is built in two copies and the second, the first article, undergoes dimensional, chemical-physical and mechanical testing, but tests are not costed (full thesis, ch. 1-3).
Storage_note: On-demand production near the user is presented as a way to digitise the warehouse and reduce inventory, without quantification (full thesis, ch. 1).
Shared_Capital_note: Read in full: the four documented criteria (Table 1.1) and the rest of the thesis contain no machine investment or utilisation element (the thesis notes only that precise criteria definition is outside its scope); a post-selection AMOtool estimate fills a build platform (16, 14, 68 parts) without showing its calculation (full thesis).
Shared_Capacity_note: Read in full: neither the four documented criteria nor the rest of the thesis discusses print capacity, sites or pooling; parts were built on one EOS M270 at IAM@PoliTo (full thesis).
Speed_note: Procurement lead time over 180 days and an unscheduled removal rate of 0.050-0.500 per 1,000 FH are screening thresholds, with AOG/AOCP as motivation; lead time is not computed (full thesis, Table 1.1).

name: EDF case-by-case AM of obsolete nuclear auxiliary-circuit parts and EDF Hydro WAAM programme
developer: EDF (R&D, nuclear fleet and EDF Hydro) with partners incl. CIH, Institut de Soudure and INOVSYS
description: EDF selects obsolete parts case by case and limits nuclear use to auxiliary circuits, not the primary circuit. Worn parts are 3D-scanned and rebuilt, either printed directly (a valve plug by SLM) or cast from a printed mould. The process is chosen by part size and use (SLM, cold spray or WAAM). EDF says it has not yet entered an industrial phase.
NRE_note: Worn obsolete parts are 3D-scanned to get a digital model and rebuilt, with material and process chosen per part, but the effort is not costed (EDF R&D pages).
Production_note: Lower manufacturing and sourcing cost and cost gains from cold spray are claimed in words, with no figures or method (EDF R&D pages).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification and use-case identification are named as the main obstacles; RCC-M does not yet cover AM and parts must match conventional mechanical properties, so EDF began with parts with few regulatory requirements (EDF R&D pages).
QA_Insp_note: Inspectability of AM parts is named as a main unknown, with NDT methods being adapted or developed, but inspection is not costed (EDF R&D page, 'les benefices pour la production').
Storage_note: EDF says it now stores only powder or wire, with part designs kept in a digital catalogue for on-demand production; no stock or holding cost is quantified (EDF R&D page, 'une revolution des modes de production').
Shared_Capital_note: EDF reports 'significant investments' in a cold-spray lab and a WAAM lab, but no source says whether machine cost or sharing enters part decisions (EDF R&D pages).
Shared_Capacity_note: EDF Hydro works with external partners (CIH, Institut de Soudure) and two EDF labs, but capacity or pooling is not discussed (EDF R&D pages).
Speed_note: Claims manufacturing lead time cut by a factor of 3-4, shorter cold-spray interventions and lower hydro unit unavailability costs, with no lead-time model (EDF R&D pages).

name: Siemens Energy (Siemens Industrial Turbomachinery) Finspang AM burner repair and spares programme
developer: Siemens Industrial Turbomachinery AB, Finspang (now Siemens Energy); Materials Solutions, Worcester (acquired 2016)
description: Problem-driven adoption: eroded burner tips are repaired by machining off the worn section and reprinting it, instead of buying new burners. A digital thread (NX, Teamcenter, MOM tracking powder reuse) supports the work. No formal part screening or business-case method is published.
NRE_note: Redesign of the burner head to combine many welded parts into one unit, with lattice and thin-wall weight reduction (22%, goal 50%), is described but not costed (Siemens blog).
Production_note: Repair is presented as a lower-cost alternative to new burners and AM as cutting material use and cost, with no cost model or figures (Siemens blog; Metal AM).
QA_Qual_note: Repaired burners are re-certified, with endurance over the required duty cycles as 'the true test'; the process is not described or modelled (Siemens blog; Metal AM).
QA_Insp_note: Burners were inspected after 20,000 operating hours, an AM monitor checks layer images for deviations, and automated 3D scanning and in-line/off-line monitoring are named as needs; inspection is not costed (Metal AM; DN Siemens feature).
Storage_note: Envisions turbines linked to a diagnostic centre where spare parts are ordered and printed on demand to minimise downtime; no stock effect is quantified (Metal AM; Siemens blog).
Shared_Capital_note: Press reports a 2016 automated facility with eight new machines and plans for more, but no source says whether investment or machine sharing enters any part decision (Metal AM; Siemens blog).
Shared_Capacity_note: The Siemens AM Network 'links part designers and AM production service providers together', with no capacity model (Metal AM).
Speed_note: Burner repair turnaround cut 70% and lead times 'reduced by up to 90 percent' are reported outcomes, not computed by any decision method (Metal AM; DN Siemens feature).

name: GE annual part audit and per-part ROI screen for casting-to-AM conversion (LM9000 bleed air adapter caps)
developer: GE Aviation (now GE Aerospace) with GE Additive; parts for Baker Hughes LM9000 turbines
description: In GE's 2020 annual part audit, the team reviewed hundreds of purchased castings, found 180 suitable for AM, and calculated ROI for each. It chose four CoCr bleed air adapter caps as the most profitable and checked them against quotes from four outside vendors. Reported results: ~35% lower manufacturing cost and 10 months from identification to prototypes.
NRE_note: Available engineering resources were a factor in narrowing nine candidates to four, and the caps needed only minor printability tweaks and a build-plate re-layout, but engineering effort is not reported as a cost term (The Fabricator 2021; 3DPI 2021).
Production_note: Teams calculated per-part ROI with internal production and financial models whose inputs are not documented, and compared AM with vendor casting quotes (about 35% lower) as a case result (trade press).
QA_Qual_note: Candidates were screened on whether the material was well characterised and previously used on the M2 machines, and printed parts matched cast quality within weeks, but no formal qualification effort or cost is described (The Fabricator 2021; 3DPI 2021).
QA_Insp_note: Two trade-press accounts describe the screen (post-processability, machining and brazing) but neither mentions inspection or whether it enters the ROI; no GE source is public (The Fabricator 2021; 3DPI 2021).
Storage_note: The press mentions de-risking the caps' supply chain for future spares as vendors drop materials or moulds become too costly, but not whether inventory is assessed; no GE source is public (3DPI 2021; The Fabricator 2021).
Shared_Capital_note: The team re-laid the build plate to fit four parts instead of three in about the same print time, spreading machine time across more parts, but machine investment or utilisation is not stated as an ROI input (The Fabricator 2021).
Shared_Capacity_note: Pandemic downtime freed machine and post-processing time at GE's Auburn additive facility for the project, a qualitative note on shared plant capacity with no capacity or lead-time model (The Fabricator 2021).
Speed_note: Time to market is quoted from the case (10 months from identification to final prototypes vs 12-18 months for castings), not computed by the screen (3DPI 2021; The Fabricator 2021).

name: Sandvik-Boliden on-demand printed drill-rig spare parts trial
developer: Sandvik Mining and Rock Solutions with Boliden
description: Proof-of-concept trial installing redesigned metal-printed parts on Boliden drill rigs to test local on-demand supply. The parts are bushes, brackets and drill parts replaced every 3,000-4,000 h. Costs, IP, warranty and liability are listed as open questions.
NRE_note: The trial prints 'a set of specially redesigned components', but redesign is not costed (Sandvik news release, Mar 2022).
Production_note: Sandvik's release lists 'What will the costs be?' as an open question, so whether the trial assesses part cost cannot be established.
QA_Qual_note: Part performance is monitored in service at Garpenberg as proof of concept, with warranties and liabilities listed as unresolved; no qualification procedure is described (Sandvik news release, Mar 2022).
QA_Insp_note: The release describes only in-service performance monitoring and does not mention inspection or testing of the printed parts.
Storage_note: Sandvik says it cannot tie up the capital that keeping all these parts in stock would need; not quantified (Sandvik news release, Mar 2022).
Shared_Capital_note: The release does not say whether machine investment or its sharing is assessed.
Shared_Capacity_note: Parts are printed at one Sandvik-managed facility in Italy, local printing is raised, and who prints (OEM, miner or third party) is left open; no capacity model (Sandvik news release, Mar 2022).
Speed_note: 'Shorter delivery times' are cited as a benefit, not quantified (Sandvik news release, Mar 2022).
